en: Now begins the fourth chapter:
Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, the twice-born man, having taken a wife, shall dwell in his house during the second quarter of his life. (4.1)

He states the meaning of the two preceding chapters in brief for the sake of recollection. The purpose of the second verse is to indicate that this is the rule for livelihood pertaining to the dharma of the householder.

Because the duration of life is indefinite, the prescription for establishing a fourth part [of life] for those in the stages of life (*āśrama*) is untenable; therefore, this verse is intended as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the time prescribed for the stages of life. Even if it could somehow be justified with reference to the statement, "Man indeed lives for a hundred years" (*AitB* 2.17), nevertheless, since another limit for studentship (*brahmacarya*) is prescribed in its own context—namely, "until the learning is complete" (*MDh* 3.1)—and since a different period for the householder stage is also understood from the text, "But when the householder sees... (*MDh* 6.2), it is inferred that this verse is merely a restatement.

The first quarter of life is the fourth [part]. Its being "first" is relative to birth. Having dwelt with a teacher and practiced the student's vow (*brahmacarya*), he should then, having married, dwell in the house during the second quarter of life—the fourth part of his lifespan. He should fulfill the stage of the householder; he should live there. 4.1.
A Brahmin should live in times of no distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no harm to living beings, or at least very little harm. (4.2)

The mental transformation consisting of distress that arises in another person who is being entreated with the words "Give! Give!"—that is intended here by the term "injury" (*droha*), and not injury in the sense of physical violence, since the latter is prohibited in all cases generally. Regarding the phrase "with little injury": if one cannot subsist without begging, then one should beg only a small amount; this is what is meant by "little injury. One should adopt—that is, rely upon—that mode of livelihood, such as agriculture or service, in which no suffering is caused to others. This is a general instruction: having fully adopted [such a way], one should live.

The rule for the tenth [stage], that of distress (*āpad*), will follow later. From this instruction, it is understood that there exists another mode of livelihood (*vṛtti*) besides those yet to be mentioned; otherwise, if the general instruction were restricted solely to the specific cases about to be described, the general teaching would be rendered meaningless. By means of that [general rule], officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*), as well as usury (*kusīda*), are obtained even though they are not explicitly listed among the "immortal" (*amṛta*) and other [permissible livelihoods].

For this very reason, that mode of life by gleaning which has been adopted is indeed attended by little harm. And so says Gautama: "Agriculture and trade, provided they are not performed by oneself; and usury" (GDh 10.5–6). This rule concerns mere subsistence; the accumulation of wealth, however, is to be achieved only through the specific occupations that will be prescribed hereafter. 4.2.
For the sake of accomplishing mere sustenance, one should accumulate wealth without causing distress to the body, by means of one's own irreproachable occupations. (4.3)

In the preceding section, the means for daily livelihood were stated; by this [verse], the rule regarding the accumulation of wealth is taught. One should effect the accumulation of wealth through one's own occupations, and those occupations will be described later. He states the purpose of such accumulation: "for the sake of accomplishing mere subsistence. The hardship of accumulating wealth should not be undertaken for the sake of enjoyment; rather, it is for the sake of accomplishing mere subsistence (*yātrāmātra*). "Subsistence" (*yātrā*) refers to the maintenance of oneself and one's family; "mere subsistence" (*yātrāmātra*) is the measure thereof; its "accomplishment" (*prasiddhi*) is its fulfillment; "for that purpose" (*tadartha*) means having that as its objective.

The performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) is indeed included within the maintenance of the self (*ātmasthiti*); for one who does not perform them, there is no maintenance of the self. And it has been said: "He who does not offer the five oblations while breathing does not truly live" (MDh 3.62). Alternatively, even if something is prescribed by scripture, if it is censured by the world, it must be avoided—just as, for example, the livelihood of a man of noble birth who has enjoyed great wealth, obtained through means such as accepting gifts from someone of low birth who has acquired fortune, even if that person belongs to the same caste.

Without affliction to the body; [one should not engage] in service or trade, which involve great affliction such as traveling long distances and so forth—such things should not be done. Accumulation is the guarding of what has been gathered into a heap. (4.3)
He now states those occupations by name:
"One may live by means of the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* or the *pramṛta*;
or even by the *satyānṛta*, but never by the 'dog's livelihood' (*śvavṛtti*). (4.4)

In some cases, praise is understood from the name alone. And the purpose [of such praise] is the engagement with those who are censured when those who are praiseworthy are absent. Among these, the dead and the deceased are extremely censured; even more so than they is the untruthful person (*satyānṛta*). For it is said: "Or even by that one lives" (MDh 4.6). The word *api* ("even") is intended to indicate a lack of approval (*aruci*). 4.4.
Having indicated them by name, he explains them according to their essential nature:
"The *ṛta* should be known as gleaning ears of grain; the *amṛta* is that which is unasked for.
The *mṛta*, however, is alms obtained by begging; the *pramṛta* is traditionally held to be agriculture. (4.5)

*Uñcha* and *śila* constitute *uñcha-śila*. That is to be known as *ṛta*, equal to the vow of truthfulness (*satya-vrata*). *Uñcha* is the gathering of ears of grain (*pulāka*) that have fallen from a field—whether from rice or other crops—as they are being carried to the house or the threshing floor, which were overlooked by the owner; that is *ṛta*. One should not entertain the thought there: "This belongs to another; I will not take it. Likewise, *śila* is the taking of grain that has fallen from a threshing floor, whether already harvested or unharvested, and which possesses many sprouts.

That which is unasked for (*ayācita*) is like nectar (*amṛta*), because it produces extreme delight; whereas begged alms (*yācita-bhaikṣa*) are like death (*mṛta*). Although the meaning is established by the word *yācita* alone, the use of the word *bhaikṣa*—ending in a collective secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—indicates that many [people] should be asked, and not a single person should be troubled. Thus it has been said: "with little harm" (*alpa-droheṇa*, MDh 4.2). Furthermore, since the word *bhaikṣa* is generally established in usage regarding prepared food (*siddhānna*), as in "one should eat alms-food for the sake of self-purification" (MDh 11.71), the inclusion of the word *yācita* is intended to indicate a general scope. Therefore, this is not merely begging for prepared food, because for one who maintains a sacred fire (*agnimat*), cooking on another's fire would contradict the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites. Nor is this begging solely for the purpose of eating; rather, it is for the purpose of maintenance (*sthiti*). And the maintenance of a householder is not accomplished by eating alone, but by whatever is necessary for the household. For this reason, even fuel, water, clothing, and so forth should be begged, as well as household utensils such as pots and covers. However, in the case of a student (*brahmacārin*), since cooking is impossible according to the rules at the time of eating, alms-food is understood to consist necessarily of prepared food. Moreover, this word *bhikṣā* also denotes the quantity of the substance being begged; thus, when asked, one says, "He does not give mere alms," or "Alms is only a handful (*prasṛti*). By this, begging for cows, gold, and the like is not permitted by the term *prasṛta*; rather, such requests are for the purpose of receiving gifts and so on.
But is not the acceptance of alms also indeed a form of receiving a gift?

It is not so; for *pratigraha* is merely taking (*grahaṇamātra*). The root *gṛh* preceded by *prati* occurs only in the sense of a specific kind of acceptance; therefore, it does not apply to mere acceptance. As in the cases, "one who is capable of receiving gifts" (MDh 4.186) and "receiving gifts is base" (MDh 10.109), *pratigraha* occurs when one receives what is given with the thought that it is for a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭa*) and accompanied by mantras. Now, in the case of alms (*bhaikṣa*), there is no recitation of mantras such as "Of thee, O God... (VS 2.11), nor is there such recitation in the giving and receiving [of food] out of affection and the like. Nor is the technical usage of *pratigraha* applied there.

Therefore, this which is designated by the terms "dead" (*mṛta*) and "immortal" (*amṛta*) is indeed a different thing from [ordinary] acceptance (*pratigraha*). Consequently, in this case, neither for one who is being asked nor for one who is not being asked does there arise, on account of their great-naturedness (*mahāsattvatā*), an expectation of some other benefit; nor is it logical for the giver to have regard for the caste and so forth of the recipient. Thus, for one who accepts what is being given out of compassion, it is not [ordinary] acceptance.
But is it not the case that giving out of compassion is solely for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)?

We say: no. In that case, there is no duty of giving (*dānadharma*); rather, it arises from the practice of compassion or from the desire to benefit others. Just as in the case of beneficial instruction and the like, the rule does not depend on the caste (*jāti*) and so forth of the recipient, so too it is with giving out of compassion. Accordingly, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) do not adhere to such a restriction of giving as that found in [Manu Smṛti 3.86]: “To a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Veda. For this very reason, even non-Brāhmaṇas, when fallen into distress, do not resort to the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa by accepting what is given by another; they do not thereby become dependent upon the acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*).

This is established. Although in the case of receiving gifts (*pratigraha*) there exists the distinction of whether they were solicited or unsolicited, the meaning of the terms *mṛta* (dead) and *amṛta* (immortal) is not determined by that alone, because another scope has been shown. This same form also applies to officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*). In some cases, one obtains the status of a priest after having officiated; in other cases, one is requested [to do so]. The same should be applied to teaching. Therefore, any livelihood obtained through begging is designated by the word *mṛta*, because it brings about wretchedness and is thus like death. Ploughing, however, is even more sinful than death. For the pulling of the plough is the bearing of a burden, and that is indeed the labor of the common folk. (4.5)
Trade consists of both truth and falsehood, and one may indeed live by it; service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it. (4.6)

It should not be thought that the scripture permits both truth and falsehood in trade. What then? This is a statement regarding the inherent nature of things. Greed itself is falsehood. Because of the expression "one lives by it," trade is for the sake of livelihood alone, not for the accumulation of wealth. Service is the "dog's way of life" (*śvavṛtti*). For just as a dog is driven about and obtains its food with difficulty, so too is the servant. Service is the state of being sent on errands; one who is sent upon any task whatsoever, whether appropriate or inappropriate, is a servant. Therefore, those who approach the king with superior activities such as the use of weapons and the like are not followers of the dog's way of life. (4.6)
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or enough for a single jar;
he may have enough for three days, or he may not even provide for tomorrow. || 4.7 ||

It has been stated: "One should accumulate wealth for the maintenance of oneself and one's family, but one should not resort to hardship for the sake of mere enjoyment. However, it was not specified whether that wealth should be acquired daily or all at once in a quantity sufficient for a long period; regarding this, the following is undertaken to address the matter of the delay in time.

The term *kusūladhānya* is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound because it is intelligible as "one who has grain in a granary. There is an alternative reading, *kuśūladhānyakaḥ*. In this case, *kusūladhānya* means "grain measured by a granary," and the suffix *-ika* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), meaning "one who possesses that. A *kusūla*—also called a *koṣṭha*—is a granary made of bricks or similar materials that serves as a receptacle for grain; here, it indicates a specific measure. In that context, one should accumulate only as much as fits [into it]. However, there is no restriction regarding the physical container itself. Even for one with a large household—including many servants, kinsmen, wives, slaves, children, cattle, horses, and so forth—the rule permits whatever amount ensures subsistence for a year. For the author will state later: "He who has food for three years... (MDh 11.7). Furthermore, the mention of "grain" is not intended to be restrictive; there is no fault for one who acquires gold, silver, and other wealth sufficient for that same period of subsistence. The meaning of the statement is simply that one must not acquire anything in excess of that.

A *kumbhī* is a small water-jar (*uṣṭrikā*). The traditional authorities maintain that this [term] refers to a store sufficient for six months. One who has food for three days is called *tryahaihika*. He is one who maintains a store of grain for the sake of the daily requirements of his family; he is *tryahaihika*. Regarding the term *śvastana*: it means "food for tomorrow" (*śvas-tanam bhaktam*); having formed a possessive derivative (*matvarthīya*) in the same manner as before, a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) should be made. One who is *sadyas* is one who possesses only what is immediate. He must spend on that very day what he has earned on that day. (4.7)
He states the established rule for this distinction:
"Among these four twice-born householders, each subsequent one is to be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of the world. (4.8)

Whichever [practice] involves a shorter accumulation of time, that is superior and more excellent in terms of *dharma*. And from this excellence of *dharma*, there arises an excellence of fruit; he becomes the most victorious over the worlds. He "conquers the worlds" means he abides in sovereignty over them and takes possession of them as objects of enjoyment. The suffix *-tama* is used here to express superlative intensity. Since no specific distinction is mentioned, "the worlds" is understood to refer to heaven (*svarga*). Therefore, the following rule applies here: one who has a large family—having many children, whose sons have not been distributed [in marriage], and whose daughters have not been wedded—is a "possessor of granary-measurements of grain" (*kusūladhānyaka*). But he who is advanced in years, who has obtained sons, and for whom the necessary rites have been performed, should resort to the other [modes of life] for as long as he attains tranquility. (4.8)
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the Brahmasattra.

Among these householders, such as those who possess granaries full of grain (*kusūladhānyaka*) and so forth, one is a practitioner of the six duties (*ṣaṭkarmā*). For him who has the great possessions previously mentioned, there are six means of livelihood (*vṛttikarmāṇi*). What, then, are they? They are: gleaning ears of corn (*uñcha*), picking up single grains (*śila*), receiving what is offered unasked (*ayācita*), receiving what is asked for (*yācita*), agriculture (*kṛṣi*), and trade (*vāṇijya*). [The remaining three are: teaching (*adhyāpana*), officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), and accepting gifts (*pratigraha*); these are included within the categories of "what is asked for" and "what is not asked for. One who has a large family should practice all the means of livelihood in combination for the sake of accomplishing his constant duties, including even agriculture and trade.

As for those who explain the six duties—beginning with "teaching and studying" (MDh 1.88)—as recited in the first chapter, their position contradicts the context; furthermore, the inclusion of study and the rest is purposeless, since they have already been prescribed elsewhere.

The second type is *kuṃbhīdhānya* (one who stores grain in a jar), which proceeds by means of three [means of livelihood]. It is declared to be useless; for as long as one continues [to live], so long does one proceed. And "proceeding" (*vartana*) means the attainment of stability. This applies to those [occupations] among the aforementioned ones, with the exception of agriculture and trade. For the *kuṃbhīdhānya* is more praiseworthy than the former [the *āśvayujīka*], since the author will say: "That mode of life is censured by the virtuous" (MDh 10.84) and "cowherds, traders... (MDh 8.102). As for what was stated by Gautama—"Agriculture and trade, provided they are not done by oneself, and usury" (GDh 10.5–6)—this refers to times of non-distress (*anāpad*). Even in that case, there is indeed a fault in the alternative of not doing it oneself, though it will be a lesser one.

One [robe] is [obtained] from two [persons]. Here too, excluding what is obtained through begging, two [robes] are taken from three [persons] as far as possible. Even that which is not begged for is accepted, provided it is sufficient for three days.

The fourth, however, lives by means of the *brahmasattra*. The *brahmasattra* is a mode of subsistence consisting of either *śila* (gleaning) or *uñcha* (gathering fallen grains). It is called a *sattra* because it occurs continuously, like a sacrificial session (*sattra*), rather than being a mode of life that must be completed on a single day; thus it is termed a *sattra* due to its daily and constant performance. The word *brahman* is a synonym for *brāhmaṇa*. This *sattra* belongs to them; therefore, this preceding elaboration on modes of subsistence should be understood as pertaining exclusively to the *brāhmaṇas*. As for the *kṣatriyas* and others, he will describe their respective modes elsewhere [in verse 35].

But how, again, is it possible to subsist by the practice of *śiloñcha* (gleaning ears and picking up grains), given that the falling of ears and grains occurs only in the fields or threshing floors during the autumn and summer seasons? If it is argued that one will gather the summer harvests from the summer crops and the autumn harvests from the autumn crops, then this would constitute a six-monthly livelihood (*ṣāṇmāsika-vṛtti*), not the state of being one who lives for the day (*āśvastanika*). Or perhaps it is possible otherwise, such that one takes whatever amount of rice and other grains has somehow fallen; true, but that is not sufficient for his food. If he were to accumulate them, he would eat only when he obtains enough, because of the impossibility of eating every five days or so. And thus, in the *Mahābhārata*, the practitioner of *śiloñcha* is described as eating at the end of the fortnight. If it is argued that in this state he is a householder who has become an ascetic (*tāpasa*), even so, the status of being one who lives for the day (*āśvastanika*) is contradicted. For he would be one who remains as long as provisions happen to be available, not one who lives for the day. Indeed, one is called *āśvastanika* who acquires what is necessary for maintenance day by day and spends it on that very day, not storing it for the second day. And if the daily meal from the practice of *śiloñcha* does not cease, how could he be one who lives for the day? And how could the life and the maintenance of wife and children belong to such a person?

For this very reason, some explain [the passage] differently, beginning with the words "another proceeds by means of three. By "three," they mean sacrificing (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and receiving gifts (*pratigraha*). By excluding receiving gifts—on the basis of the rule "receiving gifts is the lowest" (MDh 10.109)—sacrificing and teaching are the two that remain. Teaching is the "Brahma-sacrifice" (*brahmasattra*); for that is sufficient for one's livelihood. As for the statement, "subsisting by gleaning ears of corn and picking up grains" (MDh 4.10), that refers to someone entirely different, one who is distinct from these four classes.

To this it is replied: he who takes ten or twelve grains of barley or rice, equal in measure to a *śila*, from many people for as long as it takes for a single day’s journey, is one who lives by the *śila* mode. But he who gathers grain, one by one, for the sake of his journey is one who lives by the *uñcha* mode. And in another *Smṛti*, this is called the *yāyāvara* mode of life. Consequently, it is also possible [to follow this mode] for the entire duration of one's life. Nor is there any contradiction with the performance of rites such as the *vaiśvadeva*, nor is there the fault of failing to support one's sons and wife, because one accepts only an extremely small amount of begged alms. (4.9)
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭis prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.

The word *pārva* means "occurring at the *parvan*" (the end of a lunar fortnight), and *āyaṇāntīya* means "occurring at the end of the solstice (*ayana*). By adding the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense, one must apply the rule "cha after a word ending in vṛddhi" (Pāṇini 4.2.114). Thus, the *parveṣṭi* refers to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and the sacrifice at the end of the solstice is the one called *āgrayaṇa*. Because of the inclusion of the word "only" (*kevala*), optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) are excluded. Even the *vaiśvadeva* oblation and the *baliharaṇa* do not occur daily for him; for he does not always possess sufficient wealth for those. Therefore, by the inclusion of the word "only," the Great Sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) are excluded.
But surely even the *agnihotra* does not belong to him; for that too is accomplished solely by means of material substances (*dravya*).
He will perform the fortnightly offerings (*pakṣahoma*).
If it is asked, "How [then] shall he support his wife? [the answer follows].

She too shall adopt that mode of life. And when the wife is unable to maintain this vow, then the husband has no further obligation [to provide for her]. If it is asked, "How can the wife's livelihood be maintained for one engaged in the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such observances?"—this is not a valid objection, because she may eat what remains after guests and others have been served.

But surely, because of the absence of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, it is not proper for [the husband] to eat even when the wife's property (*strīdhana*) is available, since both are ordained to eat only the remains of the meal (*vighasa*). Therefore, he will perform the *vaiśvadeva* with the wife's property, because the taking of the wife's property is permitted for religious duties (*dharmakārya*). This is not so; in that state, only the *agnihotra* is the religious duty, not the *vaiśvadeva* oblation. Or, let it be granted that it is performed. But how then shall she live who has no wealth? Therefore, one whose wife is incapable is not entitled to the livelihood of gleaning ears and grains (*śiloñchavṛtti*).
Maintaining himself, sustaining his life. 4.10.
One should never follow the ways of the world for the sake of a livelihood; one should live the pure, straightforward, and guileless life of a Brahmin. 4.11

What is called *lokavṛtta* (worldly conduct) is that by which a person of ordinary nature and little strength conducts himself—through hypocrisy and the speaking of pleasant falsehoods such as, "You are Viṣṇu, you are Brahmā; victory! Live long!"—and likewise through various jesting stories. This [mode of life] should not be practiced for the sake of livelihood (*vṛtti*), that is, for the purpose of a means of subsistence. However, there is no fault for one whose nature is jesting. "Not crooked" (*ajihmām*): he who has one thing in his heart and another on the outside is called "crooked" (*jihma*). One whose soul is characterized by hatred and envy shows what is unpleasant to those who speak [to him]. "Not deceitful" (*aśaṭhām*): the performance of the *agnihotra* rite for the sake of gaining worldly favor and out of greed for receiving gifts and so forth, rather than out of faith in the meaning of the scriptures—that one is "deceitful" (*śaṭha*). Although crookedness and deceit are qualities of the self, they are designated here as "livelihood" (*jīvikā*) through metaphorical identification. Thus: "not crooked, not deceitful. "Pure" (*śuddhām*): purity consists in not being mixed with other modes of livelihood and being free from the two aforementioned faults. Although this meaning can be obtained from a single word, it is expressed by multiple words in accordance with the meter, like the expression "cattle and bulls" (*gobalīvarda*).

Now, as for the second [objection]: "How can one live the life of a brahmin?"—since the root *jīv* (to live) is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Furthermore, how can there be a double usage of the same verbal root in a single instance? For it is not the case that "one should go the act of going" (*gamanaṃ gacchet*) expresses the relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*). It is said in reply: Because of the relationship between the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), the relationship between the goal and the means is not contradictory. Just as in the expression "he has nourished the horse-nourishing" (*aśvapoṣaṃ puṣṭaḥ*). Moreover, the root *jīv* occurs here in the sense of "conducting oneself" (*vartanārtha*) as a constituent part of the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). Therefore, its transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) is established, and thus there is no fault. "One should live" means one should conduct oneself for the sake of living. (4.11)
In order to strengthen the practice of subsisting on what is obtained every third day, every day, or as soon as it is available, he states this reflection:
"Seeking happiness, one who desires ease should remain self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering. (4.12)

One should take recourse in contentment; one should not resort to the affliction of begging with the thought, "May I be a source of livelihood for many. One who seeks happiness should be self-restrained. Self-restraint is the absence of desire for more than what is necessary for one's sustenance. Contentment is the root of happiness for the wise; its opposite, discontent, is the root of suffering. It is a great wretchedness for the learned when their desired object is not attained. Therefore, one should take recourse in contentment. (4.12)
But a twice-born Snātaka living by any one of these modes of livelihood should observe these vows, which lead to heaven, long life, and fame: 4.13.

The *nidhi* (storehouse) is the object of subsistence (*vṛtti*), and it is expressed by the word *vṛtti*. Therefore, [the phrase] "by any one of these" does not depend on that [storehouse], because the rule for cessation is established by means of any one [of the modes]. Consequently, for one who lives by a combination of subsistences and has obtained paternal wealth, eligibility for the vows (*vrata*) is not appropriate; otherwise, there would be subsistence by only a single mode. These are the vows: a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is called a vow, such as: "This, prescribed by the scriptures, must be done by me, or this must not be done."

Some say that the observance of vows has as its fruits heaven, long life, and fame; therefore, they claim that only those who desire such fruits are entitled to the vows. This is incorrect, for if this were so, it would follow that the vows are non-obligatory (*anityatva*). In that case, the use of the term "obligatory" (*nitya*) in the subsequent verse would be contradicted. Furthermore, their obligatory nature is made known in the Veda by the passage: "For as long as one is joined with sin... [ŚB 12.4.1.1]. If heaven and the other fruits were construed as being optional (*kāmya*), they would merely serve as qualifications for the person entitled to the rite (*adhikṛta-viśeṣaṇa*). (4.13)
One should perform one's own duty as declared by the Vedas constantly and without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. (4.14)

Because the *smṛtis* are rooted in the *Veda*, it is heard [in scripture] that "it is declared in the *Veda*. One's own duty (*svakarma*) is the collection of observances (*vrata*) to be described hereafter; it is called "one's own" because it has been prescribed for oneself. One should perform it constantly throughout one's life. "Unwearied" means free from laziness. Performing this observance according to one's capacity—by this, he indicates that when there is capacity, the performance should be carried out as far as possible. As it has been said: "Or else, observing that entire conduct with the mind alone" (GDh 9.67). The "supreme goal" consists in the attainment of the state of Brahman. 4.14.
One should not pursue objects through excessive attachment, nor by means of contradictory actions;
nor should one pursue them when they are merely imagined, nor even in times of distress from whatever source. (4.15)

That to which a man becomes attached is what is intended by "attachment," such as singing, instrumental music, and the like; for it is there that those possessed by passion become as if stuck. Therefore, one should not seek nor acquire wealth through singing, instrumental music, and so forth. One should not perform a contradictory act—one forbidden by the scriptures and unsuitable for one's family. Nor, while wealth inherited from one’s father and others is available and sufficient for one’s maintenance, should one desire other means. Even in times of distress (*ārtyām*), one should not seek them from just anywhere; rather, one should proceed by accepting gifts from the virtuous. For the author will permit even this [seeking] for a single person in times of distress. (4.15)
One should not become attached out of desire to any objects of the senses, and one should restrain the mind from excessive attachment to them. (4.16)

The objects of the senses are their domains, such as form, taste, and so forth; one should not become attached to them—that is, one should not cultivate an excessive or constant addiction to them. These objects include captivating young women, the music of the flute, delicious flavors, the fragrance of camphor and other scents, and passionate touch; one should not indulge in these excessively. "From desire" means with a preoccupation centered on sensual pleasure. Regarding all of these, one should be like one who receives what is unasked for—even if one must constantly encounter them—one should remain detached. Furthermore, this verse describes the means for withdrawing from excessive attachment to them. For attachment to material things cannot be turned away by force; rather, it must be turned away by the mind through the cultivation of opposing thoughts (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*). First, one should consider their difficulty of attainment; even when they are present and have been experienced before, one should reflect on their nature of momentary insipidity, their perishability, and the fall into hell due to attachment, as forbidden by the scriptures. As it has been said: "These [objects] cannot be avoided in that way... (Manusmṛti 2.96). 4.16.
One should abandon all pursuits that conflict with one's Vedic study; maintaining oneself by any means whatsoever, for that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of one's purpose. 4.17

All those matters that are incompatible with the study of the Vedas must be abandoned, such as attending upon kings or ministers’ households. Furthermore, for one who is attached to this worldly course of life, there may be excessive profit from agriculture, usury, and so forth; by means of that, he will support himself, and then, possessing family wealth, his male and female slaves will become numerous. Indeed, that is the state of having fulfilled one's duties and attained one's purpose for this *snātaka*—that he, being constantly devoted to Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), somehow or other maintains his small household. (4.17)
One should conduct oneself here by practicing conformity in dress, speech, and intellect with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage. (4.18)

The genitive case in *vayasaḥ* is used in the sense of conformity (*sārūpya*). *Veṣavāgbuddhi* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The suffix *ṣyañ* in *sārūpyam* is used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*). Thus, the meaning becomes: one should adopt dress and so forth that are appropriate to one’s age. *Sārūpya* here means suitability (*aucitya*), because similarity with anything else—such as [another person’s] physical form—is impossible. *Veṣa* is the arrangement of hair, ornaments, and so on. In this regard, in the first stage of life there is the topknot (*śikhaṇḍaka*); in youth, the wearing of locks of hair (*keśa*) and the like; in old age, matted hair (*jaṭā*) or shaving the head, and so forth. Speech should be in accordance with one’s age. Likewise, the intellect: first it consists of the maintenance and practice of the three aims of life (*trivarga*); later, as one grows old, it is focused primarily on dharma alone. Dress should be in accordance with one’s occupation and wealth. For by such [conduct], even if one’s teeth are stained, one’s hair is disheveled, and so on—even if these appear ostentatious—they do not bring about arrogance, provided they are in accordance with one’s family. As it has been said: "The scope of this [work] is worldly conduct. This is what is meant: this is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because its meaning has already been established by others; rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on worldly custom: "By acting in this way, one follows the ways of the world and does not become an object of public hatred. (4.18)
One should constantly study the scriptures that quickly increase the intellect, as well as those that are auspicious and beneficial, and likewise the Vedic Nigamas. (4.19)

The Itihāsas and Purāṇas increase the intellect; the treatises on logic (tarka-śāstra), such as those of Bṛhaspati and Uśanas, are beneficial and helpful, having perceptible purposes. Medical science, astronomy, and so forth have perceptible purposes, since the Science of Polity (artha-śāstra) is taught separately [from them]. The Vedic Nigamas—the Nigama, Nirukta, Vyākaraṇa, and Mīmāṃsā—are the means for understanding the meaning of the Vedas. However, if one were to take "Ṛcas" [to mean the Ṛgveda], they would have imperceptible purposes. (4.19)
For in whatever measure a person masters a treatise, in that same measure he understands it, and his discernment finds delight in it. (4.20)

*Samadhigamaḥ* means thorough comprehension, that is to say, mastery through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). "He understands" (*vijānāti*) means he knows specifically. This is evident even in the case of a text being practiced repeatedly; at that time, knowledge (*vijñāna*) is pleasing to him. The meaning is that it becomes radiant. This is a statement regarding the root of the preceding memory (*smṛti*). Since *ruci* does not have the sense of "desire," there is no application of the rule *rucy-arthānām* [Pāṇini 1.4.33] which would otherwise require the recipient to be in the dative case. (4.20)

One should never neglect the sacrifice to the sages, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to the ancestors, according to one's ability. (4.21)

The restatement of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) prescribed in the third chapter is for the purpose of specifying particular details. That specification will be stated later: "without exerting effort" (MDh 4.22).

Others, however, hold that the repetition here under the heading of *vratas* is for the sake of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Therefore, the following formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) must be made: "As long as I remain in the householder stage, the great sacrifices must not be omitted by me."

However, one should not entertain this doubt: "The repetition is for the purpose of enjoining it twice. For no injunction is heard here; rather, it is simply stated that "one should not let [the offering] lapse. And because [the offering] is obligatory, its lapse is already established. Furthermore, there is no reason for a difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*) based on the recognition of what has been previously enjoined. [One may offer] cooked food according to one's ability, or raw food, or roots and fruits. (4.21)
Some people, who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice, constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from desire.

Some householders, who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice, offer these great sacrifices into the very senses; that is, they accomplish them [therein]. Who, then, are they? They are "those who do not strive"—those who do not desire wealth, having abandoned domestic affairs, such as those who have renounced the body and so forth.

They maintain that this same rule applies even to those who subsist by gleaning ears of grain (*śiloñcha*), as well as to the lame and others; for it will be stated regarding them that "if there should be a desire for a wife" (MDh 9.20). Furthermore, these individuals have no entitlement to perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*); because they possess no wealth, they receive only enough for their maintenance, and nothing more for the purpose of performing ritual acts.

The root *juhoti* (to sacrifice) indicates that which is brought about by the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do). For a specific action, namely *yāga* (sacrifice), cannot become the object (*karman*) of another specific action, *homa* (offering); for it does not occur that one says, "he cooks the cooking. However, it does occur that one says, "he performs the cooking," or "he performs the sacrifice. Furthermore, actions whose objects are general require substances as their means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), as in: "he desires to eat," "he is able to eat," or "he knows how to eat. Moreover, a particular instance is observed for the purpose of indicating a general category: "this cow is to be looked at with the foot."
And thus, some explain this *homa* as the very restraint (*saṃyama*) of the senses.
Others [cite] the *Prāṇasaṃvāda-upaniṣad*: "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a sacrifice; the first oblation he should offer with 'Svāhā to Prāṇa'," and so forth (ChU 5.19).

Still others, however, hold that this *homa* is precisely the method of meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) taught in the following verse; for in this way, the two are understood to form a single syntactical unit.
But is it not the case that later on, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in speech is not an organ (*indriya*)?

This is not a fault. The term "organ" is used for the purpose of indicating its internal nature. What is intended here is that it does not depend on external instruments for its accomplishment. (4.22)
Some offer the breath into speech and speech into breath at all times, perceiving in speech and breath the imperishable accomplishment of sacrifice. (4.23)

When this person exhales, he should meditate thus: "I offer speech into breath. And while speaking, [he should meditate]: "I offer breath into speech. By this much alone, the five sacrifices are accomplished. If they are obligatory, their results need not be mentioned; moreover, those who know the Self are authorized for this. For this matter has been prescribed at length in the Upaniṣads concerning the meditation on the five fires in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (KauṣU 2.5). It yields inexhaustible fruit because its result is non-return [to saṃsāra]. 4.23.
Other brahmins always perform those sacrifices with knowledge alone, perceiving with the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge. (4.24)

By means of those sacrifices—the great rites (mahāyajña) that constitute their nature—they sacrifice; that is, they fulfill their qualification regarding that [sacrificial] domain. Therefore, because there is a difference in meaning, the relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhakabhāva*) is established in the expression "they sacrifice with sacrifices," just as in the case of the term "one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma.

But how can the performance of a sacrifice be accomplished through knowledge? A sacrifice consists essentially in the renunciation of a substance for the sake of a deity, and knowledge is not of such a form.
It is replied: by the word "they sacrifice" (*yajante*), what is intended here is the accomplishment of the *effect* of a sacrifice.

If the accomplishment of the goal results from knowledge, for what purpose then is the performance of ritual actions? For it is not possible to perform rituals without an object. Now, if this thought occurs—that since knowledge is also heard of as a means to the fruit in the passage, "And he who knows this thus" (TB 3.11.8.6), there is no need for the performance of rituals—that is incorrect, because that [statement] is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) being subordinate to something else.

To this it is replied: We have already stated that those who know the Self while remaining free from desire are the ones qualified; it is precisely these men of knowledge (*jñānin*) who are intended here, not those who merely know how to perform ritual acts. For them—who, by virtue of being renunciants of the Vedas (*vedasaṃnyāsika*), remain at home—this meditation upon the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) is prescribed. Furthermore, the accomplishment of self-knowledge through the great sacrifices that require material substances is thus described. However, in the sixth chapter, the Lord will state that the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) and the libation of water (*udakatarpaṇa*) are indeed to be accomplished through ritual action.

In this context, he states an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the nature of the cause: "having knowledge as its root. Knowledge is the root of this action; knowledge is the root of the performance of every ritual act. For one who lacks knowledge is not able to perform anything at all. Thus it has been said: "One who knows should sacrifice. "Beholding with the eye of knowledge"—knowledge is like an eye. Just as form is perceived by means of the eye, so too is it known through knowledge. That "knowledge" intended here is not the Veda alone. (4.24)
One should always perform the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night,
as well as the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice likewise.

Terms such as *agnihotra* and others are well-known in the Śruti and the Gṛhya-smṛtis as denoting specific ritual acts; they are prescribed therein along with their respective procedures (*itikartavyatā*). This [text] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of them, and not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), because it mentions their established form. Only the duty regarding the oblation (*homa*) is heard here, but neither the substance nor the deity is mentioned. Furthermore, names such as *agnihotra* require a specific referent. Therefore, it is understood that these terms denote specific acts already known from other scriptures.
If this is so, then since the duty is already understood from those very sources, this [text] would be purposeless.

This is for the purpose of corroborating the present meditation (*upāsanā*) with respect to the renunciant of the Vedas (*vedasaṃnyāsika*). Just as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) are accomplished through knowledge alone—as in the passages, "Some offer the breath into speech" (MDh 4.23) and "by means of knowledge alone"—so too is this [meditation]. And what is the point of this objection, "Why is there a repetition? For such an objection would arise regarding the fact that what is stated in one part of all the Śrutis and Smṛtis is repeated elsewhere. Furthermore, a general solution has already been stated: there is no tautology because of the difference in recipients (*pratipattṛ*). Just as there is a diversity of sense organs due to the difference in recipients—since not everyone is able to see everything with a single eye, and thus many sense organs are purposeful—so too is there a division of Vedic branches (*śākhā*) and a division of Smṛtis.
Now it is asked: "Why is there no mention of *rūpa*?

This too is not a fault. There is a difference in the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) according to each branch (*śākhā*); which one, then, should be mentioned? To mention all would be cumbersome; to mention only one would involve the abandonment of the others.
That objection, too, is indeed a mere challenge.

And it has been said: "This is a restatement (anuvāda), not an injunction (vidhi). For if it were an injunction, this objection would arise: 'Since this has been enjoined elsewhere, for what purpose is it enjoined again?'"

"At the beginning and end of day and night. Here there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration; rather, [it means] at the beginning of the day and at the beginning of the night, and likewise at the end of the day and at the end of the night. By this, the times of evening (*sāyam*) and morning (*prātaḥ*) are encompassed. Among those who offer when the sun has risen, it is at the beginning of the day; among those who offer before sunrise, it is at the end of the night. The word *dhu* is a synonym for *divasa* (day). "Always" (*sadā*): the evening and morning oblations (*homa*) must be performed as long as one lives. One must supply the words "one should sacrifice with the New Moon [offering]" (*darśena yajeta*) here. For in the original injunction (*utpatti*), there is no statement "one should offer," but rather "one should sacrifice with the Darśa. This [present passage] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that; therefore, the ellipsis is supplied. For this very reason, even though no specific distinction is heard [in the text], the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) occurs at the end of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*) at the end of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). And thus says the Śruti: "One should sacrifice with the Darśa on the Darśa day, and one should sacrifice with the Pūrṇamāsa on the Pūrṇamāsa day. (4.25)
At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the sacrifice of new grain; likewise, at the end of the seasons, he should perform the ritual sacrifices;
at the end of the solstices, he should perform the animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices.

The word *sasya* denotes grains such as rice and the like; its *anta* means exhaustion. When the previous harvest has been exhausted, one should sacrifice with the *navasasyeṣṭi*, which means by means of the *āgrayaṇa*. Here, neither the exhaustion of the previous harvest nor the arrival of the new harvest is the occasion for the *āgrayaṇa*; rather, eating new grain is forbidden for one who has not performed the *āgrayaṇa*. As it is said: "One should not eat new grain without having sacrificed... (MDh 4.27). Therefore, the meaning is that one should eat the new grain by means of the *āgrayaṇa*. Thus they explain the phrase "one should sacrifice with that."

However, under this view, because there is an absence of the previous crop, or because of the presence of the new crop from elsewhere, or in the absence of a desire to eat [it], the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice does not necessarily follow. Furthermore, if "the end of the crop" (*sasyānta*) here is merely an indirect indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the arising of the new crop, then one would incur the fault of eating [the new grain] without having performed the sacrifice.

Therefore, these are two distinct sentences: "One should not eat without having sacrificed" is the first, and "at the end of the grain" is the second. By the mention of "the end of the grain," the production of the grain itself is intended; because that [production] is a fixed event, its status as a causal occasion (*nimitta*) is established. The depletion [of the grain], however, is not fixed, for even those possessing wealth may have three years' worth of grain on hand. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras says: "One should not eat the new grain without having offered the Agnihotra," and likewise, "When one is satiated by the rain, then one should sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa. Similarly, there is this other rule prescribing a specific time: "In autumn, the new grain. In that case, he whose previous supply of grain has not been exhausted observes the autumn [for the Āgrayaṇa], while the other does not. Thus, both rules possess their own purpose. Otherwise, it would have been stated simply as: "Upon the production of new grain, one should sacrifice with the New Grain Offering (*navasasyeṣṭi*). As for the one who says, "Without having sacrificed with the New Grain Offering, one should not eat food," according to him, even when new grain has been produced, there remains the necessity of waiting for autumn [to perform the Āgrayaṇa]. Furthermore, because the production of new grain is the occasion for the rite, the Āgrayaṇa must be performed as a rule even in the absence of a desire to eat the new grain.

"At the end of the season. By the observation that "the season (*ṛtu*) is the year," this performance is said to pertain to the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices; by the word *adhvara*, these very sacrifices are intended.

"At the beginning of the two solstices" means at the end of the solstices. Those two solstices are the southern and the northern. Therein, the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) is to be performed twice a year. However, the author of the Sūtra says: "Every six months, or yearly."

"At the end of the year. The word *samā* is a synonym for a year, and its "end" (*anta*) is its completion, which occurs in the cool season (*śiśira*). However, the injunction for the *saumika* sacrifice does not apply there; rather, it applies when that [cool season] has passed and spring (*vasanta*) has arrived. Thus says the Śruti: "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* every spring" (ĀpŚ 10.2.5). Such are the obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*). The overall purport is that these must be performed somehow or other, even by one who has renounced the Vedas (*vedasaṃnyāsika*). 4.26.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, desiring to live a long life, must not eat new grain or meat without first having performed the sacrifice of the first-fruits and the animal sacrifice. (4.27)

By "one who possesses the sacred fire" (*agnimān*), one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*) is intended here, because of the context concerning vows (*vrata*). For that sacrifice, there is a vow prescribed in the Yajurveda: "One should not eat meat without having sacrificed with an animal victim, nor should one eat new grain without having performed the *Āgrayaṇa* offering."

He states the fruit resulting from the observance of the rules: "one who desires to live a long life. By the word *āyus* (life), the continuous functions of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths are meant. And although the verb *jīvati* (he lives) is intransitive, the second accusative case is used here with respect to the action of *iṣ* (desiring). Even when a verbal root ends in the desiderative suffix (*san*), it expresses a desire; in this view as well, the object of *iṣ* is not something external, but rather the meaning of the root itself, while the desire is subordinate to that which is about to be seen [the object of the desire]. This is because, according to the principle that "the root and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together," this applies even outside of the desiderative formation. In this view too, time will be indicated by the word *āyus*; thus, it means "desiring to live for a long time. In that context, its status as an object is established by the rule: "Time is indeed to be understood as the object, for that which is intransitive has the designation of object."

This is the rule for one who maintains the *āhitāgni* fire regarding the *paśubandha* sacrifice, and it applies to the *āgrayaṇa* as well. For one who maintains the domestic (*gṛhya*) fire, the *āgrayaṇa* is prescribed by way of a rule in the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*.

As for the statement, "In autumn, [one offers] new grain," that refers to rice (*vrīhi*) and millet (*śyāmāka*), not to barley (*yava*). Nor does the *sasyeṣṭi* sacrifice consist of any grain whatsoever, nor of beans (*māṣa*), kidney-beans (*udgādi*), and so forth; for it has been stated that this [text] is dependent on other scriptures and is not itself an independent injunction. And in other scriptures, the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi* is prescribed with rice, millet, and barley.

However, other crops as well must not be consumed before the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi* has been performed. As for what was stated without qualification—"one should not eat crops"—if that were intended as a prohibition, he would have said simply this: "The *āgrayaṇa* [is required] for rice, *śyāmāka*, and barley; one should not eat crops without having offered the *agnihotra*. Thus it was recited by the author of the Sūtra: "The *āgrayaṇa* [is required] for rice, *śyāmāka*, and barley; one should not eat crops without having offered the *agnihotra*. Therefore, this word "crops" (*sasya*) does not refer to a restricted scope alone. 4.27.
For his fires, greedy for fresh grain and meat, if not honored with the offering of new grain and animal sacrifice, desire to consume his very life-breaths. (4.28)

He establishes the very permanence [of the sacrifice] by pointing out the fault of non-performance: "The fires of this *āhitāgni*—if not honored with new grain and if no oblations have been offered—desire to consume, that is, to eat, his very life-breaths. *Gardhin* means one who possesses *gardha*, which is an excess of longing; the suffix *-in* is used here in the sense of possession. (4.28)
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of his ability with a seat, food, a bed, water, or roots and fruits. (4.29)

This, which was stated for the sake of what follows, is now reiterated: no guest whatsoever should dwell in the house unhonored. Every guest must be accommodated in the house with honor. "According to one's ability": whether there be one, two, or many—as many as can be honored—all are to be honored with seats and other such provisions. This is intended to provide them with lodging preceded by such honor; it does not mean that the ownership of all seats, food, and beds is entirely transferred to them. Since rice-gruel, broth, meat, cooked grain, and clarified butter are mentioned separately, roots and fruits should be given when these are unavailable. (4.29)
One should not honor, even with a mere word, heretics, those who persist in improper actions, those who act like cats, rogues, sophists, and those who behave like herons. 4.30.

Regarding this, some say that because of the verbal suffix *liṅ* in the word “should dwell” (*vaset*), this is a prohibition against granting hospitality in the evening to heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*) and others.

That is incorrect. What is being precluded here is their status as objects of worship; it is not stated that the giving of food and so forth must be withheld in every way. Even for those who eat during the day, a stay of a few moments is certainly possible. Therefore, the suffix *liṅ* in “should dwell” does not indicate the evening time.

In this context, *pāṣaṇḍins* are those who wear external sectarian marks, such as the red-robed ones (*raktapaṭas*), the naked wanderers (*nagnacarakas*), and so forth. Those established in improper occupations (*vikarmasthāḥ*) are those who, when not in times of distress, subsist by the livelihood of another caste; for example, a Brāhmaṇa living by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, or a Kṣatriya by the occupation of a Vaiśya, and so on. *Baiḍālavratikas* are hypocrites who perform the *agnihotra* and other rites merely to win over the world, thinking, "We shall obtain houses and such," and not because they are their own duty (*svadharma*) as enjoined by the scriptures. *Śaṭhas* are those whose heart is one thing and whose speech is another; having promised assistance to someone, they disregard their obligation and do not act upon it. *Haitukas* are atheists whose intellect is fixed on the view that "there is no other world, there is no gift, there is no oblation. *Bakavṛttis* are also hypocrites, distinguished only slightly from the former; the difference between them will be shown later. Even with mere words—let alone the offering of a seat—they should not even say, "Welcome, please sit here," preceded by a formal salutation. As for the giving of food, it is permitted only like that of a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*). Thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, concerning the gift of food itself, recorded in his tradition: "One should not inquire about [the recipient's] birth or learning. The meaning is that one should not engage in searching for a worthy recipient (*pātra*) in this case. (4.30)

One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those householders who are learned in the Vedas, purified by their knowledge and vows, and well-versed in sacred scripture; one should avoid those who are the opposite. 4.31.

The Vedas, the sciences (*vidyā*), and the vows (*vrata*); those who have bathed by means of these are those who have reached completion therein. Various types of *snātakas* are included here. Among them, the *veda-snātakas* are those who have studied the Vedas. The *vidyā-snātakas* are those whose desire to know the meaning of the sciences has ceased; because of its proximity to the word *vidyā*, it refers specifically to the Vedas, for that alone is truly a science (*vidyā*) in the ultimate sense. As for the vows, they are those such as "lasting thirty-six years" (MDh 3.1). Even when the study of the Vedas and the desire to know their meaning are completed, the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) does not occur at that point alone; rather, there is also the view that the period of thirty-six years and so forth must be fulfilled.
Others, however, who bathe after three years even without having studied the Veda, are called *vratasnātaka*s (those who have bathed after completing their vows).
[Objection: But how can there be a "bath" for one who has not studied the Veda? This position is untenable.
[Reply: Now, for what purpose is the mention of the term *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas), since the status of a *snātaka* is already established by that very fact?
For the sake of excellence; by this, those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas, the *śrotriyas*, are included.

"Gṛhamedhinaḥ" means householders. By this, it is not intended to say that mendicants, ascetics, and religious students are unworthy of honor; rather, because they subsist on alms, the status of a guest is not possible for them. A religious student has no residence other than the house of his teacher, and an ascetic has none other than the forest. Even for a renunciant, it is said, "He should enter a village only for the sake of alms" (GDh 3.14), so he does not reside in a village. Therefore, since those in other stages of life (āśramas) reside elsewhere than in a house, although their reception might occur by some chance, the rule primarily concerns householders. Regarding "with offerings to gods and ancestors": in rites for the gods, such as propitiatory ceremonies, or in ancestral rites such as the Śrāddha, these very persons are to be honored. Conversely, those who have not performed the *snātaka* ceremony are to be avoided, even if they lack the aforementioned defects. (4.31)
A householder should give according to his ability to those who do not cook for themselves, and he should share with all beings without causing hardship to his own dependents. 4.32
It is said that those who do not cook are *brahmacārins* and *parivrājakas*;

however, this is incorrect, for giving to them is indeed prescribed as a constant duty: "And one should give alms to the mendicant" (MDh 3.84). Therefore, whatever can be given according to one's capacity—both as much as possible and as much as is cooked—should be given to those who are poor and live by begging, such as heretics (*pākhaṇḍins*) and others. Furthermore, because the occasion is the absence of the act of cooking, this refers specifically to the gift of prepared food (*siddhānna*).
And there is sharing: one should also share with others whatever wealth is useful for fuel, clothing, medicine, and so forth; some portion should be given away.

"To all beings. This word *bhūta* denotes the world consisting of conscious entities, as in the passage: "The *gāyatrī* is indeed this entire *bhūta*. Since it is impossible for non-conscious things to receive a distribution [of wealth] for the sake of benefiting them as if they were conscious, [the term] is restricted to those who possess consciousness. Consequently, according to the view that "those possessing the property of sprouting are conscious," a distribution of wealth for the purpose of watering and so forth must also be made for trees and the like. This word *bhūta* has many meanings. In some cases, it occurs in the sense of preeminence: "This *brāhmaṇī* is a *bhūta* (an eminent person) in this house. In some cases, it refers to a *piśāca*: "possessed by a *bhūta*. In some cases, it occurs in the sense of something contrary [to fact]: "he says what is true (*bhūtam*). In some cases, it refers to past time: "the meaning of the verbal root is *bhūta* (past). In some cases, it refers to a specific deity: "an offering (*bali*) to the *bhūtas*. In some cases, it denotes merely that which possesses consciousness: "one should not harm living beings (*bhūtāni*). In some cases, it denotes attainment: "the moon is a great *bhūta*. In some cases, it occurs in the sense of a comparison: "just as one who has become a poet (*kāvyabhūtaḥ*). In some cases, it denotes birth: "Devadatta’s son was born (*bhūtaḥ*). But here, the referent of the term has been explained. The dative case in *bhūtebhyaḥ* expresses purpose (*tādarthye*).

Without causing obstruction; that is, having set aside what is sufficient so that there is no suffering for oneself or one's family, a distribution [of the remainder] must be made. Thus it has been said: "Without causing obstruction to dependents" (MDh 11.9). 4.32.

A Snātaka who is perishing from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a pupil; it is the settled rule that he must not do so from anyone else. 4.33.

The mention of the "king" (*rājan*) is intended as an indicator for those of wealthy status. And so he will say: "Those who are suffering, or those desiring base metals or wealth, may beg from the lord of the earth" (MDh 10.113). Therefore, while the word "king" is primarily applied to the Kṣatriya caste, nevertheless, through a consideration of other legal treatises (*śāstra*), it is understood to denote the ruler of a territory (*janapadeśvara*). For rulers of territories possess great wealth. By this, the following is meant: one should accept gifts from those who are exceedingly prosperous in cattle, goats, sheep, grain, and wealth. This being the case, the rule "without causing harm" (MDh 4.2) is respected; for wealthy people are not excessively pained when giving. However, there would be fault for one accepting from those who have exhausted their own resources. Furthermore, if the word "king" were used in its primary sense [of the Kṣatriya caste], acceptance from Brāhmaṇas and others would be prohibited, which would result in a contradiction with all the *smṛtis*. For in another *smṛti* it is recited: "One may take uncooked food from praiseworthy twice-born men and from a Śūdra who performs service. Even regarding the prohibition, in the verse "One should not accept from a king" (MDh 4.84), the word "king" refers specifically to the ruler of a territory. Moreover, the prohibition therein does not apply to a Kṣatriya, because of the statement "from one not born of the royal lineage" (MDh 4.84). For that very reason, the prohibition there does not apply to one belonging to the Kṣatriya caste; if it did, the phrase "not born of the royal lineage" would not need to be stated. Indeed, there are no Kṣatriyas who are not born of the royal lineage. Therefore, the settled rule here is this: acceptance should be made from a Kṣatriya king who acts according to the scriptures, but not from any other.

[The genitive] in *yājya* and *antevāsin* is one based on wealth (*dhana-apekṣā*). Alternatively, [the form] *tasantau* should be read. Because these two words have action as their cause, it is implied that "one should live by means of officiating at sacrifices and teaching."

Others, however, say: because other means such as theft and so forth would result in minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and are prohibited, one may live by propitiating the Lord through a gift of favor or a recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*). Nor is this person a servant; that mode of livelihood is prohibited. Thus, even if one does not perform a sacrifice for him, one may take from the patron (*yājya*) because of the benefit previously rendered; for the obligation (*kṛtya*) persists even when the relationship has ceased.

Regarding the phrase "while sinking [into distress]": this should not be done when wealth from one's father or others is available. As it has been said: "Not while resources are sufficient" (MDh 4.15). This present rule is a restatement of that very point. Furthermore, this is not a duty for times of extreme distress (*āpaddharma*). For "distress" (*avasāda*) is not the same as "calamity" (*āpad*); rather, it is the absence of acquired wealth. Calamity (*āpad*), however, consists in the absence of prescribed means of livelihood and the depletion of wealth. Even when there is an abundance of grain and property, if food is exhausted during a famine or similar crisis, the state of having no food for guests while being tormented by hunger constitutes a calamity (*āpad*); whereas for one who is not hungry, the lack of wealth constitutes "sinking" (*avasāda*). This is the distinction between the two.
But he should not accept it from anyone else who possesses only a small amount of wealth or who is unable to provide assistance. (4.33)
A learned Snātaka shall never suffer from hunger if he has the means;
nor, while possessing wealth, shall he wear worn-out or dirty clothes. (4.34)

And if he should be thwarted in some business for the sake of wealth, he should not at that very moment resort to the duties of distress (*āpad-dharma*). Rather, he should strive again; as it has been said: "One should seek prosperity until death" (MDh 4.137). Therefore, if by some chance the destruction of crops occurs for one who is farming due to a lack of rain and so forth, he should not, because of this much loss, suddenly become dependent on the food of others through begging. Worn-out and dirty clothes are not desired when there is wealth and means available, provided a valid reason exists. (4.34)

Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure, he should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda and in what is beneficial for the self. 4.35

This is a discretionary rule (*kalpanam*) with reference to the statement, "the cutting of the beard and mustache" (*dantavāsasaḥ*). It is mandatory (*niyamataḥ*) only in this regard; for this very reason, he says "pure" (*śuciḥ*). For one with long hair, since bathing and other such acts would be difficult to accomplish, he might become lazy, and thus there would be the risk of impurity. However, if even one whose hair and so forth have grown long remains devoted to bathing, then the wearing [of hair] would not be faulty. "Tamed" (*dāntaḥ*) means free from pride. "Pure" (*śuciḥ*) refers to matters of wealth, as well as through the causes of Vedic study, such as cleansing with earth and water and sipping water (*ācamana*). And he is constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas. Although this matter has already been stated, it is repeated again and again for the sake of emphasis. "Beneficial to the self" (*ātmahitāni*) refers to remedies for disease and so forth, as well as the avoidance of eating food that is indigestible, excessively heavy, or burning, and so on. (4.35)
He should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water;
he should wear the sacred thread, a Vedic girdle, and two auspicious golden earrings.

The wearing of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the earrings (*kuṇḍala*) constitutes contact with the body. Furthermore, whichever limb is the appropriate place for the placement of an ornament, it should be applied to that very limb; for example, the earring on the ears and the sacrificial thread on the body, because the ornament of the ear is called an *earring* (*kuṇḍala*), and because the thread resting on the neck becomes the *sacrificial thread* (*upavīta*) by being drawn over the right arm.

Furthermore, because it serves a visible purpose, one always carries a staff and so forth; for the carrying of a staff is for the sake of support when one is weary, and for the sake of warding off cattle or other attackers that may come face-to-face.

Since purification is prescribed with water that has been drawn out, the *kamaṇḍalu* is specifically enjoined as the vessel; and because it serves the same purpose, it excludes jars and the like, but not earrings, bracelets, or similar ornaments. Therefore, the possession of water by the *kamaṇḍalu* is for the sake of removing the impurity caused by excrement, which is cleansed by water. And it has been said: "One should not remain impure even for a moment, provided one has the capacity" (*ĀpDh* 1.15.8). Regarding the phrase "provided one has the capacity": if the water previously carried has been used, or if otherwise an occasion for impurity arises—such as through the discharge of phlegm or spittle—and impurity results from the lack of available water, there is no fault. Nevertheless, regarding the discharge of urine or feces, he will prescribe bathing: "If one is distressed, having voided bodily waste either without water or in water, one should bathe outside with one's clothes on" (*MDh* 11.202). Furthermore, purity is prescribed in another *Smṛti* text at every step. Thus spoke the venerable Vasiṣṭha:
Fire is said to be pure in water, in the hand, and in wood;
therefore, having wiped the water-pot with both hands and water, [one should drink].
Manu Prajāpati has declared that the oblation consisting of the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) must be performed;
having completed the necessary duties, one who is most skilled in purification should sip water (*ācāmet*).
Baudhāyana also stated, beginning with: "Now, the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is to be carried..."
Therefore, having performed purification and wiped the water-pot clean,
this wiping of the object is indeed the ritual of circumambulation with fire.
Likewise:
"Even while remaining in his former state of impurity, he should carry his water-pot;
a wise man should not despise it, nor fear it, nor find fault with it."

This term [for purification] is based on a specific form and does not take the genus (jāti) into account; therefore, this very same purification applies to an object made of clay, gold, or silver, and does not depend on the nature of the material's genus. However, in the case of contact with urine and the like, the purification according to the material's genus must be observed. As for the wiping of the hand, it is due to impurity resulting from contact with a person who has consumed food-remnants (ucchiṣṭa). Thus Gautama says, "In some cases, having placed [the vessel] nearby for the sake of purification. Therefore, here too, only being placed nearby is intended, not taking hold of it by itself.

The *veda* is a handful of *darbha* grass, and its purpose is such as "the touching of the vital breaths with *darbha* grasses," and so forth. Therefore, those [substances] whose purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*) have a constant connection with the body; however, for those whose purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*), their presence is constant, but their actual taking up occurs according to necessity. [The gold must be] auspicious and beautiful in appearance, and pure by virtue of its form and its purification through heating, cutting, and the touchstone. (4.36)
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting; nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky. (4.37)

"Afflicted" means eclipsed by a planet; "in water" means reflected in water. One should see it situated in the middle of the sky—that is, in the intermediate space—but not at the time of midday. (4.37)
One should not step over a calf’s tethering rope, nor run while it is raining, nor look at one's own reflection in water; such is the rule. (4.38)

The *vatsatantrī* is a rope for tethering calves, or a row of calves; one should not leap over it nor step aside from it. Thus says Gautama: "One should not walk over a *vatsatantrī*" (GDh 9.52). *Svarūpa* refers to the physical form or bodily configuration. Because of the use of the word *sva* ("one's own"), looking at the form of another is not prohibited. This is the settled conclusion (*dhāraṇā*) in the scriptures. 4.38.
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees. (4.39)

The rule regarding the materials such as clay and so forth encountered by one who has set out is as follows: the clay and other items should be handled with the right hand; the clay that has been picked up should be treated in this manner. For another scripture reads in the section on setting out: "having turned to the right. A "divine object" (*daivata*) refers to an image painted on a cloth or similar medium for the purpose of worship. Gautama, however, states: "One should circumambulate shrines to the deities keeping them to the right" (GDh 9.66). By common worldly usage, a shrine to the deities is to be understood as a temple of the four-armed Mārtaṇḍa (the Sun) and others. He will later state: "and sacrificial halls. "Honey" (*madhu*) refers to honey from large bees due to its association with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and also because it is recited in the midst of auspicious items. "Well-known trees" (*prajātā vanaspatayaḥ*) refers to famous large trees—well-known great trees by their size or by their excellence in flowers and fruit, such as the *udumbara* and others. There is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "The *udumbara* is indeed strength" (MS 1.11.8). Those, however, who claim they refer to trees superior in quality or specifically designated [by name], are to be disregarded, as they rely solely on baseless tradition. 4.39.
Even if he is impassioned, he should not approach a woman when her menses appear;
nor should he sleep with her on the same bed. (4.40)

Even if he is intoxicated and afflicted by the arrows of desire, he should not approach her during the *ārtava*—the monthly menstrual blood well-known to flow from the female organ. Nor should he lie upon the same bed with her. If it is argued that this is already established by the prohibition against physical contact, we reply that this is not merely a prohibition; rather, this is a specific vow (*vrata*) and a particular form of penance (*prāyaścitta*). (4.40)
For when a man approaches a woman who is overwhelmed by her menses, his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan diminish. (4.41)
"Rajas" refers to the menstrual flow mentioned previously; "overwhelmed by it" means being connected with that. This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) for what precedes. 4.41.
For him who avoids her, who is overwhelmed by passion, wisdom, splendor, strength, sight, and even life itself increase. (4.42)
The mention of "increase" is merely a form of praise. 4.42.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating, sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease. 4.43.

The statement regarding purity, "The mouth of women is always pure" (MDh 5.130), and the prohibition, "The leavings of women and Śūdras" (MDh 11.152)—both of these are established through a distinction of scope. Among them, the declaration of purity is understood to refer specifically to women engaged in sexual intercourse, based on the observation of another Smṛti text: "And women [are pure] in connection with sexual pleasure" (BDh 1.9.2). Therefore, by process of elimination, the prohibition should be seen as applying to women other than those engaged in sexual pleasure, such as mothers, sisters, and so forth. For "sexual pleasure" (*rati*) here does not mean mere affection; rather, it is a specific state of being caused by *manmatha* (the god of love), consisting of desire and the like preceded by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). Consequently, there is purity in the case of women possessed of that [pleasure], while the prohibition applies to those who are the opposite.
Since eating together with one's wife would otherwise be occasioned by the purpose of sexual pleasure, this statement is undertaken: "One should not eat together with his wife.

Now, if it is argued that by the mention of "contact" (*saṃsarga*) a specific form of sexual union for one who lusts is intended, then purity would result from mere kissing; in that case, there would be no occasion for eating together with the wife.
Therefore, this repeated statement is for the purpose of making known a vow (*vrata*). Consequently, a lifelong resolve must be made such that eating together with the wife does not occur.
