And this "eating together" (*sahabhojana*)—which has a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*) and occurs at the same time and place—is enjoined as the object of the negative particle (*nañ*); thus, there is no suspicion that its meaning is already established by the prohibition against eating the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*). Furthermore, this specific sense of "together" (*saha*) is derived from other means of knowledge, such as other Smṛtis and established custom. For the meaning of the word "leavings" (*śeṣa*) is merely that which is dependent upon another. Likewise, [it is said]: "One should feed others, such as friends and so forth, together with one's wife" (MDh 3.103). In this case, a single substratum for the act of eating is not understood; rather, it is either the eater’s sharing the same location with the wife, or sharing the same time.

Others, however, explain "ucchiṣṭa" differently: *ucchiṣṭa* is that which has been left over after eating. But if it were explained in this way—that there is communal eating with one wife for a single purpose—then eating together with a Śūdra would be prohibited [by this rule], and the established usage would be abandoned. The designation *ucchiṣṭa* arises from contact with this person; that [designation] exists even through communal eating.

Some, however, maintain that eating at the same place and time is what is prohibited, because the instruction has a visible purpose: due to differences in individual nature, one man may not be satisfied by a woman who eats much, while another places his trust even in one who eats little; thus, she acts with guile, thinking, "In my presence she eats but a little."

Other rules of this kind are likewise [prohibited]. One should not look at her while she is eating; for if one sees her eating with her mouth wide open, she would not be pleasing to her husband due to the change in her appearance. A sneeze (*kṣavathu*) is the sound produced when the nose is filled by air from the head; in that case too, there would be no pleasure because of the disfigurement of the face. Yawning is the prolonged exhalation of air through an open mouth or the stretching out of the limbs and members of the body; that too is exactly the same [in its effect]. And she should sit comfortably, with her hair not loose and her limbs not cast upon the ground. (4.43)

A twice-born man who desires spiritual luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth. (4.44)

She who anoints another indeed shines forth; she is uncovered, meaning her garment is removed. For in matters of dress, people especially desire that she remain veiled. One whose limbs are entirely naked is not to be looked upon, for it is said that when one is completely without clothing, one’s beautiful form is not perceived in its entirety from all sides. [This applies to one] desiring splendor (*tejas*); *tejas* refers to the brilliance of complexion as well as the application of energy. 4.44.
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked.
One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen. (4.45)

Even though the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is always present, because it does not serve as a covering and because it is taught separately from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), he is said to be "wearing a single garment. A second garment, such as one for covering the limbs, should be used at the time of eating. [The rule] "not while urinating" includes excretion by way of illustration. On a path, on a carriage road, in a cow-pen, or wherever cattle go to graze. (4.45)
Neither on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain;
neither in a ruined temple nor ever upon an anthill. (4.46)

In a city, [this refers to] a stack of bricks for the sake of fire; the mention of "mountain" is intended to include forests and gardens as well. For thus there will be a specific prohibition: "on the summit of a mountain" (MDh 4.47). And if the prohibition were general, there would be the undesirable consequence of prohibiting even those who dwell on mountains. A *valmīka* is a mound of earth built by insects. 4.46.
Neither in pits inhabited by living beings, nor while walking, nor while standing;
neither having reached a riverbank, nor on the summit of a mountain. (4.47)

Neither walking nor standing; since walking and standing are prohibited, sitting is permitted. Nor near a riverbank, nor in the river water. "Near" (*āsanna*) refers to a place where there is apprehension of contact. "Peak" (*mastaka*) means the summit of a mountain. (4.47)
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows, one should never discharge feces or urine. (4.48)

Because wind and the other [elements] are present [in the body], one should not urinate while even glancing at the limbs [of others]. Since wind is formless (*arūpa*), its perception is to be understood through the whirling of colored clods of earth and so forth driven by it. However, this prohibition does not apply to the wind-circle (*vāyu-cakra*), for wind blows everywhere. (4.48)
The explanatory passage for this is:
"Intelligence perishes for one who urinates facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man; likewise, facing a cow or facing the wind. (4.49)
Some do not recite this verse in this chapter:

[120] "But surely, since the injunction for urination prescribes facing north, and since the sun rises in the east, how could there be a facing toward it at that time, such that facing the sun would be prohibited?

This is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), like the passage 'not in the atmosphere, nor in heaven. Or else, it might be possible [to face the sun] when one moves toward the northern direction during the northern solstice (*udagayana*). Or rather, the prohibition refers to the specific subject matter under discussion."

Some read "pratisaṃdhyam" (at the twilights). That is incorrect, because of the permission given in the verse, "And at the two twilights as during the day" (MDh 4.51), and because the suppression of natural urges is prohibited. Therefore, it should be read as "prativātam" (against the wind). This is a supplement to what precedes. [The word] "mehataḥ": it ends either in the present participle suffix -śat or the suffix -tasa. It means "of a man urinating" or "from urination. (4.49)
Having set aside wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, and so forth, he should pass by them, restraining his speech, being pure, with his limbs covered and his head veiled. (4.50)

Having set aside or concealed [the ground] with wood or other materials, one should void urine upon it. "Concealing" (*tiraskāra*) means an obstruction; having covered the ground with wood and so forth, one should discharge [the waste]. The reading with the instrumental case-ending (*kāṣṭhādibhiḥ*) is then clearer: one should discharge urine or feces using wood, a leaf, or grass. Restraining speech and being pure, one should do so with clods of earth, remaining free from food remnants. With limbs covered, meaning the body is veiled; and with head wrapped, as it is stated elsewhere: "with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) resting on the ear" (YDh 1.16). || 4.50 ||
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night and during the two twilights, one should face south, as during the day. (4.51)
The voiding and casting away of urine and excrement. 4.51.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as also when there is fear of danger to life. (4.52)

Shadow (*chāyā*) is the obstruction of the sun’s rays by walls, doors, and so forth. Darkness (*andhakāra*) is the hindrance to light caused by clouds, mist, Rāhu, or night. "Facing as one pleases" (*yathāsukha-mukha*) means that one should recite in whichever direction brings comfort. This rule applies when the direction is not known due to darkness. "Threat to life" (*prāṇabādha*) refers to the affliction of life; "fear" (*bhaya*) refers to that caused by thieves and the like. (4.52)
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it. (4.53)

The fire should be fanned with a bellows or similar means. One should not look at a naked woman, except during sexual intercourse—so says another Smṛti. One should not [throw] impure things [into the fire]. "Pure" (medhya) refers to sacrifice; that which is for the sake of sacrifice is pure. "Impure" (amedhya) refers to what is unfit for sacrifice, such as onions, urine, excrement, and so forth. One should not cast such things into the fire. Having lifted one's feet, one should not warm them directly over the fire. However, there is no fault in warming them over the fire by covering them first, for the purpose of inducing perspiration or similar needs. (4.53)
One should not place it underneath, nor should one step over it; one should not treat it with the feet, nor should one cause any injury to living beings. 4.54

One should not place a fire-vessel beneath a bed; "upadhāna" means a support or a place. "Avalaṅghana" means going by leaping. One should not act in such a way that, while not leaping, one's feet might be positioned above it. One should not engage in activities that cause harm to life—meaning those that inflict pain on living beings—such as traveling with excessive speed or exertion. (4.54)
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor travel, nor lie down;
one should not scratch the ground, nor remove a garland from oneself.

The time of twilight (*saṃdhyākāla*) is the period of transition (*saṃdhivelā*). "Lying down" means sleep. He will prohibit the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*). In another Smṛti it is said: "One should avoid these four activities during the time of twilight:
eating, sexual intercourse, sleep, and likewise the recitation of the scriptures."

Nor indeed should he scratch [the ground]. What is forbidden is digging or tearing up the earth; however, the arrangement of letters with a stylus or similar tool is not prohibited. He should not remove from himself a garland (*sraj*). A *sraj* is flowers strung together; he should not, by himself, take it off from his neck or head because it has faded or become heavy. By implication, it is stated that he should have it removed by another. Some maintain that this entire rule applies specifically to the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) period. 4.55.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or saliva into water; nor should one cast into it anything smeared with impurity, blood, or poisons. 4.56

*Lohitam* means blood. The plural form *viṣāṇi* (poisons) is used to indicate the various types of poisons, whether artificial or natural, stationary or mobile, or categorized by their specific varieties such as *gara* and so forth. [4.56]

One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person from sleep; one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice without being invited. (4.57)

An empty house is one where no one dwells. He should not wake up a superior by means of instruction based on reasons—such as saying, "This is proper for you," or "This is improper"—if he is inferior in conduct and other qualities. A *udakyā* is a woman in her menses; he should not converse with her. He should go to a sacrifice, but not uninvited; that is, he should not go to the sacrificial ground unless he has been invited. Regarding this, Gautama says: "But he may go at will for the sake of seeing it" (GDh 9.55). Therefore, this prohibition against eating and so forth applies to one who is uninvited to the sacrifice. 4.57.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.

This word *goṣṭha* signifies a dwelling place; it is a distinct term from those words that resemble compounds [ending in -goṣṭha]. The plural number in *brāhmaṇānām* is intended to be significant. The mention of "taking the hand" (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating the arms [as the locus of the action]. [The phrase *bhuñjīta*] refers to eating performed by oneself. (4.58)
One should not prevent a cow from suckling her calf, nor should one tell anyone [of it]; likewise, upon seeing a rainbow in the sky, a wise man should not point it out to anyone. 4.59

One should not prevent a cow—whether one's own or another's—from drinking water or milk, nor should one tell anyone else [to do so]. This rule applies prior to the time for milking; however, at the time of milking, letting her drink is prescribed. Because of the use of the feminine gender, there is no prohibition against preventing a male calf from drinking. Regarding the *indrāyudha* (Indra’s weapon), which is called the "bow of Śakra" or "the splendor of knowledge" in Kaśmīra: the word "in the sky" (*divi*) is a restatement. Some, however, say that there is no fault in seeing it when it is situated on mountains and the like; it is for their sake that the word "in the sky" is used. (4.59)
One should not dwell in an unrighteous village, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one reside for long on a mountain.

A village where unrighteous people—those guilty of major or minor sins—dwell in great numbers is called "unrighteous" by association with them; one should not live there. The mention of a "village" is intended to indicate any place of residence; therefore, the prohibition applies to cities as well. A marshy region (*anūpa*) is one abounding in diseases; one should not dwell in such a disease-ridden arid region (*jāṅgala*). One should abandon that country where diseases have broken out due to the influence of fate. One should not set out upon a journey alone, without a companion. (4.60)
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people; nor in one overrun by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes. (4.61)

"Sovereignty over a district" refers to a kingdom. One should not dwell in a district that is under the control of Śūdras. A kingdom consists of seven constituent elements (*prakṛti*), beginning with the minister, the commander-in-chief, and the judicial officer; this prohibition against residing there applies when all of these belong to the Śūdra caste. Now, one might object: is this not already established by the rule, "One should not dwell among the unrighteous" (MDh 4.60), since such a place would be crowded with unrighteous people?

This is not a fault. The previous prohibition refers to where they themselves reside; this one, however, applies even elsewhere—if they are present in another location, one must still not dwell in that region. Thus, the term "enclosed" (*āvṛta*) is used here: one must not stay in a region that is occupied by them. Likewise, a country overrun by heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*): even though they are unrighteous because they are outside the Veda, they are mentioned separately because they possess a sense of dharma. "Beset" (*upasṛṣṭe*) means connected with or afflicted by outcastes (*antyajana*). Alternatively, "beset" means tormented, as for example, the Vāhlīkas are by the Mlecchas. (4.61)
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice excessive gluttony;
one should not eat too early, nor too late, nor having already eaten in the evening, should one eat again in the morning. (4.62)

One for whom oil has been brought [as food] must be made to eat oil-cake, vegetable broth, and meat. For him, there will be a re-allowance (*pratiprasava*) of sacrificial remains and products of milk (cf. MDh 5.24–25). The plural number is used specifically with reference to buttermilk, curdled milk, and the like; for the direct modification [of milk] is indeed curd itself. Had it been intended to allow only that [curd], he would have mentioned "curd" alone. Therefore, this is not for the purpose of prescribing [curd]. Indeed, curd does not possess the quality of being "stale" (*paryuṣita*). Consequently, this prohibition does not apply to products of milk such as whey (*udaśvit*), buttermilk (*takra*), and curdled milk (*kilāṭa*).

One should not eat to the point of excessive fullness nor seek complete satiation. Regarding this, one part of the stomach is for solid food, another for liquids such as water, and another for the movement of the bodily humors (*doṣa*); one should eat in this manner—this is what must be done. One should not eat too early in the morning when the sun has just risen. For those who are emaciated, eating should take place after one watch of the day has passed during the forenoon; for others, it should be at midday. One should not eat too late in the evening at the time of sunset. Nor should one eat in the evening if one is already satiated from having eaten in the morning. Therefore, one should eat with desire [for more] at both times. Thus it is said: "Eating in the evening and in the morning is the meal ordained by the gods for human beings" (MBh 13.148.14). However, if one is already satiated in the morning, one should not eat in the evening.

Or rather, it is explained in this way: one should not eat in the evening or in the morning; that is, one should not satisfy oneself at both meal times. And thus Yājñavalkya speaks of a slight meal in the evening (YDh 1.114). 4.62.
One should not engage in useless exertion, nor drink water from one's cupped hands; one should not eat food while holding it in the lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity. 4.63.

Futile activity (*vṛthāceṣṭā*) is an action that provides no benefit, whether in the seen or the unseen worlds; for example, being intent on news of other lands and such. When the two hands are joined together, it is the *añjali* gesture; with that, one should not drink water. Because of the mention of "water," there is no prohibition against milk and the like. One should not [eat] in the lap (*utsaṅge*). Edibles (*bhakṣya*) refer to roasted grains, cakes, and so forth; one should not eat them while they rest upon the lap, that is, above the thighs. Because of the mention of "edibles," there is also a prohibition against fruits. However, since things such as flour-mash or boiled rice cannot be eaten without being sprinkled [with liquid], they are never even subject to the possibility of being eaten from the lap. *Kutūhala* is an excessive longing for a certainty regarding what might be, when there is no practical purpose. *Na jātu* means "never" or "at no time. (4.63)
One should not dance, nor should one sing, nor should one play musical instruments;
one should not clap hands, nor shout, nor, being impassioned, engage in conflict. (4.64)

Dancing (*nartana*) is a specific movement of the limbs, well-known in the world. Singing (*gāyana*) is the production of sound through the notes of the *ṣaḍja* scale and so forth. This prohibition applies to worldly [music], not to Vedic [chanting], because that is enjoined by scripture. Musical instruments (*vāditra*) include the lute, the flute, the drum, and others; the prohibition concerns playing them oneself. There is no prohibition against [music] being played by professional musicians, for there is no authoritative evidence that this is a causative form derived from a root ending in *ṇ*. Clapping (*āsphoṭana*) refers to the loud striking of the hands on the ground, such as clapping one's palms or striking the chest; it is that sound. *Kṣveḍā* is the indistinct sound produced with the teeth, commonly known as *kṣveḍanikā*. *Valgana* is something else. One who is impassioned (*rāgī*) should not cause discord when [another] is satisfied; he should not create opposition. This is not a prohibition when [the other] is distressed. A causative suffix (*ṇic*) must be applied to the word ending in the *ghañ* suffix. (4.64)
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal; nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its very nature. 4.65

One should not wash one's feet in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*), nor in a broken vessel—even if it is broken in only one place. In the case of vessels that are completely shattered, the prohibition follows from the very nature of the thing. However, since leaf-cups and the like are not conventionally classified as "broken vessels," there is no fault even if they have holes. "Intention" (*bhāva*) refers to the disposition within the heart; where the mind is not satisfied, or in cases where the sound is defiled, such as in a spittoon (*patadgraha*) and so forth, there too such clarity of intention does not arise. (4.65)
One should not wear sandals, clothing, a sacred thread, ornaments, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others. (4.66)

One should not use items held by others, such as one's father or other relatives. Gautama states: "If one is unable [to wash them], they should be purified" (GDh 9.6). A *karaka* is a water-pot; even if it was held by one's father or others, using it is contrary to established custom. It is intended here as something belonging to a specific relative; it is pure only for that person with whom it has a connection, and not for anyone else. An ornament refers to things such as ivory bracelets and the like. Some maintain that because these are mentioned in association with small objects like water-pots, there is no prohibition regarding jewels, pearls, and similar precious items. (4.66)
One should not travel with draft animals that are untrained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are deformed. 4.67.

Untrained and untamed oxen, horses, mules, and the like—those capable of bearing a burden—are yoked to carry that burden; this is an elliptical expression including carts and other such vehicles. The inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*) implies that travel is not desired even with those not formally yoked to the burden, provided they are merely untamed. As for the bull whose horn is broken, the growth of horns occurs only in that very animal, not in horses and the like. "Tail" (*vāladhi*) means the tail; those disfigured by it include those whose tails have been cut off and so forth. One should not travel with such an animal. Furthermore, mounting [such an animal] is prohibited in another Smṛti text. (4.67)
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfected in color and form, without excessively prodding them with the goad.

Even when being provoked to anger, some do not maintain discipline; for that reason he says: "by those who were disciplined," meaning well-trained. "Swift-moving" means going quickly. "Endowed with auspicious marks" means possessed of praiseworthy curls and so forth, and not having a bare forehead or other such defects. "Possessed of color and form": by a beautiful color, such as golden-red and the like, and by form, which is a particular excellence of configuration. And this beauty is to be known from the science of marks (*lakṣaṇavidyā*). "Violently tossing about" means causing pain. Furthermore, being excessively agitated again and again by the goad, the hook, and so forth, they break apart. (4.68)
The morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat should be avoided;
one should not clip one's nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth.

The first three muhūrtas after the sun has risen are designated as "morning sunlight" (*bālātapa*). The "smoke of the deceased" is that which rises from a corpse being cremated. A seat that is split, perforated, or broken—these are to be avoided. One should not cut one's nails or hair oneself out of mere whim; however, if they have grown excessively long, one should have them trimmed by a barber. Furthermore, one should not tear at the nails with one's teeth, even if they are overgrown.
Others, however, connect the rule thus: "One should not cut the nails or hair with the teeth. This means that one should not even strike the nails with a tooth.
For in their various fingernail-marks and arrangements, amorous women tear open their nails in many ways.
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with the fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless labor, nor any action that results in future suffering. (4.70)
"Vimardana" means breaking into pieces, such as a clod of earth associated with clay;
some, however, include even a clod of earth associated with lime and the like. "Mardana" of the clay means repeatedly tossing it up and letting it fall, or kneading it with the hand.

This act of crushing, which occurs through casual behavior, is prohibited here, but not when performed for a purpose such as purification, because the term "useless" (*niṣphala*) has been drawn forward [from the previous rule]. Since this is already established by that [previous rule], the present rule is commenced again for the sake of specifying a particular penance.

*Karaja* means nails; it does not mean action (*karman*). But [one might object]: has not fruitless action already been prohibited by the rule, "One should not engage in useless exertion" (MDh 4.63)? To this they reply: *ceṣṭā* refers to physical activity, whereas here there is an exclusion of the general category. Therefore, mental constructions such as daydreams (*manorājya*) and the like are to be avoided. *Āyati* is future time. One should not perform that action from which unhappiness or suffering arises in the future, such as eating when one has indigestion, or the expenditure of great wealth without considering the maintenance of one's family. One should not do that. (4.70)
Regarding this, there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda):
"The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, bites his nails, and is a slanderer as well as impure—he quickly goes to destruction. (4.71)

From this very mention of "clod" (*loṣṭha*) alone, it is understood that the previously mentioned term *mṛlloṣṭham* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For if both [clay and clod] were equally predominant, the mention of "clay" (*mṛd*) would have been made here just as [the clod was mentioned]. Since that [clay] is easily kneaded by the hand, its exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is established. However, because plaster (*sudhā*) is hard, its kneading must be accomplished with effort; thus, such [effortful kneading] is not even applicable when there is no purpose for it. But the kneading of clay-clods by the hand occurs naturally to some people; therefore, that is what is excluded.

The "grass-cutter" is one who is habitually inclined to cut grass. He gnaws his own nails with his teeth. A "slanderer" (sūcaka) is a backbiter (piśuna), a whisperer in the ear (karṇejapa); he is one who makes known the faults of another, whether real or unreal, behind their back. "Impure" has already been explained. He goes quickly to destruction. This result is not like other Vedic fruits, which have no fixed time for their maturation; rather, in this very life, destruction consists of a swift separation from wealth and so forth. (4.71)
One should not engage in contentious debate, nor should one wear a garland outside [the house].
Riding on the backs of cows is in every way censured. (4.72)

That mutual disputing regarding worldly treatises or matters which is carried out with dogmatic insistence or through wagering and the like, characterized by a display of self-importance—that is *vigṛhyakathā* (disputation). Regarding "outside" (*bahiḥ*): one should cover with a garment a garland worn around the neck so that it is outside the garment; such is the established custom. Others say that "outside" refers to an uncovered place; they maintain that one should not wander about in city streets and similar locations wearing a garland openly displayed.

Alternatively, it refers to external fragrance or external garlands, such that their scent is not clearly perceived. Thus another Smṛti states: "One should not wear a garland that lacks fragrance, except for one made of gold. Regarding the phrase "on the backs of cows," this prohibits mounting cows directly without a saddle. The word "in every way" means that even when there is an obstacle such as a saddle, or when the vehicle is yoked to a cart and so forth, there is no prohibition, because it is not a direct riding on the back. 4.72
One should not enter an enclosed village or house by a way other than the gate; and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar. (4.73)

In the case of an enclosed village, there is a prohibition against entering through anything other than the gate, such as by leaping over the surrounding wall; however, in the case of an unenclosed village, one may enter at will even through the gate. 4.73.
One should never play with dice, nor should one carry one's sandals oneself;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.

"Even without a wager, one should not play with dice even in jest. The mention of "even at times" is for the purpose of indicating [the prohibition of playing with] pieces such as *śalākā* (counters) as well; by this, all forms of gambling are forbidden. One should not carry leather footwear (*upānah*)—meaning shoes made of hide—from one place to another, having taken them up personally by hand or with a staff or other means. And this prohibition applies to one's own [footwear], because the word "personally" (*svayam*) is the subject under discussion; therefore, there is no prohibition regarding those belonging to a teacher or others. One should not eat while seated on a bed, a couch, or similar furniture, nor placing a morsel in the hand, nor placing food on a seat that is not separated from the vessel or other such items. Because of the immediate proximity, the reference is to the food to be eaten, not to the eater. (4.74)
And one should not eat anything mixed with sesame after the sun has set;
nor should one sleep here naked, nor go anywhere while still impure from eating.

"When the sun has set": the accusative case is used because of the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* [of the word *prati*]. And he is not "leftover" (impure). But is this not already prohibited among the duties of a student (*brahmacarya*)? And its status as a duty for all men has been made known. It is not merely for that purpose alone. True; this instruction is intended to make known its character as a formal vow (*vrata*). Therefore, a lifelong resolve must be undertaken. (4.75)
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
eating with wet feet, one shall obtain a long life. (4.76)

One should perform this rite at the commencement of an action. One should eat with wet feet; one should not sit down while rubbing one's feet until they are dry. When reclining, one should not stretch out one's limbs on the bed. "Reclining" (saṃveśana) means the joining of the limbs upon the bed. He states its fruit: "long life. This is not a rule specifically for one desiring long life; rather, it is obligatory as before. The mention of "long life" is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda). 4.76.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight; one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms. (4.77)

One should not approach, step upon, or enter a difficult place—such as a mountain or the like—that is hard to climb, nor a forest dense with trees, shrubs, and creepers. One should not let such a place come within the range of one's vision, out of fear that there might be hidden snakes, thieves, or other dangers. The mention of "vision" (cakṣus) here is intended to characterize all means of valid cognition, including scripture and so forth. One must not look at excrement or urine. "Gazing" (udīkṣaṇa) refers to a detailed examination by means of color and other attributes; since such examination occurs through prolonged observation, for that very reason it should not be performed. There is no fault if something is seen occasionally by chance. Furthermore, crossing a river by swimming with one's arms is forbidden for one who is healthy, but not when there is danger from wolves or similar threats. (4.77)
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds; nor should one step upon cotton seeds or husks. (4.78)
*Kapālikāḥ* are broken fragments. *Dīrgham āyuḥ*. The second [verse] has been explained. 4.78.
One should not dwell with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with those of the lowest castes, nor with those who live on the outskirts of society. (4.79)
But has this not already been stated [in the verse]: "Not where it is crowded with unrighteous people," and "Nor where it is infested by outcastes" (MDh 4.61)?

We say: no. In that [previous] context, residing was prohibited; here, however, it is co-residence (*saṃvāsa*). It was stated there: "One should not live as a householder in the village where they dwell. Co-residence, moreover, means social interaction with them through giving, receiving, and so forth, or cultivating friendship, as well as living near their house, such as subsisting on the shade from one side of it, and so on. Furthermore, because of the mention of "crowds" (*āvṛta*) there, a large number is understood; its meaning is that one should not live even near a village in which they are numerous. But here, even in the absence of a large number, living nearby and so forth is prohibited—this is the distinction.

The *pulkasas* and *niṣādas* are born from a *śūdra* woman. The "outcastes" (*antyās*) are the Mlecchas and others. The "outcaste-dweller" (*antyāvasāyin*) will be described as one born from a *caṇḍāla* father and a *niṣāda* mother, in the passage beginning with "a *niṣāda* woman [bearing] a *caṇḍāla*" (MDh 10.39). "Haughty" (*avaliptāḥ*) means arrogant due to pride, puffed up by wealth and so forth. 4.79.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor food prepared for sacrifice;
one should not instruct him in the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him. (4.80)

One must not provide instruction regarding what is beneficial or harmful to a Śūdra concerning matters seen or unseen; that is to say, one must not act as a counselor to a Śūdra. This prohibition concerns [counseling] for the sake of livelihood; however, there is no fault when it arises from friendship or similar motives. For Śūdras can indeed be family friends (*kulamitra*), and out of friendship, one necessarily offers advice on what is beneficial. Furthermore, friendship toward all castes is permitted for a Brāhmaṇa, as it is said: "A Brāhmaṇa is called a friend" (MDh 2.87).

As for those who explain, having introduced the point that one should not speak to one who does not ask—on the grounds that it is logical because it is established in other treatises, such as: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked" (MDh 2.110)—[they are mistaken].

That is incorrect. For in that context, regarding the subject of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), one should not speak unasked—such as saying "you have corrupted [the text]" or "it has been destroyed"—when someone else is performing something unrelated, such as a matter concerning accents or phonemes. And thus, in this specific instance where it is said "these are not to be taught," the statement "one should not speak when unasked" was made. Its meaning is that one should say nothing at all to a non-pupil who, even when unasked, recites with wrong accents or wrong syllables.

Regarding the term *nocchiṣṭam* ("not leftover"): this word *ucchiṣṭa* denotes a state of impurity (*aprāśastya*) caused by eating. Even one who has voided urine or feces is called *ucchiṣṭa* until he has sipped water (*ācānta*), as we shall explain: "One who is *ucchiṣṭa* should not touch [anything] with his hand" (MDh 4.142). Generally, the usage of *ucchiṣṭa* is connected to the act of eating. For when one is eating, that which remains inside or outside becomes *ucchiṣṭa* through contact with the interior of the mouth. Thus, the rule "hair on the beard does not enter the mouth" (MDh 5.139) indicates that anything other than the beard-beard hair—that which enters the mouth—renders one *ucchiṣṭa*. Consequently, the designation *ucchiṣṭa* applies to the eater, the food being eaten, and the vessel or locus from which it is taken. In some instances, however, it also means "the remainder of what has been used," as in "the sacrificial remnant (*havirucchiṣṭa*) is the priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In that context, according to established practice (*samācāra*), that which is held in a vessel, associated with a person who is *ucchiṣṭa*, and slightly tasted, is called *ucchiṣṭa*. Even clear rice and such items remaining in a vessel, though untouched by the eater, are avoided due to their association and established practice. In this regard, the injunction "even the *ucchiṣṭa* should be given" and the prohibition "not the *ucchiṣṭa*" refer to the same subject; they may be treated as alternatives based on the distinction between a true Śūdra and a false Śūdra, or based on the difference between the sacrificial remnant (*haviḥśeṣa*) and other types of remnants. Alternatively, *ucchiṣṭa* refers to what remains in the cooking pot after guests and others have eaten—essentially stale food—and that must not be given to a Śūdra. To this it is replied: because of its association with "worn-out clothes" (*jīrṇavasana*), it is more appropriate to understand it in this way. Furthermore, since the root *śiṣ* (to leave over) signifies "that which is other than what has been used," and the prefix functions in accordance with that meaning, the usage "the sacrificial remnant is the fee" is not contradictory. In this manner, there will be no contradiction between these two Smṛti texts, even though in common usage (*rūḍhi*) those things requiring sipping of water (*ācamana*) are generally seen here in the text. As for the statement "and the rules of purification are like those of a Vaiśya" (MDh 5.138), that refers to the case of a servant-Śūdra (*dāsa-śūdra*). We shall demonstrate that it is understood as referring specifically to what is left over after eating.

"Not *haviṣkṛtam*. That which is "made for the oblation" (*haviṣe kṛtam*) means prepared for the purpose of the oblation. This is a compound with a plural sense because of the prohibition against what is merely intended for that purpose. By the principle of the "stick-and-cake" (whereby the mention of one thing implies its related counterparts), everything that possesses even a trace of being an oblation is prohibited. Thus, the prohibition is established for: (1) that which has been formally resolved as being for the sake of the oblation; (2) the remnant of an oblation already in use; and (3) an oblation that has been left over after being partially consumed. Furthermore, the verb *kṛta* ("made") is employed here as a term denoting action in general. The expression "that which is made for the sake of the oblation" means "that which has been resolved [as such]. Therefore, it is understood that the prohibition applies to all states—even to the leavings—as long as they are designated as *haviṣkṛta* by their original formal resolution.

Others, however, have explained *haviṣkṛtam* as "mixed with sacrificial oblation" (*havirmiśram*). Furthermore, because of the prohibition against [food] that has been commingled, there is also a prohibition against [food] that is merely [contaminated]. It has been stated that when there is a prohibition regarding what is commingled with a Brahmin, it refers to the food of the Brahmin himself.

But how can there be a negation of the simple when there is a negation of the mixed? By means of the negation of the simple, the negation of the mixed—which is subordinate—can sometimes be expressed. Where even two things that are mixed appear as distinct, or where, while a form is appearing to the eye, its application occurs through taste and so forth, even there the linguistic usage based on that [mixture] certainly takes place. For example, in the case of balls of parched grain mixed with wine and the like, even though the form of the wine is not concealed, because of the cognition of that [taste], the penance for drinking wine indeed applies.
But even so, since it has not taken on a liquid form, it is not possible to drink the liquor that has attained unity with the solid lumps.

This is not a fault. The drinking is mentioned here by way of a general statement of propriety; however, what is actually prohibited is consumption (*abhyavahāra*) itself. For this section concerns what may and may not be eaten (*bhakṣyābhakṣya-prakaraṇa*), and eating is simply the act of consuming. Its specific varieties include drinking, chewing, masticating, and so forth. Furthermore, since a smell is perceived even when it has no [perceptible] substrate, one cannot infer the existence of a substance from it alone. Even when camphor and the like are at a distance, their smell is perceived. If one were to postulate that there must be an apprehension of subtle particles of a substance, then that substance would have to possess parts and a certain magnitude. However, where two things have merged into a single state and there is no cognition of them as distinct, injunctions and prohibitions cannot apply to the individual substrates alone. For example, regarding the rule "milk is to be drunk," when milk and water are mixed and both are drunk, it is neither milk nor water, because it is a different substance. For in that case, there exists a different color, taste, configuration, and other factors that cause the cognition [of something else]; thus, it is indeed a different substance.
If this were so, then if liquor and water were drunk together, one would not incur the penance for drinking liquor, because they are different substances.

This is not a fault; for liquor overcomes other tastes, just as a bitter taste does. Therefore, due to the recognition of that specific taste, the penance for it certainly applies. However, where there is a large amount of water and only a small amount of liquor and such, we shall carefully explain the penance for such contact in the section on "One Part" (Ekādeśa).

Therefore, a negation whose locus is the individual alone may indeed extend to the combination; for example, when it is said, "Beans are not to be eaten," even those mixed with other things are not permitted. But for what reason would a negation whose locus is the combination apply to that which is not combined? When it is said, "Bring water from the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā," one does not bring water from the Gaṅgā alone, nor from the Yamunā alone. If you say, "It is simply a matter of established usage," then such usage itself must be cited as the authority. One should not, however, teach this as a matter of Dharma.

But is it not the case that, because of the general prohibition against giving excessive gifts—whether for visible or invisible purposes—to a Śūdra in the rule "not to a Śūdra," the prohibition against instructing him in Dharma is already established?

True; however, the repetition is for the sake of a remainder (*śeṣārtha*). From this, the instruction regarding expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) becomes permitted. We shall demonstrate this in the context of the verse, "Having abandoned one who has come for refuge" (MDh 11.197).
Others, however, say that one should not teach the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, *pākayajña*, and so forth, in the capacity of a priest (*yājaka*) and the like.

Regarding this, they raise an objection: if the instruction of Dharma is forbidden for a Śūdra, how then can he possess knowledge of Dharma? And since one who lacks such knowledge cannot possibly perform religious duties, the Dharma-śāstras would be rendered useless by having a Śūdra as their practitioner. This objection is not valid; for it is possible for a Brāhmaṇa—who has transgressed the prohibition—to act as an instructor out of a desire for gain. Indeed, the injunction to give away all one's property [as a penance] for killing a Brāhmaṇa does not necessitate the acceptance of that gift; rather, it is the desire for gain that acts as the motivator. But is there not the statement: "And he may teach others"? (MDh 10.2)

Regarding the acquisition of the means of livelihood, for this very reason the present subject is stated thus: "A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] according to the rule, and he should proclaim them to the others" (MDh 10.2). However, instruction must certainly be given to one who has taken refuge as a Śūdra; for cohabitation with an ignorant person is forbidden because of his transgression of injunctions and prohibitions, as it is said: "Not with fools, nor with the arrogant" (MDh 4.79).

As for what they explain—that by these two rules, namely "nor should one teach him," [the teaching of] the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*) or the exposition of their meaning is prohibited; that by one rule the study of the treatises is forbidden and by the other the exposition of their meaning—[they are wrong], because for those who speak thus, since it is already established by the rule "his investigation of the treatises" (*tasya śāstravicāraḥ*), this would be a mere redundancy. Furthermore, informal instruction (*upadeśa*) that is not based on a formal text is not prohibited by anyone.
Thus, for those who argue in this way, the present statement is redundant.

Regarding this, they say: the word *dharma* refers to treatises such as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), which have the purpose of awakening one to *dharma*. For that [grammar] is not a treatise on *dharma* in the sense of having supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), since there is no instruction [in it] regarding prohibitions. Nevertheless, it does serve the purpose of awakening one to *dharma*; for a grammarian is indeed able to extract the profound meaning of a sentence by following the meanings of individual words. Furthermore, because it is a treatise on *dharma*, it is mentioned separately here, even though it would already be included under the term "treatise" (*śāstra*).

This is correct, provided that no one were to say: "How can there be an application for one who has no authority over the primary [rite] in regard to its subsidiary parts? For the Veda and the Smṛti-śāstra constitute the primary [rites], and the Śūdra has no authority therein.

Nor should one prescribe a vow for him. By the word "vow" (*vrata*), the *kṛcchra* penances are meant, as seen from the usage in the passage, "by these vows" (MDh 11.101). One should not prescribe those for one who desires prosperity. However, instruction is indeed intended when they serve the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). As for the vows of a *snātaka*, there is no possibility of their application because he is not a *snātaka*. Likewise, the *Sāvitrī* and other such rites do not apply due to the absence of Vedic study; and study is absent due to the absence of initiation (*upanayana*), since the three castes are mentioned in the injunctions for that initiation. (4.80)
For he who expounds this doctrine to him, and he who likewise prescribes the vow, sinks into the darkness called "the unrestrained" along with him alone. (4.81)

This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the preceding prohibition. By the phrase "together with him," he states the fault of both—the one who listens and the one who causes [the listener] to hear. "Sinks" means he plunges into it; that is to say, he incurs that [consequence]. 4.81.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food, nor bathe without using water. 4.82.

The prohibition applies simultaneously with both hands joined, pressed together, and mutually touching. By the word "with the hands" (*pāṇibhyām*), he prohibits the arms from being joined. By the word "of oneself" (*ātmanaḥ*), he excludes another person; therefore, there is no fault in scratching with both hands joined by someone else. Because of the mention of the "head," there is no fault regarding the back and so forth. "And one should not touch the head"—some say this means with the hand or with some other part of one's own body;
but that is not correct, because "with the hands" (*pāṇibhyām*) is the subject under discussion.
And one should not bathe without [covering] the head; this is the rule for both the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) baths. [Objection:
But why should this apply to a common bath taken by one who is perspiring?
[Response: Because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction for bathing.
The requirement for a prescribed bath is logical due to its proximity [to the specific context]. However, in common worldly usage, because there is no such injunction, it is not applicable.

Furthermore, this verb *snāti* (to bathe) refers to the washing of all limbs with water, cow urine, and so forth, as well as to bathing excluding the head. In that regard, when one has been touched by a Caṇḍāla or similar person, even the bathing excluding the head—which might otherwise occur by chance—is prohibited: "One must not bathe without [washing] that [head]. Moreover, there exists a worldly form of bathing that excludes the head, by which the "bathing of the head" is mentioned in the rule: "But one who has bathed his head [may anoint it] with oil" (MDh 4.83). || 4.82 ||
One should avoid seizing the hair and striking others on the head;
and having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil. (4.83)

Some authorities maintain that this prohibition applies without distinction to one’s own hair or that of another; others, however, connect it with the subject at hand, namely "one's own" (*ātmanaḥ*). Furthermore, this prohibition concerns seizing hair when motivated by anger; however, the grasping of a lover’s hair during sexual union is not forbidden. Regarding the term *śiraḥsnāna*, the inversion of the word order occurs because it belongs to the class of *rājadanta* and similar compounds (cf. Pāṇini 2.2.31), meaning "that by which the head has been washed. The compound *śiraḥsnāta* is formed by way of *bāhulaka* (general rule). One must not seize one’s own limb. (4.83)
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya lineage, nor from those who possess slaughterhouses, oil-presses, or taverns, nor from those who live by prostitution. 84.

It has been stated: "One should seek wealth from the king" (MDh 4.33). This word *rājan* is observed to be used for the Kṣatriya caste, but it is also seen applied to a ruler of a realm (*janapadeśvara*) who is not a Kṣatriya, as in the expression "the kingdom of Brāhmaṇas. In that context, regarding both the injunction for accepting gifts and the prohibition thereof, the term is understood to refer to the ruler of a realm; for this reason, the text says "from one not born of a Rājanya. For sovereignty over a realm can arise from any of the social classes (*varṇa*) through desire for power. Therefore, he specifies: "one should not take [wealth] from a king who is a ruler of a realm and is not born of a Rājanya—that is, whose birth or origin is not from a Kṣatriya. Furthermore, even from a Kṣatriya, one should not take [wealth] if he is greedy or acts contrary to the scriptures, according to the prohibition that will be stated later (MDh 4.87).

A *sūnāvan* is one who lives by the purchase of meat preceded by the slaughter and immolation of animals; he is well known in the world as a butcher (*khaṭika*). A *dvaja* is a liquor merchant, one who lives by the buying and selling thereof. A *veśa* is the profession of prostitution; one who lives by that, whether woman or man, [is a *veśavan*]. (4.84)
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a banner is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten banners; and a king is equal to ten brothels. (4.85)
This is for the purpose of making known that each subsequent [offense] is more serious than the preceding one; the remedy for such cases in times of distress will be explained later. 4.85.
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is a terrible thing.

A butcher (*śauṇika*) acts with a knife; he drives [the animals], meaning he employs them for the accomplishment of his own ends. This [act] is terrible and fearsome, because it is a cause for rebirth in hell and other such states. (4.86)
Through a figurative statement, there is a censure regarding the acceptance of gifts from a king:
"He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall, in succession, go to these twenty-one hells. (4.87)

"Greedy" means one who has the habit of seizing [wealth] from neighboring lords and others. "Acting contrary to the scriptures" means that he conducts himself by transgressing such scriptural injunctions as, "Having ascertained his learning and character" (MDh 11.22), by inflicting unjust punishment, abducting the wives of others, and so forth. "In turn" means that after experiencing the fruit in one place, he goes elsewhere. The word *naraka* denotes unsurpassed suffering; alternatively, it denotes a specific location based on the implication of hearing only of suffering. The number twenty-one is a figurative exaggeration (*arthavāda*). 4.87.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka. || 4.88 ||
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana,
Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pūtimṛttika.
The iron spike and the parched husk, the path and the Śālmalī river,
the forest of sword-leaves, and likewise the iron bristles.
The three verses [4.88–90] have a clear meaning.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king. (4.91)

This is the conclusion of the preceding injunction prohibiting the acceptance of gifts from a king: knowing that accepting gifts from a king is the cause of various sufferings in hells and other realms, learned Brahmins should not accept gifts from a king. "Those who desire"—that is, those who long for—"welfare," meaning spiritual well-being, in the afterlife, in a future existence. The word *pretya* is a distinct term that resembles a gerund (*lyabanta*). "Those who speak the Veda" means those who recite it; the mention of both "learned ones" (*vidvat*) and "those who speak the Veda" (*brahmavādin*) is intended to show the extreme gravity of the suffering involved. For them, there is an excessive fault resulting from such acceptance. As he will say: "Therefore, even a learned man should be afraid" (MDh 4.191). 4.91.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha, as well as those bodily hardships rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas. (4.92)

The night consists of three watches; its final portion is the *brāhma-muhūrta*. At that time, one should abandon sleep. Having awakened at that hour, one should reflect upon the Dharma and its purpose (*artha*). Furthermore, one should consider what kind of physical hardship arises from practicing a particular Dharma. If a Dharma produces great bodily suffering while being of little value, or if it contradicts other Dharmas, one should avoid it.

Even wealth obtained through service and the like causes excessive suffering and must therefore be avoided; for it is said, "One should protect oneself from everything" (GDh 9.34). One should do nothing without having reached a firm decision, nor should one indulge in mental constructions such as daydreams. For this is the nature of men: when there is no external activity, mental constructions arise in the form of a longing for the property of others and so forth. This [instruction] is for the purpose of human welfare in order to prevent that.

At that time, one should contemplate the true meaning of the Veda through the relationship of the goal and the means; one should contemplate the secret knowledge of the Self and practice it according to the method of Vedānta.

Alternatively, even regarding the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Veda, one should determine its meaning: "This is an injunction; this is the purpose; this rite has such a form; this is the deity here; this is the material; this is the qualified person here; this is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)," and so forth, deciding by means of one's own intellect. One should investigate the reasons for the differing opinions of commentators, determining that "this is correct knowledge" and "that is an error. (4.92)
Having risen and performed the necessary duties, purified and composed,
he should stand for a long time reciting the prayers at the morning twilight, and likewise at the evening twilight at its proper time.

Immediately thereafter, when the night has turned to dawn, he should leave his bed. He must attend to the bodily necessity of voiding urine and excrement; for at that time, men generally perform this. In this context, "attending to the necessity" refers to the voiding [of waste] as well as the cleansing of the mouth and teeth and so forth. Having performed these and completed the purification, he should sip water (*ācamana*) according to the rule beginning with "one [application] on the penis" (MDh 5.134). Being composed—by setting aside all other mental distractions—he should stand for the twilight prayer (*saṃdhyā*). While reciting the *Sāvitrī*, he should fix his mind upon the Blessed Sun for a long time. The period for the twilight prayer is said to last until the appearance of the sun; however, one who desires long life should recite it for even longer than that. For this purpose, the previously mentioned rule for the twilight prayer has been restated here. And he should also perform the subsequent twilight prayer at its proper time, beginning from the moment of sunset and continuing even after the rising of the stars. (4.93)
By virtue of their prolonged twilight devotions, the seers attained long life, as well as wisdom, glory, fame, and spiritual luster. (4.94)

He now shows for what purpose this rule is intended: one who desires the fruits such as longevity should perform the recitation during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) for a long duration. Although [the twilight rite] is obligatory (*nitya*), this specific fruit arises from the quality of its length. This is possible for one who is without a sacred fire (*anagnika*) or one who is away on a journey; for another, however, there would be an obstruction of the time for the *agnihotra* due to the performance of the lengthy twilight rite. "Lengthy twilight" is stated here as a quality. The word "twilight" (*saṃdhyā*) is used here in reference to the rules for recitation and so forth that accompany the twilight rite. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose twilight is long. The mention of the "sages" (*ṛṣi*) is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). (4.94)

Having performed the ritual commencement (upākarma) according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being self-restrained, should study the Vedas for four and a half months. 4.95.

The full moon day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa is called Śrāvaṇī; likewise for Prauṣṭhapadī. Having performed the rite known as Upākarma on those days, one should study according to the prescribed rule. The previously mentioned rule beginning with "with the tips [of the grass] pointing eastward" (MDh 2.75) is here recalled. "Yuktaḥ" means intent upon that. "Chandāṃsi" refers to the Vedas; this word *chandas* denotes the Veda and does not refer to the Gāyatrī and other meters. Therefore, this is the primary injunction even for one studying the Brāhmaṇas and so forth. This applies to both cases alike, as there is no difference in the suffix (*pratyaya*). This option is settled thus: "The Chāndogas perform the Upākarma on the Prauṣṭhapadī day, while the Bahvṛcas and Adhvaryus do so on the Śrāvaṇī day. (4.95)
Under the Puṣya asterism, a twice-born man should perform the external rite of the suspension of Vedic study (utsarjana);
or he may do so on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, during the forenoon.

When four and a half months have passed, the rite of *utsarjana* (the suspension of Vedic study) should be performed under the asterism Puṣya. The ritual for the *utsarga* has been handed down by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras. "Outside" means in an unenclosed place. The specific nature of these two rites, the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*, is to be understood from the Gṛhyasūtras. (4.96)
Having thus performed the ritual dismissal of the Vedic meters outside according to the scriptures, one should cease [recitation] for the intervening night and that very same day and night. (4.97)

Having performed the *utsarga* (the ritual suspension of Vedic study), one should not study for two days and one night; that constitutes a day and a night. Alternatively, for the second [period], it is only the day and not the night; one should abstain from study for this much time. A night that includes parts of two days is called "bird-like" (*pakṣiṇī*). Or else, on whichever day the *utsarga* is performed, that day and that very night are for non-study; on the second day, however, one should study. According to the first view, the second day is a period of non-study, while study is said to take place at night. (4.97)
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights, and one should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights. (4.98)

Therefore, after this rite of renunciation has been performed, one should study the *chandāṃsi*—the Vedas consisting of the collection of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas—during the bright fortnights; and one should study the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), such as phonetics, sacrificial ritual manuals, and grammar, during the dark fortnights. || 4.98 ||
One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night while fatigued, one should not sleep again. (4.99)

That in which the manifestation of syllables and accents is not clear is "indistinct" (*avispaṣṭa*). And that generally occurs in the rapid (*druta*) mode of recitation. At the end of the night, in the final portion of the night, when one who has risen from sleep should study, he should not then go back to sleep lest he become exhausted again. The reading should be construed thus: "But having studied the Veda at the end of the night while still exhausted, one should not go to sleep. (4.99)
A twice-born man who is disciplined should always recite the Vedic meters according to the prescribed rule, as well as those composed in the *brahma-chandas*, except in times of distress. (4.100)

The *chandāṃsi* (Vedic meters) intended here are the *gāyatrī* and so forth. The *brahma* (sacred text) composed or joined with these—namely the *ṛk* and *sāman*—is what is meant. Because the root *kṛ* has multiple meanings, its sense here is explained as "to join" (*yuj*). Just as one says "make cow-dung" (*gomayān kuru*) in the sense of collecting it, or "make a back" (*pṛṣṭham kuru*) in the sense of massaging it, so too does this term function here in the sense of "joining. *Brahma* and *chandas* together form *brahmacchandasī*; that which is composed or joined by these two is *brahmacchandaskṛtam*. *Brahma* refers to the *brāhmaṇa* portion; in the *Yajurveda*, *brahma* refers to the *yajus* formulas and the mantras associated with the *gāyatrī* and other meters. They recite [these] in a single location. It is not as in the *Bāhvṛcya* and *Chāndogya*, where the mantras are in one book and the *brāhmaṇa* in another, divided apart. Previous commentators have explained that the Vedas are thus constituted because of such differences in their modes of arrangement.

As has been stated, the previous rule is set aside in cases of distress (*āpad*). In times of distress, it may happen that the teacher is absent, or that one who is looking for a division among many deities might—being deficient in that regard—forget it. Therefore, in times of distress, this [strict] division is not to be observed. 4.100.
One who is studying [the Veda] should always avoid these occasions when study is forbidden, as should one who is teaching students according to the prescribed rule. (4.101)

One who is studying should avoid these following occasions of suspension (anadhyāya), as well as when performing the act of teaching. The mention of "teaching" is intended to include those who are not currently engaged in formal study, for the purpose of grasping and practicing the material. This is not permanent from the very beginning; rather, it applies even during the four and a half months starting from the Upākarma ceremony. This is a restatement for the sake of the students. (4.101)
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when it stirs up clouds of dust by day—
those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions during the rainy season to be times unfit for study.

*Anila* means wind (*vāyu*). When it blows with force, a sound is heard due to the friction of one wind against another; that wind is called *karṇaśrava*. It is termed *karṇaśrava* because it is heard by the ears (*karṇābhyām śrūyate*); this is a compound formed according to the rule *sādhanakṛtā* [Pāṇini 2.1.33]. The mention of "ears" (*karṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating a specific state [of the wind], for it is indeed heard by the ears. Therefore, whenever such a sound of wind is heard, one must not study. *Pāṃsusamūhana* means that which sweeps together or collects dust (*pāṃsu*); *pāṃsu* refers to dust. This is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*), meaning either such dust or such a wind. Thus, when it rains from here and there, if the wind blows in this manner, that duration of time is a period of non-study (*anadhyāya*). Those who know the lesson (*adhyāyajña*) are those who know the rules for teaching. (4.102)
Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when there is a falling of great meteors, there shall be no study for the remainder of the day. 4.103.

*Vidyut* means lightning; *stanitam* means thunder. Because they are mentioned as a copulative compound (*dvandva*), there is no study when these occur together simultaneously. *Maholkā* refers to the radiance of celestial bodies falling from the sky; their *saṃplava* is their falling here or there. The word *ākālika* denotes the period beginning from the time of the omen until the same time on the following day. The mention of *manu* is for the purpose of completing the verse; others say it is for the sake of indicating an option. 4.103.
But when these have arisen while the fires have been kindled, one should know that there is no study; likewise, even outside the rainy season, when clouds appear.

This is not a time unfit for study at any hour when these [phenomena] have arisen; rather, it refers to when the fires have been made manifest—meaning at the time of the twilights (saṃdhyā). For at that time, the fires are invariably made manifest with the desire to offer oblations. The word *prāduḥ* signifies manifestation. "Out of season" (*anṛtau*): the season (*ṛtu*) is the rainy season; other than those, autumn and so forth. In that case, it is when clouds are seen, provided that the fires have been made manifest, as required by the context. (4.104)
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the luminaries,
one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study until the same time the following day, even during the proper season.

A *nirghāta* is a thunderous sound from the atmosphere; an *utpāta* is a portentous noise. Among the luminaries—the moon, the sun, Jupiter, and so forth—there is the phenomenon of *upasarjana*, which is the appearance of halos, as well as their mutual eclipsing. The phrase "even in the proper season" (*ṛtāv api*) includes the intention that, according to tradition, portents are not counted during the rainy season. (4.105)

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, the suspension of study shall last as long as the light remains; for the remainder of the night, it is as it is during the day.

In the case of the "threefold conjunction" (*trisamnipāta*), it was previously stated that the period lasts until the next dawn (*akālika*). By this [present rule], however, it is said that even when two [of these three] meet, the period lasts as long as the light (*sajyotis*). "Thunder and its sound" refers to thunder and its resonance; "lightning and thunder and its sound" is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). When these two have arisen during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*), the period of non-study (*anadhyāya*) lasts as long as the light. During the day, the sun is the light; at night, fire is the light. If [thunder and lightning] arise during the morning twilight, there is non-study only during the day, but not at night. Likewise, if they arise during the evening twilight, there is non-study during the night, but there is no fault in studying in the morning.

Regarding the three topics under discussion—lightning, thunder, and rain—there is a separate mention of lightning and thunder. Rain is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*); when that third [phenomenon] is observed, the previously mentioned suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasting until the same time [the next day] applies. With reference to that, it is stated: "as by day, so also by night. *Jyotis* refers to the well-known [sacrifices] such as the Jyotiṣṭoma. The reading is *śeṣam*; the meaning is that the remaining day during which the oblation is being offered becomes a cause for the suspension of study.
Now, why was it not stated thus: "but the remainder is remembered as being until the same time"?
Manu’s composition of verses is diverse. 4.106.
For those who desire proficiency in dharma, there shall be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, and in the presence of any foul odor whatsoever. (4.107)

Those who desire proficiency in the Dharma should not study in villages or towns. The word *dharma* here refers to the fruit of Dharma, such as heaven and the like; or rather, proficiency in Dharma consists in its being unobstructed by non-Dharma (*adharma*), whereby the purpose of the injunction is performed in its most perfect form. Consequently, this constitutes an authorization for one who is incapable [of full observance]. "Foul odor" means a contemptible smell; when that reaches the path of the nose, there is no studying. "In every way" means even in the case of the smell of a corpse. (4.107)
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a *vṛṣala*, nor while one is weeping, nor in a gathering of people. (4.108)

"In which [place] a corpse is contained" means one in which a corpse remains in the middle of a village and has not yet been carried out. "[Of a] *vṛṣala*": here *vṛṣala* does not mean a Śūdra, because that has already been prohibited by the rule: "Not in the presence of a Śūdra person" (MDh 4.99). What then? Unrighteousness (*adhārmikatva*) is indicated by his predominance of unrighteousness (*adharmaprāyika*). Therefore, the prohibition applies to one who is of sinful conduct, and [the study is forbidden] due to being in his presence. "While there is weeping" means when the sound of weeping exists. The word *rudyamāna* refers to the mere state [of the action]. "The assembly of people" (*janasamavāya*): in such a place where many people have gathered together for some purpose, one should not study. Alternatively, the meaning is "while there is weeping in the assembly of people," i.e., while people are weeping; the prohibition applies when many are weeping. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used in the sense of the agent, as is Vedic (*chāndasa*). 4.108.
While in water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine, while impure from food, or after eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony—one should not even think [of forbidden things] in one's mind. (4.109)

Midnight consists of four *muhūrtas*; that indeed is the "great night. [The time for recitation is forbidden] from two *muhūrtas* after the first midnight until two *muhūrtas* after the latter. Regarding water: one situated in a river, pond, or similar body of water; however, recitation while submerged in water—such as the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn—is not prohibited, because it does not constitute a formal occasion for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). Others read "at sunrise" (*udaye*); this refers to the time of the sun's first rising, which is a period of non-study. One who is "impure" (*ucchiṣṭa*) is one who has not yet performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) following a meal. Even one who has voided urine or excrement is called impure until he has performed the *ācamana*. Others say the term refers merely to the state of being unfit for *ācamana*; by this, even one who has spat or done similar things is included. Even mentally: elsewhere, mental reflection is permitted during times other than those of suspended study. What then? These causes are mentioned for the purpose of emphasizing the gravity of the offense. (4.109)

Having accepted an invitation for an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days during the period of impurity following the death of a king or during an eclipse of Rāhu.

That which is intended for one person alone is called *ekoddiṣṭa*, namely the *navaśrāddha* (the first funeral rite). Having accepted the invitation—that is, having agreed—to that [rite], there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) for three days, starting from the time of the invitation. Likewise, "the king" refers to the Moon; his "impurity" (*sūtaka*) is the flowing of nectar toward Rāhu. By the word "and" (*ca*), the Sun is also included. Alternatively, the "impurity" of the king who is the lord of the realm refers to the festival of a son's birth. The "impurity" of Rāhu is the eclipse of the Moon and the Sun, commonly known as a *grahaṇa*. 4.110.
As long as the fragrance and the smear of food offered at a single funeral (ekānudiṣṭa) remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should he not recite the Veda. 4.111

An *āmaśrāddha* (an ancestral rite performed with raw food) is intended for a single individual; for that rite, there is a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*) for as long as the scent and the stain remain on the performer. This is a different rule than the preceding one. On the second day, having bathed and removed that scent, he becomes fit for study. Furthermore, this is an illustrative rule: even in the absence of scent and stain, one should not study as long as the food consumed has not been digested. By the word "of the learned" (*viduṣaḥ*), the text reiterates that only such a person has the entitlement to partake in the *śrāddha* meal. (4.111)

One should not study while lying down, nor with one's feet raised, nor while sitting with a cloth tied between the knees; nor after eating meat, nor food from a household in which a birth or death has occurred. 4.112

"With legs extended" means with one foot placed upon the other; "or with feet joined" refers to sitting on a bed, chair, or similar seat with the feet together. "Avasakthikā" is the binding of the knees and the middle [of the thighs] with a cloth or other material. "Āmiṣa" means meat. The mention of *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) is intended to indicate impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) and so forth as well. (4.112)
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the new moon and fourteenth days, and on the full moon and the Aṣṭakā days. (4.113)

*Nīhāra*, *diṅmoha*, and *dhūmikā* are synonyms; that by which the quarters are made as if covered with mist and dust. *Bāṇa-śabda* means the sound of arrows. Others read and explain the labio-dental [variant] as *vīṇā-bāṇa*; for its usage is seen in the *Mahāvrata*: "The lute (*vīṇā*) has a hundred strings, the lute has many strings. On the fourteenth day of both fortnights, and on all the *aṣṭakās*—that is, all the eighth days—according to other Smṛtis and established custom. However, others read simply "on the eighth days" (*aṣṭamīṣu*). (4.113)
The new moon day destroys the teacher, and the fourteenth day destroys the disciple;
the Brahma-aṣṭakā and the full moon day likewise destroy them; therefore, one should avoid those days.

The preceding statement is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) for the sake of establishing the obligatory nature [of the rule]. Therefore, in cases where there is nothing indicating its obligatory character, that non-study (*anadhyāya*) is subject to optionality. And he will state later: "One should always avoid only these two" (MDh 4.127). One should completely avoid those [days] from the act of study. 4.113.
A twice-born man should not recite while there is a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, and camels are barking in a row.

The jackal is the *gomāyu*. Its howling is the making of sound. There is no study when dogs, donkeys, and camels are standing in a row and making noise; this applies to each individual animal in a row of its own kind. (4.115)

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting food offered at a śrāddha ceremony. (4.116)

The word *antaḥ* denotes proximity; [it means] near a cremation ground and near a village. A *govraja* is a place where cows go to graze, or it is a cow-pen. One should not study while wearing that very garment which was worn at the time of sexual union with a woman; because of its association, the word *maithuna* (sexual intercourse) refers here to the garment used at that time. Having taken even dry food and other items prepared for a *śrāddha* ceremony, one should not study. (4.116)

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha ceremony—having touched even that, there is a suspension of study; for the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth. (4.117)

That which is given for the purpose of a *śrāddha*, such as cooked rice and so forth, is commonly known as "śrāddhika"; it is for the sake of excluding this that the following is stated. Not only is the acceptance of rice, grain, and the like a cause for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) during a *śrāddha*, but even other things—whether living beings such as cows and the like, or non-living things such as a pair of garments—are included. Having touched even those at the time of acceptance with one's hand, one should not recite; for that [acceptance] itself constitutes his meal. He is called "pāṇyāsya" because his hand is his mouth. This shows that eating at a *śrāddha* and the acceptance of goods for its sake are equivalent. (4.117)
