When a village is plundered by thieves, during a panic caused by fire, and during all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is no study for the duration of the day. (4.118)

*Upapluta* means afflicted or beset. Where many thieves fall upon a village for the purpose of slaughter, there one should not study. *Saṃbhrama* refers to a state of agitation where fear is produced by fire, such as when a house is set ablaze; even if the house and so forth have not been burnt, the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasts until the same time on the following day, starting from the time the event occurred. Furthermore, this applies to other extraordinary portents (*adbhuta*), whether celestial, terrestrial, or atmospheric, such as the floating of stones and the like, or the appearance of such things during the daytime. (4.118)
At the commencement and the conclusion of the Vedic term, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
likewise for the Aṣṭakās, and for the nights at the end of the seasons, it is for one day and night.

Regarding the *utsarga* (the ritual closing of the term), a period of one day and night has been previously mentioned; this [present rule] provides an option with a period of three nights. Regarding the *upākarma* (the ritual opening of the term), this is a new injunction. The *aṣṭakās* are the three or four eighth days (*aṣṭamīs*) in the dark fortnight following the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī. Although a period of one day and night has been prescribed for all eighth days, nevertheless, this commencement is rightly made for the sake of establishing a constant rule. Furthermore, throughout this section, the option depends on the requirement that the purpose be fulfilled. The phrase "on the days marking the end of the seasons, a period of one day and night" is supplied [from the previous rule]. There are six seasons. When one of these ends and another begins, there is no study (*anadhyāya*). The mention of "night" is intended as an illustration (including both day and night). (4.119)

One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant; nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on the ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle. 4.120.

A barren tract (īriṇa) is a place outside the village devoid of water and grass, another term for which is "saline soil" (ūṣara). "Vehicle" refers to a cart, a carriage, a palanquin, and so forth; there is a prohibition against traveling by such means. 4.120.
Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when there is sour eructation. (4.121)

*Vivāda* is an initial verbal dispute; *vyākrośa* is mutual abuse. *Kalaha* is the mutual striking with sticks and other weapons. An *senā* consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. A *saṅgara* is a battle. Even when not in a battle, there is a prohibition for one who is stationed within an army. Regarding "having just eaten," another *smṛti* text states, "as long as the hands are still moist. *Ajīrṇa* refers to food eaten on the previous day that has not yet been digested on the following day. *Vamana* (vomiting) is well known. In the case of sour eructation (*śuktaka*), even if there is no indigestion, [the rule applies] on that very day or the next. (4.121)
Nor having failed to take leave of a guest; nor while a strong wind is blowing;
nor when blood flows from the body; nor when one is wounded by a weapon. (4.122)

The mention of the *atithi* (guest) is intended to indicate the *śiṣṭa* (the learned or cultured person). A *śiṣṭa* who arrives unexpectedly is an *atithi*; when he has come to the house, he should be requested [with the words], "We shall study. Having been permitted by him with the response, "So be it," one should study. And so says another *smṛti*: "And when a *śiṣṭa* has arrived at the house" (YDh 1.150). Regarding the phrase "when the wind blows with force":

although it was already stated that "within earshot" (MDh 4.102) and so forth, that is true; however, this prohibition applies to even stronger winds, and also prohibits study during the rainy season and at other times as well.

Alternatively, [the term *vāti*] means "becomes parched," because *vāna* has the sense of drying up. And the mention of *māruta* (wind) is intended as an illustration for wind in general. Even when the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are wasting away due to the fatigue of study, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). In the phrase "when the wind increases" (*mārute vardhamāne*), the two locative cases are used with different referents (*vyadhikaraṇa-saptamī*) to indicate that the one who performs the rite and the one who studies are distinct. When blood has flowed out due to leeches and so forth, or when blood has flowed from the body wounded by a weapon; this forms a single syntactical unit with the verse concerning the limbs and so forth. (4.122)
One should never recite the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda while the sound of the Sāmaveda is being heard;
nor after having completed the study of the Veda, nor after having studied the Āraṇyaka. (4.123)

One should not recite the *ṛc* verses or the *yajus* formulas while the sound of the *sāman* chants is being heard. There is no prohibition against the *ṛgveda* and the *yajurveda-brāhmaṇa*. Furthermore, when the *pañcaviṃśa* (the twenty-fifth book) is being heard, this prohibition applies to both the *ṛc* and the *yajus* as well. "The end of the Veda" refers to where the Veda reaches its conclusion—the end of the mantras and the end of the *brāhmaṇas*. The *āraṇyaka* is a specific portion of the Veda; having studied that, one should not study another text. (4.123)
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda, however, belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure. (4.124)

It is stated that when the sound of *sāman* chanting occurs, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for the *ṛg* and *yajus*. Regarding this, the following is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). "Devadaivatyam" means having the gods as its deities; the meaning is that it is intent upon the praise of the deities. Since *ṛc*s are generally characterized by praise, it is therefore called "devadaivatyam. Because humans are characterized primarily by action (*karman*), and because the *Yajurveda* teaches a great abundance of rituals, the *Yajurveda* is called "human" (*mānuṣa*) on account of this similarity. The word "human" (*mānuṣa*) denotes the human species. Through the superimposition of identity (*abhedādhyāsa*), it is said that the *Yajurveda* is human. "Pitrya" means beneficial to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Or rather, it is heard to have the ancestors as its deities through some connection with the word "ancestor" (*pitṛ*). There are three worlds, and there are exactly three presiding deities over them: the gods (*deva*) of heaven, humans (*manuṣya*) of the earth, and the ancestors (*pitṛ*) of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Thus, there are three Vedas. Since two [the *Ṛgveda* and *Yajurveda*] have been mentioned as connected to gods and humans respectively, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the *Sāmaveda* is "pitrya. Its sound is impure (*aśuci*). One should not understand the impurity of its sound to be absolute in a metaphysical sense. Rather, just as one should not study in the presence of something impure, so too in its presence; thus, the basis for the impurity is common. And this prohibition against the *ṛg* and *yajus* while the *sāman* is being sung arises from the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the rules for Vedic study, not during the performance of a sacrifice (*yajña*). (4.124)
Knowing this, the wise, having daily practiced first the extraction of the essence of the three Vedas in due order, subsequently study the Veda itself. (4.125)

Knowing that this constitutes a connection with the presiding deities of the three worlds—as expressed in such passages as "The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deity"—the wise and learned first practice the essence extracted from the three Vedas, namely the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Sāvitrī, in the manner previously described; thereafter, they study and recite the Veda. By means of that study of this triad, the three worlds and the three deities become fully encompassed.

Although this matter has already been stated in the second chapter, it is stated again here: just as one does not recite [the Veda] during forbidden periods (*anadhyāya*), so too one does not study the *trayīniṣkarṣa* before [the Veda] has been previously learned. 4.125.
If a domestic animal, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat passes between [the teacher and the pupil], one should know that the study is suspended for a day and night. (4.126)

"In the case of interrupting [the study] by going between [teacher and pupil], it refers to the interval between the teacher and the student, or among those who are studying together. 'Day and night' means an entire day and night. But in the Gautama Dharmasūtra it is said: 'A three-day fast and living apart [from one's teacher] have been prescribed' (GDh 1.59). And this same rule applies to studying in a cremation ground. Here, an option is to be understood. || 4.126 ||
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study: an impure place for Vedic recitation and himself when he is impure. (4.127)

Because of the inclusion of the word "constant" (*nitya*), there is an option regarding the non-study periods mentioned previously. Even among those, it has already been shown that for some there is merely constancy, as where the term "constant" occurs or where there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), such as: "The new moon day kills the teacher" (MDh 4.114). Furthermore, the impurity of the ground consists in contact with impure things such as bones, female genitals, or phalli. As for the impurity of oneself, it will be explained in the fifth chapter. Although these two [types of] non-study periods occur within the context of the injunction for formal study, they apply to the daily obligatory (*naityaka*) recitation as well; for one who is impure is not entitled to perform [the rite]. And thus says the *Brāhmaṇa*: "For this sacrifice, there are indeed two non-study periods: when one is impure oneself, and when the place [is impure]" (TĀ 2.15). Moreover, the *brahmayajña* is a constant recitation (*japa*). (4.127)
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth, a twice-born Snātaka should always remain celibate, even during his wife’s fertile season. (4.128)

"He shall be a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*). The duty of a student—namely, the abstention from sexual intercourse—is extended [to these days], but not [the duties] such as wandering for alms and so forth; for, due to the connection with the phrase "even during the season," that [abstention from intercourse] is what first comes to mind. Others, however, desire the abstention from honey and meat on these days as well; in that regard, another *smṛti* passage should be cited:
"The sixth, the eighth, the new moon day, and the fourteenth of both fortnights..."
One should avoid [these acts] on the full moon day, as well as with regard to oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and shaving.

Others, however, say that *brahmacārī* is the name for a person belonging to a specific stage of life (*āśrama*). Therefore, when it is applied to a householder or others who abide in a different stage of life, it serves as an extended application (*atideśa*) by means of the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the duties intended for the acquisition of the Veda. [The injunction] "one should be a *brahmacārī*" implies that all the duties of a *brahmacārī* apply; yet, because of the statements "he should perform them until his return [from studentship]" (MDh 2.108) and "the householder eats the remains" (MDh 3.107), those specific acts such as tending the sacred fire, kindling the wood, and wandering for alms are directly set aside. Only the prohibitions against honey, meat, and sexual intercourse are extended [to the householder].
But the word *brahmacārin* is well-known as referring specifically to the cessation of sexual intercourse; therefore, this [objection] is trivial. 4.128.
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with one's clothes on, nor in an unknown body of water. (4.129)

This is not a prohibition regarding the obligatory daily bath, because for one who has already eaten, there is no occasion for its performance. For in another Smṛti, the sequence of activities is heard as: "bathing, the great sacrifices, and eating the remnants. Nor does this apply to bathing necessitated by touching a Caṇḍāla and so forth, because that would contradict the rule: "One should not remain impure even for a moment. Therefore, this prohibition refers to bathing characterized by personal desire, which is caused by the removal of heat and other such factors.

The afflicted person is one seized by disease. Even though he is impure, bathing in every form is forbidden for him according to the rule: "One should protect oneself from everything" (GDh 9.34). What, then, is his purification? Wiping, sprinkling with water accompanied by mantras, discarding clothes, and so forth—these must be performed.

The "great night" (*mahāniśā*) consists of four *muhūrtas* on both sides of midnight. As for those who explain it as "the great night is that time [of the year] such as the beginning of winter," their interpretation is a false exposition because it contradicts the rule for the morning bath during the months of Māgha and Phālguna. Nor is there any authoritative basis for the claim that this is a prohibition regarding the nights of the winter season, since a second occurrence of the word "night" (*niśā*) is absent [in the text].

Regarding the phrase "with garments": when there are many garments available for purposes such as protection against cold, which are indicated by their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), this is a prohibition. For it has already been ordained that one should bathe with at least one garment, according to the rule: "One should not bathe naked" (GDh 9.60–61; cf. MDh 4.45). With two garments, there is no restriction; with many, there is a prohibition. "Water-reservoir" (*jalāśaya*) means a source of water. "Unknown" means its depth—whether shallow or deep—is uncertain, as well as whether it poses a danger from crocodiles and the like. "Constantly" (*ajasram*) means at all times. || 4.129 ||
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a teacher, a king, a *snātaka*, an *ācārya*, a tawny person (*babhru*), or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice. (4.130)

The images here are the deities, because their shadows are produced [therein]. The *guru* is the father; the *ācārya* is the initiator (*upanetā*). The separate mention [of these terms] is for the purpose of removing the extended application (*atideśika*) of respect [that might otherwise apply to all elders]. Therefore, this rule does not apply to maternal uncles and others. Some say: "This is not correct because it contradicts established practice; the distinction should be understood as being like the expression 'oxen and bulls' (*govalīvarda*). *Babhru* is a tawny color; the substance endowed with that quality is meant. Here, *babhru* refers either to a cow or to the *soma* plant, since both are seen to be used by the word *babhru* in the Veda. Regarding the phrase "intentionally," there is no fault if it was done unintentionally. (4.130)
At midday and at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.

At midday, at midnight, or during the dead of night, having eaten a *śrāddha* meal that includes meat, one should not indulge [in sexual intercourse], nor should one remain there for a long time. If, while traveling to a village or elsewhere, there is no other path except through a crossroads (*catuṣpatha*), then a mere passing through it is not forbidden. Some, however, connect the word "and" (*ca*) in this way: "having eaten a *śrāddha* meal, and also any other food containing meat. Regarding this connection, established custom (*samācāra*) must be consulted; otherwise, a disjointed connection cannot be maintained. (4.131)
One should not intentionally step upon the remains of a bath with fragrant unguents, the water used for ritual bathing, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit. (4.132)

Udvartana refers to fragrant powders such as flour and the like used for rubbing the body. Apasnāna refers to water that has already been used. Niṣṭhyūta refers to things such as betel leaves that have been spat out after being consumed, even if they do not consist of phlegm. Adhiṣṭhāna means standing upon those [substances]. "Intentionally" (kāmataḥ): there is no fault if it was done unintentionally. (4.132)
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy, nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another. (4.133)

One should never engage in sending gifts, sitting or standing in the same place, or conversing about matters such as housing and honors with an enemy—that is, a foe—nor with one who is unrighteous (*adhārmika*), a sinner (*pātakī*), or one who lives by deceitful means. A "thief" (*taskara*) is a robber. And because of this specific mention of "distinction" (*bheda*), not every unrighteous person is intended; rather, it refers to those as explained. The term "another's wife" (*parasya yoṣit*) refers to a woman. By using the word "woman" (*yoṣit*), it is indicated that it is not only a legally wedded wife (*patnī*), but also a concubine (*avaruddhā*), since both cause enmity and are prohibited due to the visible faults associated with them, as they are mentioned together. Furthermore, the use of the word "wife" (*dāra*) later on is for the purpose of showing an excess of invisible fault (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*).

Furthermore, it should not be said that "in the general designation 'woman,' a specific understanding is reached because of the explanatory statement (arthavāda) regarding the meaning of the word *dāra*. This is not an explanatory statement for this; rather, this is a distinct sentence altogether. 4.133.
For there is nothing in this world so detrimental to long life as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this world. (4.134)

Neither indigestible food and the like, nor the theft of gold and the like, are so detrimental to longevity or so destructive of life as is sexual intercourse with another's wife; for it entails fault both in its unseen and its seen consequences. (4.134)
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak. 4.135
Disrespect, lack of regard, absence of reverence, and contempt—even toward those who are emaciated and currently incapable of showing affection. (4.135)
For these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt. (4.136)

He shall consume the man who treats these three with contempt: the Kṣatriya by his glance and his weapon, the Brāhmaṇa by his muttered prayers, burnt offerings, and invisible spiritual power. Therefore, the conclusion is that these three must always be honored. Having set forth the vision of their potential for harm, this final summary is intended to ensure they are avoided with great effort; and from this exceeding care, one may infer the gravity of the expiatory rites required for offending them. (4.136)
One should not despise oneself on account of former failures; until death one should seek prosperity, nor should one consider it unattainable. (4.137)

Failure (*asamṛddhi*) refers to the lack of success regarding wealth and so forth at the time of acquiring wealth through agriculture and other means. In such a situation, one should not despise oneself by thinking, "I am unfortunate and have not performed meritorious deeds; I have not obtained wealth on this occasion, so how shall I obtain it at another? One should not harbor despondency. One should seek prosperity until death. Until the very last breath, the desire to acquire wealth must not be abandoned. Nor should one consider that prosperity is difficult to attain. Thinking, "My resolve will certainly succeed," one should proceed toward its acquisition without taking into account unfavorable planetary positions and the like. There is a wise saying by someone:
Those deficient in personal effort calculate the influence of the planets;
for those who lack the vigor of being, nothing is impossible for those who are resolute.

By this, he demonstrates the following: "I am not in a state of misfortune; since I possess the wealth that can be acquired through the afflictions of ritual duties such as the *ādhāna*, I am not qualified for them. Therefore, I have escaped the hardship of performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice"—he who possesses such a thought does not think correctly. Consequently, one should strive for that [true understanding]. (4.137)
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant; nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma. (4.138)

Speech employed for a purpose is regulated by truth. Truth is that which is seen and heard exactly as it occurred. One should speak what is pleasant; this is the second rule. One should recount the virtues of another, such as magnanimity and so forth, even on some occasion when they have not been witnessed. Likewise, regarding the birth of a son and similar events—as in "O Brahmin, a son has been born to you"—even if one has no personal interest in it, if it is true, it should be spoken. If he does not know of it, there is truth that may be either pleasant or unpleasant. The pleasant has been illustrated by "O Brahmin, a son [has been born]," and so on. The unpleasant is, for example, "O Brahmin, your daughter is pregnant. One should not speak that which is untrue. Even if it is true, the fact of a daughter’s pregnancy should not be disclosed because it is unpleasant. When there is a way out, one should remain silent.

"Surely, out of affection, one should say of a pregnant woman that she is 'not pregnant'; therefore, he says: 'And one should not speak an untruth that is pleasant. Thus, he who has had his first direct realization is not permitted to remain silent regarding it; this is the eternal law (*sanātano dharmaḥ*). Since the Veda is eternal (*sanātana*) and constant, the law (*dharma*) ordained by it is likewise eternal. (4.138)
One should say "bhadra, bhadra" or simply say "bhadra"; one should not engage in groundless enmity or dispute with anyone. (4.139)

In this context, they explain the first word *bhadra* as involving the elision of the negative particle (*nañ*). One should say that what is *abhadra* (inauspicious) is *bhadra*. The use of the particle *iti* is for the purpose of illustration; established words such as *kalyāṇa*, *maṅgala*, *siddha*, and *śreya* should be employed.

If the preceding word is also intended for the sake of illustration, then expressions such as "one with eyes" for a blind person or "wise" for a fool are obtained. Alternatively, the word *bhadra* itself should be used in such cases.

One should not engage in "dry enmity"—that is, boastful speech devoid of any purpose such as wealth or other interests. In this way, a dispute in a royal court becomes merely "dry" and so forth, even if it is initiated by someone who is incompetent. (4.139)
One should not travel too early, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with outcasts.

The word *atikalya* refers to the break of dawn; one should not go out at that time. Nor should one go out too late in the evening at the time of the western twilight, nor with an unknown man, nor alone with *vṛṣalas* or *śūdras*. (4.140)
One should not despise those who have missing limbs, those with extra limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those destitute of beauty or wealth, or those of low birth. (4.141)

Those with deficient limbs are those who are one-eyed, leprous, hunchbacked, and so forth. Those with redundant limbs are those who have extra members, such as those suffering from elephantiasis (*ślīpadī*) and the like. Those deficient in learning are fools. Those who have passed their youth are the extremely aged. Those deficient in form are those of ill-proportioned appearance, such as the flat-nosed, the squint-eyed, and so forth. Those deficient in wealth are the poor; "wealth" (*draviṇa*) means riches, and they are those excluded or bereft of it. Those deficient by birth are those of low castes, such as the *kuṇḍas*, *golakas*, and others. One should not revile them. Reviling (*ākṣepa*) is contempt; addressing these people by these very names is itself an act of contempt. (4.141)
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire;
nor, while remaining in his natural state, should he look at the hosts of luminaries in the sky while he is impure.

"Ucchiṣṭa" refers to one who has eaten and not yet rinsed his mouth, or one who has voided urine or excrement; here, the word "ucchiṣṭa" denotes impurity in general. Thus, the touching of cows and other such beings by one who is *ucchiṣṭa* is forbidden. By the word "impure" (*aśuci*), he will later prescribe the penance. The mention of "limbs" is not restrictive; touching with any other part of the body is also not desired. There is no prohibition if the contact is mediated by clothing or similar objects. One should not look at the host of luminaries in the sky while healthy and not afflicted by illness. Because of the specific mention of "in the sky," there is no prohibition against looking at terrestrial luminaries, such as fire. (4.142)
Having touched these while impure, one should always touch the vital breaths with water, as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand. (4.143)

Even though the term is used without qualification, the "vital breaths" (prāṇas) referred to here are specifically those located at the head, such as the eyes and so forth. The word *prāṇa* is seen in the Veda in the sense of the eyes and other senses, as in the *Prāṇasaṃbhava Upaniṣad*. The "limbs" (*gātrāṇi*) refer to the shoulders, knees, feet, and so on. Having taken water with the palm of the hand, one should touch [the body]. 4.143.
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own bodily apertures without a specific reason; he should avoid touching all the hairs of his private parts as well. (4.144)

Without a cause—meaning without a reason such as itching—one should not touch one’s own *khāni*, that is, the apertures such as the eyes and so forth. One should avoid touching the private parts located in the armpits and the genitals by means of the aforementioned contact. The use of a different verbal form (*ākhyātāntara*) is for the purpose of completing the verse.
Others, however, say that because of the mention of a different verbal form, looking [at them] is prohibited. (4.144)
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should constantly mutter prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness. (4.145)

Auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is the attainment of desired longevity, wealth, and so forth. For that purpose, one should always be devoted to and engaged in *maṅgalācāra*—the practice of auspicious conduct—which consists of touching yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), forehead marks (*tilaka*), auspicious fruits, and the like.
Now, it has indeed already been stated that such conduct possesses authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*).

True. By this, an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*) is stated. For someone might become indifferent upon seeing a deviation in that which is performed with the notion that it is merely visible; therefore, it is stated again. Just as at the time of departure, when [auspicious signs] are present—such as saluting curds and the like, seeing white garments, the cry of a *kapiñjala* bird to the right, or a crow on a fruit-bearing tree to the very right—these and similar things are to be heeded for the sake of auspiciousness, while the opposite is to be avoided.

One who has conquered the senses and is free from longing for sense-objects—although this has been stated repeatedly as being for the sake of human purpose, it is stated again here for the sake of avoiding failure. Since an oblation can be offered elsewhere than in the fire, he says "he shall offer into the fire"; the term "unwearied" is a restatement of what was already mentioned. 4.145.
For those who are endowed with auspicious conduct, who are ever self-restrained,
and who constantly recite prayers and offer oblations, no downfall exists.

"Calamity" (*vinipāta*) refers to divine affliction caused by ordinary inauspicious omens, such as disease, loss of wealth, separation from loved ones, and so forth. Such [calamities] are averted by these auspicious observances (*māṅgalyaka*). By this [statement], its obligatory nature (*nityatā*) is also expressed, even though it serves a specific purpose (*phalārthatva*). For no one seeks merely the cessation of divine affliction; therefore, the mention of "obligatory" (*nitya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Even if someone were not desirous of [this result], this injunction would still remain obligatory. Thus, it has a dual purpose: its application consists in both the fulfillment of an obligatory duty and the cessation of calamity. (4.146)
One should constantly recite the Veda at the proper times without weariness; for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty. 4.147

It has been stated: "One should both recite [the Veda] and offer oblations. Regarding that, he first states the means for the recitation: "One should recite the Veda itself. The remainder is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). "At the proper time" (*yathākālam*) means at whichever time; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of repetition. For one should recite precisely when one's worldly activities do not interfere. Other rites, such as the *agnihotra*, have fixed times; however, for recitation, purity alone is the time.

This is the primary *dharma*; [the other] is a secondary *dharma* (*upadharma*). A secondary *dharma* is that which is near to *dharma*. This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the proximity is the predominant factor, not an *avyayībhāva*, as in the rule "comparisons [are compounded] with words expressing common properties" (Pāṇini 2.1.55). The censure of other *dharmas* is for the purpose of praising the recitation of the Vedas, not for the purpose of prohibiting them. 4.147.
By constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth. (4.148)

Non-malice is non-violence. "Beings" refers to those that are stationary and those that move. These four types of actions, when practiced throughout one's entire life, result in the recollection of past births. "Birth" (jāti) means another existence; "prior" (paurvikī) means belonging to a former life. (4.148)
Remembering his former birth, the twice-born man practices the Brahman;
and through the constant practice of the Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss. (4.149)

Now, one who desires a specific result strives for everything; yet, the recollection of previous births is not invariably a source of happiness such that it could be described as the fruit of the fourfold practice beginning with the study of the Veda. To this he says: remembering his former birth, he knows Brahman, and therein he becomes possessed of faith. [The sense is: "Such is the practice of Brahman by which a previous birth is remembered. Remembering, he again engages in that practice. And from that practice cultivated over many births, he subsequently enjoys—attains—the bliss characterized by the attainment of Brahman, which is eternal and from which there is no return. By the word "infinite" (*ananta*), a specific kind of bliss is indicated: the soul's complete satisfaction without further means. By the word "eternal" (*ajasra*), its permanence is established. Such bliss is attained, and it does not perish.

Two words may have the same meaning yet not be redundant, as in the example: "He carries *vṛttaka* and *purīṣa*. Here, *vṛttaka* means water and *purīṣa* means excrement; in this context, one is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) and the other is an etymological term (*kriyā-śabda*). *Purīṣa* is that which is capable of filling (*pūraṇa*), and *vṛttaka* is water. (4.149)
He should constantly perform oblations for Sāvitrī and propitiatory offerings on the change-moon days (parvan);
and he should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and the Anvaṣṭakā days. (4.150)

The nature of the previously mentioned *homās* is now stated. The *sāvitrāḥ* are those whose deity is Savitṛ; they are to be performed on the *parvan* days, namely the full moon and the new moon. These *homās* for the sake of pacification (*śānti*) have the purpose of averting misfortune. Regarding the substance, clarified butter (*ājya*) alone is prescribed here for all *homās* where no specific substance is mentioned, as it is heard in the scripture: "Indeed, that which is taken in the *dhruvā* vessel as clarified butter is for the sake of the entire sacrifice" (TB 3.3.5.5). Furthermore, the locative case in the word *parvasu* should be understood in the sense of the accusative. Fire is the locus of the *homa*, never its object. The substances to be offered are recited as parched grain, clarified butter, meat, flour-cakes, curd, milk, grains, ground meal, and so forth. And these *homās* are *apūrva* (producing transcendental results). Whatever procedure (*itikartavyatā*) exists according to traditional practice has been shown previously. The *aṣṭakās* are the three eighth days of the dark fortnights following the *āgrahāyaṇī* festival. According to some, there is the statement: "Of the four dark fortnights of the winter and dewy seasons" (ĀśG 2.4.1). Therein, one should honor the ancestors (*pitṛs*) with a *śrāddha*. The word *pitṛ* refers to one's father and others who have passed away before. The *anvaṣṭakās* are those same ninth days. (4.150)
One should perform the voiding of urine at a distance from the dwelling, the washing of the feet at a distance, and the disposal of the remains of food at a distance as well. (4.151)

That by which the feet are moistened, such as water and so forth, is "pādāvasecana" (water for washing the feet). One should throw that away from a distance; or rather, one should perform the washing of the feet itself at a distance. "Niṣeka" means sprinkling. Even the water used for bathing with oil and other substances can be designated by the word "niṣeka. This refers to the disposal at a distance of what remains after use and is to be discarded; for that is more commonly known by the term "niṣeka. (4.151)
One should perform the preparation of unguents, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and the worship of the deities during the forenoon alone. (4.152)

In the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages), it is heard in the praise of the limbs of the sacrificial animal that "the anus is Mitra. Therefore, here too, by way of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), Mitra is the anus; purity pertaining to that is *maitra*. "Adornment" (*prasādhana*) refers to the arrangement of hair, anointing with unguents, and so forth. Alternatively, the two words form a qualifier-qualified relationship: "*maitraṃ prasādhanam*" (Mitra-like adornment). Even though no feces have been produced, the washing of the anus must be performed in the morning. For just as the rinsing of the mouth is prescribed because the flow of saliva and such is inevitable for one who has slept, so too this washing of the mouth and the two lower limbs must necessarily be performed even without a specific cause.

Others, however, say that *maitra* refers to the service of a friend; that should be performed before all other duties, even those that are more internal. Even in that case, since there is no possibility for one who is impure to remain [in that state] for even a moment, its priority should be understood in relation to one's own duties. And in that context, the word "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) is intended merely as an indication of priority over other duties, and not for the purpose of prohibiting the afternoon. Alternatively, *mitra* is the sun; the worship of him is *maitra*. (4.152)
On the sacred festival days (parvan), he should visit the deities, righteous and most excellent brahmins, the Lord for the sake of protection, and his gurus. 4.153.
He should salute his elders and offer them his own seat;
he should attend upon them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them as they depart. (4.154)
One should, unwearied, constantly practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma, properly set forth in one's own duties as declared by the Śruti and Smṛti. 4.155.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. (4.156)
Nor is this person being established as one endowed with qualities such as learning; for these qualities are sought after by subjects. As it has been said:
"What is the use of that cow which is neither a milch-cow nor pregnant?
What is the purpose of a son who is born neither learned nor righteous? (Pañcatantra, Prelude, verse 3).

Even that which is inexhaustible and abundant—indeed, that which remains undiminished even by unfortunate calamities—is destroyed by improper conduct (*ācāra*). Even an inauspicious mark (*alakṣaṇa*) upon the body, such as a mole (*tilaka*), which indicates misfortune such as poverty, is likewise destroyed by proper conduct. For through devotion to proper conduct, unrighteousness (*adharma*) perishes. (4.156)
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he is constantly a partaker of suffering, afflicted by disease, and short-lived indeed. (4.157)
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct, is full of faith, and free from malice, lives for a hundred years. (4.158)
Whatever action depends on others, that one should avoid with effort;
but whatever depends on oneself, that one should practice with diligence. (4.159)

That which is performed for the benefit of oneself and others through the solicitation of another is considered dependent on others (*paravaśa*) and is to be avoided; however, this does not apply to activities such as officiating at sacrifices (*ārtvijya*), which are accomplished through one's own livelihood (*vṛtti*). For that is indeed under one’s own control. It is precisely with regard to such matters that the employment of servants and the like is permitted. Nor does this [text] prohibit even those acts dependent on others for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), because it is improper for a Smṛti to subvert a Śruti, and because the Smṛti has its scope only within the aforementioned subject matter. However, whatever is under one’s own control—even if it be a very small amount of wealth—if it can provide some slight benefit to another, one should perform that action oneself. If the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) cannot be fulfilled and there is no wealth available for the maintenance of one’s family, begging must indeed be resorted to when no other means exist. But it should be done with the thought: "I shall sacrifice specifically," or "I shall give specifically. The intended meaning is that, provided some measure of wealth exists, one should remain contented. (4.159)
Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering. (4.160)
He censures begging: "Whatever is dependent on another is entirely suffering. Let alone the standing at the door of another's house, such compliance is a wandering both in this world and the next.
But even the mere thought of begging does not prevail over the heart;
surely this is an unmistakable illusion, not the creation of the Self-Existent One."
In brief, this is the definition of suffering: whatever there is of begging; and this is happiness: the absence of longing. (4.160)
Whatever action brings satisfaction to one's inner self while performing it, that one should perform with effort; but one should avoid the opposite. (4.161)

The repetition of "satisfaction of the self" mentioned previously is for the sake of recollection. Its scope is indeed its manifestation: that action which, when performed, does not give rise to hesitation or doubt, is to be done; but that in which the heart finds no satisfaction is to be avoided. (4.161)
One must not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever. (4.162)

The *ācārya* is the one who initiates [the student]. The *pravaktṛ* is the teacher (*adhyāpaka*) or the expounder (*vyākhyātṛ*). The *guru* is someone other than these two, such as a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, and so forth. The term "all" (*sarva*) includes ascetics (*tapasvin*), those engaged in penance (*prāyaścitta*), and even outcasts (*pātakins*). For violence against all living beings without distinction is prohibited in various contexts;

some maintain that this repetition is for the purpose of prohibiting [violence] even against *ācāryas* and others when they act as aggressors (*ātatāyin*). However, the explanatory passage beginning with "Whether it be a teacher, a child, or an elder" (MDh 8.350) is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to this very rule.

But the Teacher says: this is not a prohibition; rather, it is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), intended for the purpose of enjoining a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), just like [the rule]: "One should not look at the rising sun" (MDh 4.37). Therefore, when an effort has been made [to look], this becomes a prohibition of the mental resolve. Alternatively, speaking ill is indeed violence, because we see such usage as: "He struck her with various words. Or else, the root *han* is used in the sense of acting in a hostile manner. (4.162)
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities; one should also avoid hatred, arrogance, pride, anger, and harshness. (4.163)

Nihilism (*nāstikya*) is the determination that the objects established by the authority of the Vedas are false. Censure (*nindā*) is the presentation [of them] through words [in a derogatory manner]. Regarding tautology, it is due to a defect of intention—thinking "the Veda contradicts itself; there is no truth here"—and not as a rhetorical device for a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). The deities are Agni and others; their disparagement is indeed censure, just as speakers say regarding fate, "We have been struck down by a cursed fate. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is displeasure caused by envy and other such motives. Arrogance (*stambha*) is the lack of humility due to egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). Pride (*māna*) is egoism, the conceit of self, such as "I am learned," "I am wealthy. Resentment (*amarṣa*) is anger, sharpness, and harshness; it is anger preceded by hatred. (4.163)
One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike him down; except for a son or a pupil, whom one may strike for the sake of instruction. (4.164)

That by which one is subdued is *daṇḍa*—such as the hand, a stick, a whip, a rope, a split bamboo cane, and so forth. Being angry, one should not exert oneself toward another, nor should one brandish such an instrument; nor should one strike even obliquely for the purpose of inflicting a blow. A "blow" (*nipātana*) is the forceful contact with that limb. One may strike a son or a pupil with a whip, a bamboo splinter, or an open hand-palm, as will be stated in the eighth chapter, but not with a staff. And these two should not be struck out of anger; rather, it is for the sake of correction and instruction, if they act with restlessness due to childishness. As in the rule, "But on the back part of the body" (MDh 8.300), they are to be struck only slightly. The mention of the "pupil" is intended to include female and male slaves as well, since their duties are similar. (4.164)
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him revolves in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years. (4.165)
Since striking in general on all objects has been forbidden, these five verses are intended to show the excessive gravity of the offense when committed against a Brāhmaṇa.

Having "menaced" (avagūrya)—that is, having merely raised a staff or similar weapon with the intent to kill or the desire to strike—without actually bringing it down, one is cooked in hell for a hundred years; that is, one undergoes the transformation [of suffering] and experiences its fruit. (4.165)
Having intentionally struck [a living being] even with a blade of grass out of anger, one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in states of woe. (4.166)

"Aggression" (*saṃrambha*) means an outburst of anger, not in jest. "Intentionally" (*buddhipūrvam*). "Twenty-one births": *jāti* means birth. The syllable *ā* is meaningless, as in the word *pralambate*. "Wombs of the wicked" refers to animals, who abound in suffering. Let alone objects that cause pain such as a staff; even for striking with a blade of grass, there is the experience of hell for a long duration. (4.166)
A man who, through lack of wisdom, causes blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting, incurs very great suffering after death. (4.167)

"Blood" means *lohita*. When one causes it to flow from limb after limb—such as by striking a Brahmin with a sword or similar weapon while he is not fighting—it results in very great suffering in another birth after death, such as in hell and the like. The phrase "through lack of wisdom" is a restatement; for a wise person, knowing the meaning of the scriptures, would never act in this way under any circumstances. (4.167)
For as many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth, for that many years shall the shedder of blood be devoured by others in the next world. (4.168)

In the case of a slight blow, the aforementioned fruit [applies]. But in the case of a more severe one, for as many particles of dust, grit, or specks of soil as the blood—fallen from the body of the Brāhmaṇa onto the ground—takes up or absorbs, for that many years in the next world, the striker who caused that blood to flow shall be devoured by dogs and jackals. (4.168)
Therefore, a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body. (4.169)

This is the conclusion of the preceding rule, which prohibits the three actions concerning the lifting and striking [of a weapon]; the meaning is that one must never do so, even in times of distress. (4.169)
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood, and who always delights in violence—he does not prosper in happiness here in this world. (4.170)

This is a general supplement to the prohibition against all violence. Adharma is that which is forbidden by the scriptures, such as approaching women who should not be approached; one who practices this is an unrighteous person (*adhārmika*). Furthermore, there is he for whom falsehood itself is wealth—meaning one who, by speaking untruth in witness testimony, legal proceedings, and the like, acquires wealth through bribes. And he who delights in violence, being intent on harming others either due to a persistent enmity or for the sake of material gain—he does not thrive in happiness, nor does he attain happiness in this world. (4.170)
Even when suffering for the sake of dharma, one should not turn the mind toward adharma, seeing that the wicked who act contrary to dharma quickly meet with their downfall. (4.171)

Dharma is the boundary established by the scriptures; one who abides by it should not set his mind upon unrighteousness even when suffering or falling into distress. For although unrighteous people may be seen to possess great wealth through theft, bribery, hypocrisy, and the like, their ruin—such as the loss of wealth—is nevertheless quickly observed. Therefore, one should not deviate from dharma. (4.171)
Having become a friend, he has shown the matter as it was seen. Now he states the meaning of the scripture:
"Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow;
but returning slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer. (4.172)

This is said because the times for Vedic actions that yield auspicious or inauspicious fruits are indefinite. Unrighteousness (*adharma*), when practiced—that is, performed—does not bear fruit immediately; it does not grant its result at once. For in the Veda, only the fact that enjoined and prohibited actions result in pleasure and pain is heard; however, no specific time is understood. Indeed, the function of a scriptural statement, even though its primary aim is to make known what ought to be done, culminates merely in making known the connection between an action and its fruit; it does not imply a specific time for those actions that possess fruits. As for obligatory (*nitya*) duties, their obligation does not arise from a desire for a fruit. Furthermore, regarding the avoidance of prohibited acts, one is not entitled to perform them out of a desire to avoid the suffering of hell and so forth; rather, it is by the force of the scriptural prohibition itself. That prohibition makes known that the performance of what is forbidden has suffering as its fruit. To explain this more precisely would entail an excessive expansion of the text, so we shall desist.

"Like a cow. This is an illustration by way of both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Just as the earth, when sown with seed, does not immediately become possessed of various crops, but rather requires ripening—such is the similarity of Vedic action. By way of dissimilarity also: just as a cow or a beast yields fruit immediately through carrying or milking, so it is not with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). The mention of "demerit" is for the purpose of showing that there is no fixed rule regarding the time for the yielding of fruit even for merit. "Revolving" means accumulating over time. It "cuts," that is, severs, the "roots" of the agent who performs prohibited acts. By the severing of the roots, the total destruction of everything is indicated; just as trees and other stationary beings do not grow again once their roots are cut, so it is for those who commit unrighteousness. (4.172)
If it does not ripen upon oneself, then upon one's sons; if not upon the sons, then upon one's grandsons; yet an unrighteous act never fails to bear fruit for the doer. (4.173)

This is improper: that it is said the fruit of an action performed by one person goes to another. Vedic actions grant their fruit to the agent. The principle of Vaiśvānara does not apply here, because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect]. Indeed, the fact that [the fruit] is for the sake of a son or others is not heard in this context.

True. When a son is afflicted, the father who suffers for him experiences even greater pain; therefore, the suffering belongs to the doer alone. It is not contradictory that for the son as well, that result arises from his own actions performed in a previous body. This should be understood to apply to grandsons (*naptṛ*) as well—grandsons being sons of sons. Because the *saṃhitā* (the continuous text) is identical in form, both "dharma" and "adharma" are included by the term "adharma. (4.173)
By unrighteousness one prospers for a while; then one sees auspicious things;
then one conquers one's rivals; but finally, one perishes along with one's very roots. (4.174)

One prospers—that is, attains growth—through unrighteousness, such as by betraying one’s master and the like. At that very time, having obtained wealth or a village, one then beholds and experiences auspicious things characterized by the possession of many servants, cattle, horses, and so forth. Thereafter, one conquers and overcomes rivals and enemies who are impoverished. Thus, those established in righteousness obtain nothing from any source due to the absence of such deceit; therefore, for them, the term "poverty" is a synonym for sovereignty. Having remained thus for some time, they are eventually destroyed along with their roots—including their sons, kinsmen, wealth, and relatives. Therefore, righteousness must not be abandoned. (4.174)

He should always take delight in truth, righteousness, and noble conduct, as well as in purity; and he should instruct his disciples in accordance with dharma, restraining his speech, his arms, and his belly. (4.175)

Truth (*satya*) is the speaking of things exactly as they have been perceived. Dharma consists of injunctions and prohibitions concerning what has been heard in the Vedas. Although truth possesses that same nature, its separate mention in the Veda is for the sake of emphasizing its excellence. Untruth is inherent in human nature; therefore, it is repeatedly prohibited with great effort. Noble conduct (*āryavṛtta*) is the practice of the virtuous; "nobles" (*āryāḥ*) refers to the cultured (*śiṣṭāḥ*), and their "conduct" (*vṛtta*) is their behavior. One should take delight (*āramet*) therein. "Delight" means satisfaction. By this, satisfaction in these matters is enjoined. Having observed other such practices as well, one should cultivate a clarity of mind. Disciples—namely wives, sons, servants, and students—are to be instructed according to dharma, following such rules as "behind the back of the body" (MDh 8.300). One should be restrained in speech, arms, and stomach. Restraint of speech (*vāk-saṃyama*) means not speaking excessively, whether there is a purpose or not. Restraint of the arms means not causing pain to anyone by relying on the strength of one's arms. Restraint of the stomach (*udara-saṃyama*) is the absence of gluttony (*anaudarikatā*), meaning not eating too much. Gluttony is excessive eating due to greed for specific foods, or eating frequently at the houses of others.

"Even though a matter has already been stated, it is stated again; for that which is beneficial should be spoken even many times. This is the resolution of the charge of tautology in all cases. (4.175)
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness, and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future suffering and is censured by the world. (4.176)

The threefold aggregate of human goals (*trivarga*) has been described. Someone, however, might consider them to be equal, thinking: "Just as *dharma* is practiced by setting aside wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*), so too are sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which are in opposition to them; for that [sacrifice] is opposed to wealth because of the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the like, and it is opposed to pleasure because of the injunction of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for the initiated one. Likewise, one should not pursue wealth and pleasure by setting aside *dharma*. In this regard, where a desire for injury to living beings is intended to be expressed—such as in the case of 'one should not harm living beings'—that is for the purpose of prohibiting that specific object, because of the connection with enmity; but where wealth and pleasure are intended through the injury of someone, there is no fault of injury"—thus he argues. To remove this misconception, the following is said: [The verse: "One should not injure living beings. [Commentary: In this context, when a desire for injury arises due to the persistence of enmity, and someone wishes to express it, that [prohibition] is for the sake of forbidding that particular object. However, where wealth and pleasure are sought through the injury of someone, there is no fault of injury. To dispel such an error, this is stated: "But one should perform the prescribed acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity for the sake of heaven. This means that while the aforementioned injury is prohibited, the injury performed for the sake of heaven is not prohibited. Furthermore, regarding the statement "one should not injure living beings," if someone were to argue that this is a general prohibition against all injury, and that therefore even the injury required for the sake of heaven would be forbidden, then to refute that, it is said: "But one should perform the prescribed acts... This shows that the injury involved in performing sacrifices and the like is not prohibited. Moreover, since the term "living beings" (*bhūta*) is used here, it follows that injury to non-living things is not prohibited. For example, when one says, "Bring the cow," if someone objects, "No, you should bring the horse," and another replies, "I am bringing the cow, not the horse," the word "cow" is understood to exclude the horse. Similarly, the word "living beings" excludes non-living things. Thus, the injury to non-living things is not prohibited. Furthermore, if the injury to living beings were prohibited without exception, then the injunction to perform sacrifices and the like would be meaningless. Therefore, it is established that injury for the sake of heaven is not prohibited. Alternatively, the meaning may be explained as follows: the injury to living beings that occurs during the performance of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited, whereas other injuries are prohibited. Why? Because the injury occurring in the context of sacrifices and the like is for the sake of heaven, and since heaven is a desirable goal, its cause—the injury—is not prohibited. On the other hand, other injuries are not for the sake of heaven, and thus they are prohibited. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is enjoined by scripture (*śruti*). Since it is enjoined by scripture, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are not enjoined by scripture. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is accompanied by a desire for heaven. Since it is accompanied by a desire for heaven, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are not accompanied by a desire for heaven. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is connected with a scriptural injunction. Since it is connected with a scriptural injunction, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are not connected with a scriptural injunction. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) to the primary act. Since it is a subordinate factor, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are not subordinate factors. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*). Since it is a necessary concomitant, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are not necessary concomitants. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a duty (*dharma*). Since it is a duty, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are not duties. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a means to achieve heaven. Since it is a means to achieve heaven, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are not means to achieve heaven. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of merit (*puṇya*). Since it is a cause of merit, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of demerit (*pāpa*). Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of liberation (*mokṣa*). Since it is a cause of liberation, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of bondage. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the cessation of suffering. Since it is a cause of the cessation of suffering, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the increase of suffering. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of the self. Since it is a cause of the attainment of the self, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the obscuration of the self. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the purification of the self. Since it is a cause of the purification of the self, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the defilement of the self. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the realization of the truth. Since it is a cause of the realization of the truth, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the obscuration of the truth. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of knowledge. Since it is a cause of the attainment of knowledge, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the destruction of knowledge. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of power. Since it is a cause of the attainment of power, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the loss of power. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of sovereignty. Since it is a cause of the attainment of sovereignty, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the loss of sovereignty. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of bliss. Since it is a cause of the attainment of bliss, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the attainment of misery. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of peace. Since it is a cause of the attainment of peace, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the attainment of agitation. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of contentment. Since it is a cause of the attainment of contentment, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the attainment of discontent. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of virtue. Since it is a cause of the attainment of virtue, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the attainment of vice. Alternatively, the injury to living beings that occurs in the context of sacrifices and the like is not prohibited because it is a cause of the attainment of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). Since it is a cause of the attainment of the highest good, it is not prohibited. Other injuries, however, are prohibited because they are causes of the

One should abandon—that is, avoid—those objects of wealth and desire where there is a conflict with *dharma*. Having thus stated that *dharma* is stronger than all else, he speaks of its necessity to be avoided even in certain instances: "and even a *dharma* that results in unhappiness. *Udarka* means the subsequent time; that whose result is unhappy—for example, when one gives away all one's possessions [thinking], "This man is righteous and of great merit," or when one performs a ritual bath at riverbanks or secluded spots where many common people are watching, such that the bath becomes merely for show, performed out of a desire for public acclaim while seeking to acquire merit. Or, for instance, giving gifts to the "crane-monks" (*tīrthakāka*); though the gift is technically a *dharma*, it differs from true giving because its purpose is merely to produce the reputation of being a donor. Alternatively, whatever the world censures due to its blameworthiness—for example, the killing of a cow which is not to be killed, or the eating of its meat—that is more reprehensible in the world than the killing of other animals. Furthermore, this prohibition is based on visible grounds, like the prohibition against touching a snake. If common people, lacking knowledge, were to think "this act has been enjoined" and thus proclaim the unrighteousness of the sacrificer, then, because of their numbers, even the learned, failing to understand the basis of the tradition, might likewise avoid him. Thus it is said: "When the king is righteous... (MDh 11.10).

This has been stated and explained by the predecessors; thus it is understood that it is not right for a direct Vedic injunction (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) to be sublated by a Smṛti rule. However, this is a more appropriate example: the duty of officiating at sacrifices (*niyoga-dharma*), though enjoined by Smṛti, is not performed because it is censured by the world. Likewise, when someone out of compassion supports a young woman who has no protector, if there is apprehension of public censure—thinking, "He finds her desirable precisely because she is a woman"—that is a duty censured by the world. (4.176)
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor crooked; one should likewise not be fickle with speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others. (4.177)

"Fickle with hands and feet": the compound is formed by a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) from Pāṇini 2.1.30, which prescribes the use of the third case. Fickleness consists in grasping and moving objects even when they are not useful for the hand; fickleness of the eyes consists in gazing at another's wife, looking at paintings, and so forth; and one must not form the intention to perform actions intended to harm others. (4.177)
By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that way, he does not come to harm. (4.178)

Whatever practice has been performed by one's father and others, with whom affection was cultivated, with whom the marriage of daughters and so forth was contracted, and whichever Vedic branch (*śākhā*) was studied—that very path is to be followed. By acting thus, one does not come to harm, is not oppressed, and is not censured in the world.

Others, however, who are ignorant, regard this as a mere expedient among human duties such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the like—like a royal drum for barbarians and others. But rites such as the *agnihotra* depend solely upon one's own conviction.

On this point, they raise an objection: if a practice performed by one's father and others is without foundation, how can it possess the nature of *dharma*? Or, if there is a foundation, that will apply to the son as well; what then is the purpose of mentioning "the father and others"?
This is answered by stating that this is an instruction intended for those who are ignorant and do not know the foundation.

Others, however, say that where doubt does not cease even when investigating with great care, and where the meaning of the sentence can be understood in two ways, then the path practiced by one's father and others should be followed.
This too must be considered: there is no such thing as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is eternally doubtful. For a statement must necessarily be fixed upon a single meaning.
Regarding the various options for actions, one should follow the practice performed by one's father and others, because they have practiced it;

thus he says "the path of the virtuous" (*satāṃ mārgam*). If some improper act was previously performed by one's father, grandfather, or others in some way, that is not to be resorted to; therefore he says "the path of the virtuous. (4.178)

[One should not eat] with officiating priests, family priests, and teachers; with maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; with children, the elderly, and the sick; and with physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and blood relations. (4.179)
One should not engage in dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brothers, sons, wife, daughters, or the group of servants. (4.180)

"One should not act [thus]" is to be connected with each [term]. "Dependents" refers to those who have come for refuge and those who live off one's support. "Physicians" means the learned or medical practitioners. "Kinsmen" (jñāti) refers to those on the father’s side. "Relations" (saṃbandhin) refers to those by marriage. "Relatives" (bāndhava) refers to those on the mother’s side, such as the daughter of one’s maternal aunt and so forth. "Female relatives" (jāmī) refers to sisters and female residents of the household. "Dispute" means opposition, hostile behavior, or verbal quarreling. One should not engage in these with them. (4.179–80)
By abandoning disputes concerning these, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds. (4.181)

Regarding the sinful connection that arises from these disputes being engaged in, the one who does not perform them has no such connection. It is said that "he is liberated from all sins. Furthermore, the statement that "by conquering and disregarding these, he conquers and appropriates all worlds" is an *arthavāda* (a commendatory exaggeration). 4.181.
The teacher is the lord in the world of Brahmā; the father is the master in the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord in the world of Indra; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods. (4.182)

The teacher is the lord and master of the world of Brahmā; when he is satisfied, the world of Brahmā is attained. Therefore, by virtue of his qualities, he is called the Lord of the World of Brahmā. In the world of Prajāpati, the father is the master. (4.182)

Sisters-in-law are the kinsmen of the Apsarases in their world; maternal uncles and mothers are the kinsmen of the Viśvedevas in their world; and maternal aunts and maternal uncles are the kinsmen of the Waters in their world and of the Earth in hers. (4.183)
The young, the old, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as lords over space (ākāśa).
An elder brother is equal to a father; a wife and son are one's own body. (4.184)
A wife and a son are one's own body, one's very own physical frame; (4.184) One's own shadow, the group of servants, and a daughter are even more wretched.
Therefore, when insulted by these, one should always endure it without feverish agitation. (4.185)

The circle of servants is one's own shadow. Just as a shadow is constantly following and is not an object of anger, so too is the circle of servants. One should endure—that is, be patient—when reviled by these aforementioned harsh words, dragged about, or provoked to anger. "Free from fever" (*asaṃjvara*) means that fever is absent; and by the absence of fever, the lack of agitation in the mind is indicated. For just as there is agitation of the mind for one who is feverish, so it is for one who is angry. Alternatively, there is another reading: *asaṃjvaraḥ*. *Saṃjvara* means "torment" (*saṃtāpa*; Amarakośa 1.1.60); this is negated by the particle *nañ*. (4.185)
Even if one is capable of accepting gifts, one should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, one's spiritual luster (brāhmaṃ tejaḥ) is quickly extinguished. (4.186)

That which is obtained from another person prompted by an unseen motive (*adṛṣṭa*) is a gift (*pratigraha*). In that regard, even if one is capable and able, one should avoid the occasion for its repeated occurrence. Capability consists in the perfection of Vedic learning, study, and character, as well as knowledge of the rules regarding the object of the gift. Although this has already been stated in the verse, "Therefore, the ignorant man should fear" (MDh 4.191), it is reiterated here for the sake of what follows. 4.186.
He shows this:
"Without knowing the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of material gifts, a wise man should not accept them, even if he is perishing from hunger. (4.187)

One should not accept gifts for the sake of enjoying sensual pleasures and the like without understanding [the proper purpose]. This is what is meant: one should accept gifts for the maintenance of one's own family and for the fulfillment of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), but not otherwise. Even if one is perishing from hunger, one should not accept gifts even if that leads to exhaustion. "Exhaustion" (*avasāda*) refers to the lack of nourishment for the body.
Alternatively, the connection may be made thus: "the lawful rule regarding substances in the acceptance [of gifts]."

What is that righteous procedure? Having understood the righteous purpose, one should [know] the mantras for receiving gifts and the deities of the substances, such as "gold for Agni, a cow for Rudra," and so forth. (4.187)
He states the excessive fault incurred by an ignorant man in accepting specific types of gifts:
"But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood. (4.188)

He is reduced to ashes like wood. Just as wood consumed by fire is turned to ashes, so too a Brahmin who is not endowed with knowledge is reduced to ashes when he accepts these objects, such as gold and the like. 4.188.
Gold and food increase life; land and a cow nourish the body;
a horse [increases] the eyesight, clothing the skin, ghee the vital luster, and sesame seeds progeny. (4.189)

The earth (*bhūḥ*) and the cow (*gauḥ*) burn (*oṣataḥ*) the body (*tanum*); *śarīram* is a synonym for *tanum*. Gold (*hiraṇyam*) burns (*oṣati*) life (*āyuḥ*), with the case ending changed; thus, "burning" is to be supplied as the verb. In the same way, the verb must be supplied in the phrases "the horse [burns] the eye" (*aśvaś cakṣuḥ*), and so forth. (4.189)
But that twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study the Vedas, and who delights in accepting gifts, sinks along with him in the water as if using a stone for a raft. 4.190.

He who possesses no austerity (*tapas*), and who, not being a student, does not study—by "study," the aforementioned state of learning (*vidvattā*) is indicated; for both learning and austerity together constitute the grounds for the entitlement to receive gifts. One who has fallen away from both qualities, yet still desires to accept gifts, sinks down—that is, goes downward—along with him. With whom? Since no other person is specified and the giver is present, it is understood that he sinks along with the giver. The recipient relies upon such a person as one would rely on a raft for his own rescue. But he who is such an unworthy vessel leads both the giver and himself downward, just like a stone-raft in water. A raft made of stone is a "stone-raft" (*aśmaplava*). That by which one crosses to the further shore is a raft, such as a boat and so forth. In this regard, just as one who has boarded a stone for the purpose of crossing a river sinks in the water and goes down along with the stone-raft, so too both the giver to the Brahmin and the Brahmin who accepts from him go to hell. (4.190)
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear whatever gift he might receive; for even by means of a very small one, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud. (4.191)

Therefore, out of fear of hell, the ignorant fool should be afraid of accepting gifts; that is to say, he should tremble and not accept them. Let alone gold and other such substances—even by accepting a small amount of worthless material such as tin or lead, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in a mire. (4.191)

A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who observes the "vow of a cat," nor to one who observes the "vow of a heron," nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Vedas. (4.192)

The duty of the recipient has been stated; now the duty of the giver is being declared. By the word "even" (*api*), the giving of all things is prohibited. Where even water is not permitted to anyone, that too must not be given to these [persons]; how much less so other substances? This is a prohibition against giving other substances by way of hyperbolic expression (*atiśayokti*). However, there is no prohibition regarding water, because water is for the sake of all purposes. But is it not already stated: "One should not honor those who act like cats (*baiḍālavratika*) even with mere words"? (MDh 4.30).

True. In that context, worship was forbidden; here, however, it is the giving of gifts. And that refers to wealth, not anything else. In this way, the double prohibition becomes meaningful. Accordingly, he will state later: "Even wealth acquired according to the rule... (MDh 4.193). Therefore, the giving of food with contempt to heretics and the like is not prohibited.

Regarding this, someone says: "Even though it is heard [in the text] that 'to one who does not know the Veda' (*avedavid*), it should nevertheless be understood as 'one who has not studied it' (*anadhīyāna*). For instance, giving to those who merely study the Veda has been prescribed; however, it is not proper to give for the sake of desire (*kāmya*) to those who are hypocritical (*dāmbhika*). He should be asked this: "Where, then, is giving prescribed for one who merely studies the Veda but lacks knowledge?
If he replies, "In the passage: 'Gifts are to be given only to a *śrotriya*'" (MDh 3.118).
