However, in the case of the phrase "to the most worthy of Arhatship" (MDh 3.118), since [the recipient] has not yet attained that status, there is no entitlement [to the gift] without knowledge. Furthermore, other sentences within the same context, such as "the sacrificial fee for the learned man" (MDh 3.133), certainly exist. Therefore, by considering those [texts] and through the application of both qualifiers, it is understood that [the gift] must be given [only to one who possesses both qualities]. Consequently, we see no reason to abandon the meaning explicitly stated in the scripture (*śruta*). As for the claim that parity is improper—what indeed is improper regarding a matter understood through the authority of the verbal testimony?

One who acts according to the "vow of a cat" is a *baiḍālavratika*. One who possesses the vow of herons is a *bakavratika*. When the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed, the locative case is used; when the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is intended to be expressed, the dative case is appropriate. [4.192]
For wealth, even if acquired according to the rules, when given to these three types of persons, leads to misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world. (4.193)

This implies that the giving of food is not prohibited by the acceptance of wealth. Even if acquired according to rule—meaning through such means as receiving gifts from the virtuous or buying—as permitted by the scriptures, such a gift results in harm for both the giver and the receiver in the next world. (4.193)
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks, so too do the ignorant donor and recipient sink to the depths. 4.194

*Auṣala* and *āśmana* [refer to those made of stone]. A *plava* is a boat or similar vessel for crossing water; he who crosses by means of it, or proceeds to cross, sinks beneath the water—that is, he is submerged. In this same way, both the ignorant giver and the recipient [sink]. Regarding the word *pratīcchaka*: since one performs the act of receiving (*pratīcchā*), one should form the derivative with the suffix *ṇvul* after applying the causative marker *ṇic*. There is an alternative reading, *pratīpsaka*; in that case, the suffix *ṇvul* is added to the root *āp* (to obtain) following the desiderative suffix *san*. However, the meaning of both terms is exactly the same. (4.194)
One who carries the banner of Dharma while being always greedy, hypocritical, and a deceiver of the world;
such a person is to be known as one who observes the "cat-vow," being violent and a deceiver of all. (4.195)

These two words are employed by way of figurative designation (*upacāra*). And among the various grounds for figurative designation, that very one which serves as the cause for their application is possible here; it is intended for the purpose of establishing the object of the restriction and the negation.

"Dharma" is like a banner (*dhvaja*). Because *vyāghra* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa*, a compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.56. Sometimes it is a *karmadhāraya* for the sake of terms such as *sarvadhaṇa*. From that, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is added in the sense of "one who has this. He who performs dharma solely for the sake of reputation, and not out of devotion to the scriptures, is described in this way. He is one who performs dharma only where people can see him and causes it to be proclaimed by his own men, thinking: "By becoming famous for my righteousness, I shall obtain gifts and other benefits."

He is greedy, envious, and miserly. He deceives and cheats the world; thus he is a "deceiver of the world" (*lokadambhaka*). He acts with guile; thus he is a "guileful one" (*chādmika*). *Chadma* means pretense or artifice. While appearing righteous in public, he steals what was entrusted to him in private; he makes public what should remain secret. It is observed that someone, having been inspired by trust because of the thought, "This man is righteous; what is said in his presence will not go elsewhere," speaks to him, only to find that what was meant to be kept secret was spoken right to his very face—this is malice toward others (*paradroha*). Furthermore, being a detractor who seeks to deceive everyone, he cannot tolerate the virtues of others. Such a person is to be known as a "cat-vowed one" (*baiḍālavratika*). [The term] *abhisaṃdhaka* means "one who deceives" (*abhisaṃdhatte*). The suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.136 (*ātaś copasargaḥ*). Then, another *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe ka*). Thus, *sarveṣām abhisaṃdhakaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Some recite a verse on this point:
"He whose banner of righteousness is always raised high like the banner of the gods,
yet whose sins are concealed— that is called the 'cat-vow' (baiḍāla-vrata)."

This very point is stated in brief: one who is connected with even a single such quality should be known as a "cat-like hypocrite" (*baiḍālavratika*). From this very verse, it is inferred in this way: since no specific distinction is heard regarding the phrase "hidden sins," and because all of these are indeed sins, the Teacher has instructed his disciples in both ways.

Some have been taught this verse, while others have been taught the previous one; both are authoritative. Therefore, although in the statement “Devadatta has armlets, earrings, broad shoulders, and a broad chest” the status of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is understood to belong to the collection as a whole, nevertheless, in this context, these are each individual defining characteristics. (4.195)
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own self-interest, crafty, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow. (4.196)

The characteristics of the "cat-vow" (*bakavrata*) are looking downward; that is, having a lowly gaze. A "lowly" person is one who is wretched. Such a person is always occupied with some task, somehow obtains something from somewhere, and even accepts it from a base person. "Niṣkṛti" means cruelty; one who acts with that, being dominated by it, is a *naiṣkṛtika*, one who speaks improperly. One who is falsely humble (*alīkavinīta*) adopts courtesy and modesty, yet acts as an obstacle to what needs to be done. A cat feigns sleep when desiring to seize its prey. In this way, one who practices dharma with deceit is called a "follower of the cat-vow" (*baiḍālavratika*).

The same applies to one who practices the "heron-vow" (*bakavrata*). For herons, while seizing fish, display contempt for other aquatic creatures; yet, they possess nothing but the intent to catch fish. By the word *vrata*, an action habitually practiced is meant. Thus, the non-redundancy of the terms has been demonstrated. Furthermore, there may be no fault here because it is a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); for a defining characteristic is that which is not [already] known. Through repeated mention, the meaning becomes easy to grasp.
But what, then, is the difference between one who follows the "cat-vow" (*baiḍālavratika*) and one who follows the "heron-vow"?

It is said: This one is intent on accomplishing his own purpose and does not obstruct the work of another; the former, however, out of envy, destroys the work of another even when his own purpose has not been achieved. (4.196)
Those Brahmins who observe the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed.
This verse has been explained by its own words. 4.197.
One should not perform a vow after committing a sin under the pretext of dharma;
for by concealing one's sin with a vow, one practices deception upon women and Śūdras. (4.198)

Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow as an expiation while merely invoking the name of dharma to proclaim it in the world, saying: "I perform this vow for the sake of dharma; it is not for the purpose of expiation. In reality, however, he performs it solely for the sake of expiation. This must not be done. One should not deceive women or Śūdras by concealing or denying the sin through that vow. Expiation should be performed openly, except in cases where it is secret. (4.198)
Such Brahmins, both in this world and after death, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda; and any vow performed through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas. (4.199)

In this world, by the very nature of things (*padārtha-svābhāvyena*), whatever result arises from an action performed even with another objective in mind, that indeed comes to pass. For instance, one engaged in obeying a teacher's command does so thinking, "I am carrying out the teacher’s word for the sake of merit (*dharma*)," and not for the sake of sensual desire; yet, due to the inherent nature of the matter (*artha-svābhāvyāt*), it nevertheless produces sensual desire.

Thus, someone might think: "Vows are for the purpose of removing evil; even when performed with another intention, they do not abandon their inherent nature. Therefore, this expiation of mine will serve both purposes: I shall become renowned in the world as an ascetic, and my evil will be removed. It is for the sake of turning back such a person who possesses this mindset that the following is undertaken.

In that case, this vow, though performed and observed under a pretext, goes to the Rākṣasas; it becomes fruitless, meaning it does not remove sin. Not only is there a failure to accomplish the purpose, but such Brahmins who practice the vow are censured and condemned by those who discourse on the Veda—by the learned who know the authority of the Vedas. (4.199)
He who, being without the marks, subsists by the livelihood of one wearing the marks, takes upon himself the sin of those who bear the marks and is born in the womb of an animal. (4.200)

The wearing of emblems (*liṅga*) pertains to each stage of life (*āśrama*). For example: the student (*brahmacārin*) wears a girdle and so forth; the householder (*gṛhastha*) carries a bamboo staff, earrings, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and so on; the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) wears skins, rags, matted hair (*jaṭā*), and so forth; and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) wears saffron-colored garments, a staff, and so on. He who, though not belonging to any stage of life, wanders through the world for the sake of alms and subsists upon a livelihood by means of such a dress, takes upon himself the sin of those who bear these emblems and satisfies their debt. [As a result], he is born in the womb of an animal—namely, among animals such as dogs, jackals, and the like.

Nor should it be suspected here that the sin of those who bear the marks [of a religious order] departs from them and migrates into that [person]; such a thing is impossible. It is understood that wearing the external marks of another [order] is not to be done; even though there is no explicit prohibition, this is understood from the deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) alone. 4.200.
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others; for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the person who constructed the reservoir. (4.201)

A *nipāna* is a reservoir of water from which one drinks or by which one approaches; it includes ponds, wells, tanks, and the like. One should never bathe in such a reservoir belonging to another that has been constructed for the other's own benefit and not relinquished for universal use. All bathing—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*) due to contact with *caṇḍālas* and others, or for the purpose of removing sweat—is prohibited there. Regarding the transgression of this rule, he states the fault: one becomes tainted—that is, connected—with some portion or share of whatever evil deed belongs to the maker of that reservoir. This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serving as a supplement to the prohibition. (4.201)
One who enjoys his vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, and houses when they have not been given shall incur one-fourth of the sin. (4.202)
One who makes use of vehicles and other items belonging to another that have not been given shall incur a fourth part—that is, one-quarter—of the sin pertaining to that owner.
Regarding this, someone says: "Because of the word 'not given,' even things prepared for the sake of all [the community] must not be used.

That is incorrect, because the context concerns what belongs to another (*parakīya*). Nor are those things [prepared for the community] "belonging to another," for they have been properly relinquished. Furthermore, it has already been explained previously that the mention of "a fourth part" is not intended to be restrictive. (4.202)
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs. (4.203)

All rivers are "dug by the gods" (*devakhāta*). Therefore, since it is impossible for them to be both [dug by gods and dug by humans], that characteristic mark must be recited as being expressed by the term "dug by the gods. For tanks and the like may be both dug by the gods and dug by humans; yet they are not actually dug by the gods. Rather, their greatness is indicated solely by the fact that their makers are not remembered. (4.203)

A wise person should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not the observances (niyamas) exclusively; for one who fails to perform the restraints while devoting oneself solely to the observances falls. (4.204)

The *yamas* are of the nature of prohibitions, such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," "Liquor must not be drunk," and so forth. The *niyamas* are of the nature of observances, such as "One should always recite the Veda alone" (MDh 4.147), and so forth. [The verse] does not mean that one should never practice the *niyamas*; rather, it means that the *yamas* are more obligatory than the *niyamas*. Thus he says: "By failing to perform the *yamas*, one falls. When there is a lapse in the *yamas*, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, one falls; because of that fallen state, one is no longer entitled to perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other rites. But it is not so in the case of a lapse in the *niyamas*. And thus is the traditional teaching of the learned (*śiṣṭas*):
"One who possesses the observances (*niyama*) but is not devoted to the restraints (*yama*) falls; however, one who possesses the restraints but is lazy regarding the observances does not perish.

Without first examining the observances with his intellect, he should not apply his mind excessively to those consisting mostly of restraints. Thus it is for those whose *yamas* and *niyamas* are merely technical designations.
Non-violence, truthful speech, celibacy, freedom from guile,
and non-stealing— these five are both the restraints (yamas) and the observances (vratas).
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in diet,
and vigilance— these are the five observances (niyamas) and the minor vows (upavratas).

The relative gravity or lightness of these [transgressions] is also established by this verse. Therefore, by this [verse], neither the practice of the *yamas* nor the non-practice of the *niyamas* is being enjoined, because both are prescribed by those [other] scriptures. (4.204)
The section on religious observances (*vrata*) was concluded by the preceding verse. Now, the section concerning prohibitions begins:

A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), nor at one performed by a priest who officiates for an entire village (*grāmayājika*), nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch (*klība*). (4.205)

In this context, first of all, eating food obtained from just anyone out of mere desire is prohibited. A Brāhmaṇa should not eat at a sacrifice that has been commenced by one who is not an *śrotriya*—that is, one who has not studied the Veda—or at one commenced by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are not *śrotriyas*. Nor should he eat where a village-priest (*grāmayājī*, one who performs sacrifices for an entire village) offers oblations, nor where a woman performs the *homa*. For in the *Chāndogya*, the authors of the Gṛhya-smṛtis have prescribed the *agnihotra-homa* for women; therefore, seeing this [practice], he prohibits it.

Alternatively, this prohibition applies to that sacrifice where the woman is the principal figure, the husband is afflicted by defects such as poverty, and the woman is arrogant due to her dowry and the influence of her kinsmen.
A *klība* is a eunuch. (4.205)
This is offensive to the virtuous wherein these people offer oblations;
it is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it. (4.206)

This is an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) to the preceding prohibitory rule. "Unseemly" means unworthy of the virtuous or the refined. For where they offer oblations and perform sacrifice, that place is "contrary to the gods," meaning adverse to them. Therefore, one should avoid going to such a place. (4.206)
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor that which is infested with hair or insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched by a foot. (4.207)

As long as these [faults] such as intoxication persist in them, so long is their food unfit to be eaten. Others consider it to be a matter of frequency: the food of one who becomes intoxicated by liquor through frequent consumption—that is, a drunkard—should not be eaten. Likewise, the food of one for whom anger predominates, of one who is exceedingly prone to wrath, and generally of one who is sickly, afflicted by disease or illness.

[Food] that has been defiled by hair or insects, or rendered impure through contact—wherein some insects cause defilement when dead, such as flies and house-lizards, while others cause it even while alive; the mention of "insects" (kīṭa) is intended to indicate small creatures, including worms and moths; the mention of "hair" (keśa) [includes] nails, body hair, and impurities such as eye-secretions, according to established custom; [food] touched intentionally with the foot out of desire—there is no fault, however, if it was done through negligence. (4.207)
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog [is unfit to be eaten]. (4.208)

A *bhrūṇahan* is a slayer of a Brahmin; by him [the food] has been looked at—that is, scrutinized. This is merely an illustration [of the rule]; it applies to other outcastes (*pātakin*) as well. However, there is a prohibition regarding that which has been touched by outcastes. Indeed, the prohibition for that which has been touched by them is already established by the very injunction for bathing. A *udakyā* is a woman in her menses; there is a prohibition for that which has been touched by her, but not for that which has been looked at. Now, one might object: since the author will state later that even one who touches such a person must bathe, impurity is thereby established by that alone; so how could there be any possibility of eating that which has been touched by such a person?

It is said: that food should be eaten after being washed. Alternatively, it has been stated that the mention of the "fœticide" (*bhrūṇahan*) is for the purpose of illustration. In this regard, someone might think that it is for the purpose of illustrating those mentioned in the verse concerning the *divākīrti* (MDh 5.84). Consequently, there would also be a prohibition against food looked upon by a woman in her courses (*udakyā*). By this, the case of food touched by a dog is explained. Therefore, it was stated [that the mention of the fœticide] is for the purpose of illustrating others, such as outcasts (*patita*). Thus, in this context, the mention of "outcasts, women who have recently given birth," and so forth, is appropriate. The mention of the woman in her courses is for the purpose of indicating the woman who has recently given birth.

"By a winged creature": a winged creature is a bird; and according to common usage, this refers to carnivorous ones such as vultures, crows, and the like, but not to swans and similar species. (4.208)
Food smelled by a cow, and especially food [announced] by proclamation; the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned—[these one should avoid]. (4.209)

*Ghuṣṭānna* is that which is given after being publicly announced to some petitioner who has not been invited, without specifying particular recipients such as those residing in a monastery (*maṭha*) or those attending a sacrificial session (*sattra*). Alternatively, it refers to food that is given to one person after having promised it to another. For this verbal root is taught in the sense of "accepting" or "taking possession. In the absence of that [specific intention], they record an exception [to the prohibition] regarding eating at sacrifices, weddings, and so forth, when one is not formally invited.

And this [term] *gaṇa* denotes a collective; therefore, among brothers who have not divided their property, there is no designation as a *gaṇa*. This is because of the statement: "Among brothers who have not divided, one single duty prevails" (MDh 9.215). And since that single duty for them is precisely the performance of rites such as hospitality, it is shown in the ninth book: "The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety" (MDh 9.105). This indicates that his entitlement extends to those duties which must necessarily be performed. There is also a prohibition against others belonging to that group, even if they are common property. A *gaṇikā* is a courtesan. *Jugupsitaṃ* means censured. By a "learned man" (*viduṣā*) is meant one who knows the meaning of the Vedas. Even edible things, such as lotus stalks (*bisakhalyādi*), [are forbidden]. 4.209.
The food of a thief and a singer, of a carpenter and a usurer, of one who has been consecrated for sacrifice, of a miser, and of one who is bound or fettered—[these are not to be eaten]. (4.210)

A singer is one who lives by means of singing; however, for others, singing such as that of the *aparāntaka* style and so forth is indeed prescribed. A miser is one who is stingy. The distinction between one who is bound and one with fetters is this: the former is restrained merely by word, while the latter is constrained by ropes and iron shackles. Others read the text as "and of one who is clear" (*viśadasya ca*), and they explain that "clear" (*viśada*) refers to what is painful (*kaṣṭa*). 4.210.

[One should avoid] the food of one who has been accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite; likewise, food that is fermented, stale, and the leavings of a Śūdra. (4.211)
A *puṃścalī* is any woman who engages in sexual relations with anyone at all.
But is it not the case that the food of a courtesan (*gaṇikā*) is already forbidden?
This is not so; for one is a courtesan and the other is a *puṃścalī*. A courtesan lives by the profession of a prostitute, whereas a *puṃścalī* is merely one whose senses are unsteady.

A hypocrite is one who practices religion with deceit, such as those who follow the "cat-vow" (*baiḍālavratika*) and others. The eating of the leavings of a Śūdra is forbidden specifically for the sake of particular penances, since the eating of leavings is forbidden for everyone. Others, however, say that "the leavings of a Śūdra" refers to food remaining in the cooking vessel (*sthālīstha*), whereas "leavings" (*ucchiṣṭa*) means what remains after a Śūdra has eaten. There is, however, an alternative reading: "likewise the leavings of one who is not a Guru. "Leavings" (*ucchiṣṭa*) is defined as that which becomes impure through contact with another, as well as what is discarded after being eaten. For if it were one's own [food] that had not been eaten or discarded, there would only be the eating of a single mouthful. Nor is it the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) that, having eaten food once given, one should sip water again and eat what is taken from another vessel. Thus, one should not eat food in that manner. Likewise, there is a prohibition against other intervening actions, such as rising from the seat. Therefore, there is no fault in touching [the food] before sipping water until satiety; but as for eating together (*sahabhojana*), even though there is contact with another, it is not "eating leavings" because it is a different matter. In this context, what is left over by a father is eaten together with sons and others. Accordingly, Āpastamba and others, by mentioning the region, censure "eating together with one who is uninitiated" (*anupanīta*) as a general rule (cf. BDh 1.2.3), but not with one who is initiated. Under this view, however, the prohibition applies to eating with those of a different caste (*vijātīya*); another form of intervention must be assumed. But what is discarded after being eaten is called "leavings" (*ucchiṣṭa*) due to its connection with the root meaning (*dhātvartha*), even if it belongs to another. (4.211)
The food of a physician, of a hunter, of a cruel person, or of one who eats leavings;
the food of a fierce man, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and that which has been tasted by another before being served—these must not be eaten for ten days after the birth. (4.212)

A specific distinction is heard in another *Smṛti*: "The *śalya* is one who lives by dancing. A *mṛgayu* is a deer-hunter; he is one who kills deer for the sake of sport or for the purpose of selling meat. A *krūra* is one of a cruel and crooked nature, difficult to propitiate. An *ucchiṣṭabhojī* is one who eats forbidden leavings. An *ugra* is a particular caste; the use of this term is seen in the Veda: "Like the fierce *madhyamaśīr*" (*Ṛgveda* 10.97.12). There is no other prohibition against him, nor is it heard in the manner of a demonstration of fault; rather, the prohibition is derived from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "The food of a king takes away one's luster" (*Mānava Dharma Śāstra* 4.218).

*Śūtikānna* (the food of a woman who has recently given birth) refers to that which is prepared for the sake of the *śūtikā* by members of her own family; even such food is unfit to be eaten. It is *anādya* (not to be consumed) during the *anirdaśa* period—that is, for ten days. Therefore, although for Kṣatriyas and others the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts beyond ten days, nevertheless, [their food] must not be eaten for those ten days. There is an alternative reading, *sūtakānnam*; by the word *sūtaka*, the persons possessing that status are indicated. Those in whose family there is *sūtaka* are such that their food is not to be eaten for ten days. This prohibition applies to the view where the *sūtaka-āśauca* lasts for ten days for everyone. However, when the view is that the *sūtaka* belongs only to the parents, or specifically to the mother, then it is not to be eaten as long as the *āśauca* persists. The inclusion of the term *anirdaśa* is intended to indicate the cessation of the *āśauca*. Consequently, for Kṣatriyas and others, one whose period of *āśauca* lasts for a certain duration is unfit to provide food for that long. Although the text should have been read as *sūtakānnam anirdaśam*, it is separated by the word *paryācānta* due to metrical requirements.

Others, however, have explained the mention of "not ten days old" as being independent [of the preceding rule]. By the word *sūtaka*, the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) is indicated. "Not ten days old" refers to the milk of cows and other animals. Regarding "partially consumed": if one has begun eating and, for some reason, sips water for purification (*ācamana*) while the meal is unfinished, then what was left over after that sipping must not be eaten again. (4.212)

Food that has not been honored, meat not prepared for a purpose, the food of a woman who has no male relatives, the food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of an outcast, and food upon which someone has sneezed—[these one should avoid]. (4.213)

That which is given with contempt to one worthy of honor is "unhonored" (anarcita), but not so when given to a friend or the like. "Vain meat" (vṛthāmāṃsa) is that which is not a remnant from the worship of the gods and so forth, but is prepared for one's own sake. An "unvirgin woman" (avirā) is one who has neither a husband nor a son. An "enemy" (dviṣat) is an adversary. A "city" (nagarī) refers to the ruler of a city, even if he is not a king. "Sneezed upon" (avakṣuta) is that over which a sneeze has been made. (4.213)
The food of a slanderer and a liar, of one who sells the sacrifice, of an actor, of a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person—[these should not be eaten]. (4.214)

A slanderer (*piśuna*) is one who betrays a matter told in confidence, or one who speaks of another's faults behind their back. A liar (*anṛtī*) is one who gives false testimony. A seller of sacrifices (*kratuvikrayaka*) is one who, having performed a sacrifice (*kratu*), sells it—giving its fruit to another for a price by saying, "Let my fruit of the sacrifice be yours. Although in the ultimate sense there is no selling of a sacrifice, nevertheless, this is a prohibition against one whose livelihood is of such a kind, or whose activity proceeds through the deception of others. A *śailūṣa* is an actor; according to others, it refers to one who makes a living from his wife. A tailor (*tunnavāya*) is a seamster. An ungrateful person (*kṛtaghna*) is one who destroys a benefit received; rather, he engages in harming the benefactor, even though he is capable of returning the favor. (4.214)
Of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player, a goldsmith, a bamboo-worker, and likewise a seller of weapons; 4.215.

A *karmāra* is an iron-smelter. A *niṣāda* will be mentioned in the tenth [chapter]. A *raṅgāvataraka* is one other than actors or singers, such as a wrestler and the like; or alternatively, one who attends the stage out of curiosity. A *veṇa* is one who lives by playing musical instruments. A *śastravikrayin* is a seller of weapons, whether they be finished products such as swords or unfinished ones such as iron bars. (4.215)
[One must not eat the food] of dog-keepers, of liquor-sellers, of a washerman, of a dyer, of a cruel man, or of one in whose house a paramour resides. (4.216)

Those who keep dogs for the purpose of hunting and the like are "dog-keepers" (*śvavantaḥ*). "Liquor-sellers" (*śauṇḍikāḥ*) are those addicted to intoxicants or those who live by the trade of selling them. He who "cleanses cloth"—that is, washes it—is called by the name of a craftsman; he is a washerman (*rajakaḥ*), one who applies blue and other dyes to garments. A "cruel man" (*nṛśaṃsaḥ*) is one who praises or flatters men, who is well known in the world as a bard (*bandī*); or alternatively, a cruel man is one who is merciless. An "adulterer" (*upapati*) is a paramour; [the term refers to] one in whose house a paramour of his wife resides. (4.216)
Those who tolerate a paramour, those who are entirely conquered by women, food from one recently deceased (within ten days), and that which causes dissatisfaction—[these are forbidden]. (4.217)

The former [type of person] is one who does not know of his wife’s paramour; this one, however, knowing of it, tolerates it and does not exercise restraint over his wife. Nor is the food of that ignorant man—who has a paramour elsewhere than at home—to be eaten. Those who are "conquered by women" (strījitāḥ) are those for whom the wife alone in the house is the doer and the taker, and who themselves have no mastery over their own retinue; they are under her control in every respect. "Food of the deceased" (pretānna) refers to the period of impurity following death; those belonging to that family are persons whose food is not to be eaten. The mention of the "ten-day period" (anirdaśa) is intended to indicate the duration of time. While the previous mention of the "ten-day period" independently prohibited the food of those related by impurity without distinction, here the prohibition concerns the food provided for the deceased (pretānna), even in cases where there is no formal impurity, such as for friends or relatives who have begun the fourth-day śrāddha and so forth out of compassion. This is described in the *Rāmāyaṇa* and by other authors of Gṛhya-sūtras: "The tenth-day [rite], the ninth-day, the fourth-day śrāddha, the eighth-day," and so on. "Causing dissatisfaction" means that while eating it, there is no satisfaction of the mind. (4.217)
The food of a king takes away one's vital energy; the food of a Śūdra, one's spiritual luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's lifespan; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame. (4.218)

Now, he demonstrates the fruit of transgression: for those who eat the food of a king, their vital energy (*tejas*) is destroyed. This is to be understood in all cases. Words such as "goldsmith" and so forth denote those who live by specific crafts. Those who fashion gold for the sake of their livelihood are called "goldsmiths. The same should be understood regarding washermen and others. One who cuts or slices leather is a "leather-cutter" (*carmāvakartin*); this is a conventional designation for those who live by that work. In this context, for those whose prohibition was not previously stated but of whom only the fault is heard, a prohibition must be inferred from that very fact. (4.218)
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength; the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the worlds. (4.219)
Artisans such as cooks and the like perform occupations that are not excessively censured; this is their distinction from craftsmen. The "destruction of progeny" means its non-production. (4.219)
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; the food of a seller of weapons is filth. (4.220)
The food and meal of a physician is equal to pus; semen is the sense-faculty; and excrement is simply impurity. 4.220
Regarding those others who have been described in succession as persons whose food should not be eaten,
the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair.

Regarding those others who have been declared unfit to be fed in this section, their food consists of skin, bone, hair, and so forth; whatever fault there is in consuming their skin, that same fault applies to their food as well. (4.221)
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one must fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance. (4.222)

"Fasting for three days" means not eating for three days. "Unintentionally" means without prior awareness; however, if done intentionally, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance. And because it must be consistent with other *smṛti* texts, that *kṛcchra* is the *taptakṛcchra*. Regarding the consumption of semen, feces, or urine, the *taptakṛcchra* is prescribed: "If one drinks [these] unintentionally, milk, ghee, water, or air, each for three days, constitutes the *taptātikṛcchra*; thereafter, his purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is performed" (GDh 23.2). Furthermore, the statement regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) outside of its specific context is intended to demonstrate the gravity of the offense.

Because of the use of the genitive case in the phrase "of any one [of these]," they consider this expiation to apply only to food that is defiled by its ownership (*parigraha-dūṣita*), and not to that which is defiled by time, its own nature, or contact (*kāla-svabhāva-saṃsarga-dūṣita*). For there are four kinds of food unfit for consumption: that which is defiled by time, such as sour or stale food; that which is defiled by contact, such as food touched by intoxicants; that which is defiled by its own nature, such as garlic and the like; and that which is defiled by ownership, namely the food of those whose food is inherently unfit to be eaten.

To this it is replied: True, there are four kinds of food that should not be eaten. There is also the mention of the "sixth" [type of forbidden food]. However, if this expiation did not apply to sour gruel (*śukta*) and the like, then their inclusion in this specific context would be entirely purposeless; for in the fifth [chapter], there is no prohibition regarding those two. Therefore, their inclusion here is solely for the sake of prescribing expiation. If that is so, then for what purpose are they mentioned there?

We shall explain that very point there. Although it is said, "Eating forbidden or unfit food" (MDh 11.56), and "Having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten" (MDh 11.151), all of that will be determined in detail according to its divisions in the eleventh chapter. 4.222.
A learned twice-born man shall not eat cooked food from a Śūdra who does not perform śrāddha rites;
however, in the absence of other means of subsistence, he may accept from him raw grain sufficient for one night.

The consumption of food from a Śūdra is prohibited without distinction; now, its specific scope is stated: [it applies] to one who does not perform the *śrāddha*. But where was the Śūdra’s food prohibited?
In this passage: "And likewise the leavings of a Śūdra" (MDh 4.211).
But is it not the case that in that context, "the food of a Śūdra" refers specifically to his leavings?

We say: no. The connection there is as follows: one should not eat the food of a Śūdra, nor the leavings of anyone else. As for what was explained previously—that it represents the view of earlier authorities—we have also recorded that as their opinion.

By the word *śrāddha*, the performance of *pākayajña* and other rites prescribed for a Śūdra is indicated; thus, [the prohibition applies] to one who does not perform those rites. One should not eat cooked food belonging to anyone other than a virtuous Śūdra.

Or the reading may be *aśraddhinaḥ*, meaning "one who lacks faith. Thus, in the following verse, he declares the very primacy of faith: "of the generous man" (MDh 4.224). *Āmam* refers to unhusked grain, such as rice and the like; likewise, *ekarātrikam* means sufficient for one day, not more. 4.223.
Having deliberated upon both the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer, the gods ordained that their food be equal. 4.224

The Brahmin who is endowed with all virtues—since the term *śrotriya* is intended to illustrate [the possession of learning]—is one learned in the Vedas and devoted to the performance of prescribed duties. However, he may be a miser (*kadarya*), a wretched person who does not welcome friends, kinsmen, guests, or supplicants, and who makes no effort to give anything to anyone. Or, there may be another who is a usurer (*vārdhuṣi*), one of evil conduct who lives by lending at interest. On the other hand, there is the generous (*vadānya*) and noble man, full of faith, who rejoices when those come to his house and honors them with food and other offerings out of faith. Regarding the food of these two, the gods weighed them equally and established that they were the same. Even if one is virtuous and of good conduct, he is nonetheless marred by his miserliness; for it is said: "Greed [destroys] all virtues" (MBh 7.74.53). As for the other, even if he is faithful, he is nevertheless disparaged due to the defect of his profession. Having thus deliberated and reflected, the gods made this determination: "These two are equal. (4.224)
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal;
that which is purified by faith from a generous man is [true], while the other is slain by lack of faith. (4.225)

Prajāpati came to the gods and said, "Do not do this; such an unequal leveling is unjust. The gods asked, "Which of these two is superior? Prajāpati replied again: "The food of one who is generous and full of faith is pure and sanctified by that faith, even if it comes from a usurer; whereas other food, even that of a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), is defiled by his actions and is not commendable. This dialogue between the gods and Prajāpati is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). One must not eat the food of one who lacks faith, even if he possesses good qualities; however, the food of even a Śūdra may be eaten if it is offered with respect. (4.225)

With faith, one should constantly perform sacrifices and works of public utility without sloth; for when performed with faith and with wealth acquired through righteous means, those two become inexhaustible. 4.226

*Iṣṭa* is the sacrificial act and the like performed within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*). *Pūrta* is that which is performed elsewhere than that for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), such as acts of hospitality and so forth. These two must be performed with faith (*śraddhā*) and with "well-earned" wealth—that is, wealth acquired by means of learning, heroism, austerity, or [the marriage of] a daughter, and so on. In this way, they both become inexhaustible, yielding inexhaustible fruits. However, those [deeds] which are not performed with well-earned wealth do not yield inexhaustible fruits; yet, they are certainly not fruitless. For even by those [means], ownership of wealth is produced, and by that wealth, sacrifices and other rites must be performed. Furthermore, no prohibition against usury and the like is heard in the context of sacrifice and giving, such that it would constitute an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of them. Therefore, sacrifices and other rites must be performed with wealth acquired by whatever means are causes for the production of heaven (*svarga*). It is only the excellence or deficiency of the result that varies.

What, then, are those praiseworthy means of acquiring wealth? To this it is said: "Wealth acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, inheritance from a daughter, from a sacrificial priest, from a pupil, or by lineage—these seven kinds of wealth are pure; both [the giver and the receiver] are likewise [pure] in such cases. (NSm 1.41)

In this context, learning (*śruta*) and austerity (*tapas*) serve as the grounds for receiving gifts (*pratigraha*). Although there is only one act of receiving a gift, it is spoken of as distinct due to the difference in its causes. Furthermore, the qualities of the recipient (*pratigrāhya*) are to be understood therein by implication: if the giver is not extremely corrupt, then what has come from him is pure. By the words "sacrificer" (*yājya*) and "pupil" (*śiṣya*), officiating at sacrifices and teaching are respectively included. "Inherited" (*anvayāgata*) refers to property belonging to one's father, grandfather, and so forth. That which is obtained from the house of the father-in-law at the time of giving away a daughter in marriage belongs to the *kanyā* category. For a Kṣatriya, that acquired through valor (*śaurya*) belongs to the *anvaya* category. Both *kanyā* and *anvaya* are common to all [classes].

That which is obtained through usury, agriculture, trade, crafts, service, or following [another], as well as from one who has rendered assistance, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala). (NSm 1.42) Service consists of acting as a messenger or servant, being subject to employment at will, and following [another]. Following means being agreeable and compliant. Among these, usury, agriculture, and trade are not for the non-Vaiśya; however, they are indeed recommended for the Vaiśya. Service consisting of attendance upon the twice-born is specifically recommended for the Śūdra, whereas other forms of it are censured for him. By the use of the term "spotted," it is indicated that the fruit does not endure for long; rather, that fruit lasts only as long as one lives.
That which is acquired through gambling with dice, theft, distress, forgery, violence, or by means of fraud is declared to be "black" wealth. (NSm 1.43)

A *pārśvika* is one who stands by the side; he acquires wealth through bribes and the like. Having learned of someone’s acquisition of wealth, he says, “I will cause it to be given to you, but you must give me something,” and he who accepts this is a *pārśvika*. He is neither the doer nor the instigator; he stands on the sidelines and does not accept [the wealth] out of ignorance. For example, having accepted it, he remains as a guarantor (*pratibhū*) for a debtor. A *pratūpaka* is a hypocrite. A pretext (*vyāja*) consists of the sale of saffron and other items adulterated with safflower and the like. Affliction (*ārti*) is the causing of pain to others. Concealed taking is theft (*caurya*). Taking by force is violence (*sāhasa*).

But surely, through theft and force, ownership itself does not arise, because they are not enumerated among the causes of ownership: "One becomes an owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding" (GDh 10.39), as well as "Learning, craft, wages, service... (MDh 10.116), and likewise "Seven lawful ways of acquiring wealth" (MDh 10.115). If it is argued that these two [theft and force] are causes of ownership based on this very statement [regarding the seven lawful ways], then how is it said: "What is enjoyed by force is not digested"?

Some, however, say that this reading does not exist as "dyūtacauryārti," but rather as "vairyārti. That which is taken from an enemy at the time of making a treaty—when one says, "If you give me this much, then I shall make peace with you"—is given because of a lack of power. Furthermore, "sāhasa" (rashness) is not taking by force; rather, it is that which is acquired at the risk of one's life through sea voyages, or by the secret sale of goods prohibited by the king.

Others, however, think: ownership is not at all contradicted by forcible seizure, nor is the lapse of time (jaraṇa) contradicted by possession (bhoga). For while force exists first at the time of the initial seizure, even in the absence of force, possession through neglect establishes ownership there. But where there is forceful enjoyment from the very beginning throughout all time, it is said that the property "lapses" (jīryati). Therefore, both [possession and lapse] are not contradictory.

This is logical: that ownership does not arise through theft or force, because these are excluded from the classification of [legitimate] acquisitions, and because other authors of the Smṛtis do not include them among the causes of ownership. (4.226)

One should constantly practice the duty of giving—both that pertaining to sacrifices and that pertaining to public works—with a spirit of complete contentment, whenever a worthy recipient is encountered, according to one's ability. (4.227)

The "duty of giving" (*dānadharmah*) refers to things such as tanks and so forth; it is a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound). Alternatively, it means "that which is both giving and that duty. By the inclusion of the word "duty," he indicates the state of being governed by joy and other such factors. Furthermore, with a mind that is satisfied and serene, having encountered a worthy recipient (*pātra*), there is the giving of vows and so forth. Thus, [the merit] is both internal and external to the Vedic ritual. (4.227)
Whatever may be asked for should be given by one who is free from malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who can deliver one from all [suffering]. (4.228)

Whatever may be asked for, even if it be very little, it must be given when one is entreated. When there is doubt regarding whether a person is a worthy recipient (*pātra*) or not, and no certainty exists, something should be given, but not too much. Furthermore, if there is doubt due to the nature of the request, one should not give, thinking: "A worthy recipient might arise at some point; he will become such a one. What kind of recipient? One who rescues and protects [the giver] from all sins that cause a fall into hell. As it is said: "To a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas" (MDh 3.86); in that regard, this exception concerning a small amount of wealth is based on doubt. 4.228.
The giver of water attains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision. (4.229)

Satisfaction is freedom from the affliction of hunger and thirst; and that belongs to one who is wealthy and free from disease. By this, having abundant wealth and being healthy are stated to be the results. "Inexhaustible happiness": since no specific qualification is mentioned, the happiness resulting from the means [of enjoyment] is not what is intended; rather, "inexhaustible" means lasting as long as life. A giver of food includes both prepared food such as barley-meal (*saktu*) and boiled rice (*odana*), as well as raw materials such as unhusked rice (*taṇḍula*). The gift of a lamp should be given at a crossroads or in an assembly of Brahmins. (4.229)
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life; the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty. (4.230)
He attains sovereignty over the earth; he obtains gold and fine gold; from silver, he receives the most excellent form. 4.230
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of an ox attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of the Sun.

He is looked upon like the moon; he becomes pleasing to behold for everyone. According to the *Itihāsadarśana*, one attains a specific celestial realm called the Moon-world (*candraloka*). By giving [the gift], one attains the same world as the Aśvins—the possessors of horses—meaning one acquires many horses. Furthermore, by the mere sight [of the recipient], one attains the world of the Aśvins. One who gives a bull (*anaḍvān*), a draft-animal capable of pulling a cart, gains abundant and great prosperity (*śrī*), consisting of the wealth of cattle, goats, sheep, grain, and so forth. One attains the station (*viṣṭapa*) of Bradhna, the Sun; one becomes possessed of great splendor and stands above all. Alternatively, the "station of Bradhna" refers to heaven. In another Smṛti, a specific reward based on a particular quality of the cart is heard: *anasaḥ pūrṇasya dānena phalaṃ prāpnoti mānavaḥ | tathā dhānyānnapūrṇasya tathā vastraprapūrṇasya ||* *ratnapūrṇasya ca tathā dānād bhavati bhogavān | tathā hiraṇyapūrṇasya dānāt svargaṃ samaśnute ||* *gosahasreṇa saṃpūrṇasyānasas tu pradānataḥ | phalaṃ prāpnoti puruṣo yathoktaṃ munibhiḥ purā ||* *evaṃ dharmavidhānajño yo dadāti gavāhanam | sa gacchati vimānena svargaṃ lokam anuttamam ||* *na ca kṣayo 'sya bhavati phalasya dvijasattama | yathākālaṃ yathāyogaṃ yāvad ābhūtasaṃplavam ||* By the gift of a cart full [of grain], a man obtains the fruit; likewise by one full of rice and food, and likewise by one full of clothing. By the gift of one full of jewels, one becomes a possessor of enjoyments; by the gift of one full of gold, one enjoys heaven. By the gift of a cart filled with a thousand cows, a person obtains the fruit as described by the sages of old. Thus, he who knows the rules of dharma and gives a vehicle for cattle goes by means of a celestial chariot to the unsurpassed heavenly world. And there is no exhaustion of that fruit, O best of the twice-born, according to time and circumstance, until the dissolution of all beings.
A milch cow with golden horns and silver hooves, well-behaved, covered with cloth, accompanied by a bronze vessel, and given along with a sacrificial fee, should be bestowed. (YDh 1.203)

In the reading "sudakṣiṇā," other items such as gold and so forth should also be given there; or, the word *su-* may be read in the sense of "excellent. That cow is excellent, and [the phrase refers to] the giving of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). There is an alternative reading, "kāṃsyopadohā"; *kāṃsya* is a specific measure of capacity, meaning that she yields much milk when milked with that vessel. The procedure seen in another Smṛti, beginning with "having covered the earth with ornaments of pearls and decorated with ploughs," should be adopted by one who desires a particular result. Likewise:

If she is a tawny cow (*kapilā*), she delivers [the donor], along with her calf, for as many ages (*yuga*) as there are hairs on her body, up to the seventh generation of his kin. This is the fruit of the gift of a tawny cow accompanied by her calf. A tawny cow given while "facing both ways" causes one to attain heaven for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on her body; she "delivers," meaning she liberates one from sins. In the *Bhārata*, it is stated that the gift of a cow yields all fruits. It is also heard in scripture that even water and other such gifts yield the fruit of heaven.
Having given land, cattle, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter, a house, and gold, one is honored in heaven. (YDh 1.208) "Naiveśika" means a dwelling. 4.231.

The giver of vehicles and beds obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty; the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda obtains equality with Brahman. (4.232)

*Sovereignty* (*aiśvaryam*) means lordship or dominion. *Happiness* (*sukhitvam*) means bliss. *Grains* (*dhānyāni*) refer to rice, mung beans, green gram, and so forth. Regarding sesame seeds, a different fruit has been mentioned. *Brahman* is the Veda; he who imparts it and explains it is the giver of Brahman. *Sārṣṭitā*: "Flowing" (*arṣaṇam*) is *ṛṣṭi*. One whose flow (*ṛṣṭi*) is equal (*samā*) is *sārṣṭi*. Due to Vedic usage, the form *sabha-* is substituted for *samāna-*. The root *ṛṣ* means "to go. Alternatively, *sārṣṭi* is the act of flowing (*arṣaṇam*). That which arises from this is *sārṣṭitā*. In either case, this refers to having an equal course with Brahman; that is to say, equality with him. (4.232)
Of all gifts, the gift of the Veda is preeminent over the giving of water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter. (4.233)

This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding injunction. "Gifts" (*dānāni*) refers to things to be given, that is, objects fit for donation; or, "giving" (*dāna*) may refer to the very act of giving itself. "The gift of the Veda" (*brahmadāna*) consists in the study and exposition of the Vedas. The mention of water and the other items is because they constitute the most excellent of all gifts. (4.233)
With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift, with that very same disposition one receives it in return, duly honored. (4.234)

This word "state" (bhāva) refers to a mental factor. With whatever state of mind—one characterized by clarity, faith, and respect—one gives, with that very same state one receives. Alternatively, if one gives without faith, with contempt, and with a defiled mind while treating the recipient with disdain, one likewise obtains the result accordingly.

Furthermore, this does not refer to the specific type of substance; rather, it refers to the result. This is what is being said: he obtains that very joy which is produced by each respective substance. For if the intention were directed toward the generic class (*jāti*), then in the case of giving medicine to a sick person, one would obtain only medicine; and since that is useless for one who is not ill, even that [act of giving] would be rendered ineffective. Therefore, whatever kind of joy he experiences through exhilaration and the like, he obtains exactly that. And thus, it is stated that the gift of medicine always results in health.

Alternatively, "bhāva" is the desire for a result, thinking, "May this be mine. Whatever substance one gives while aiming for a particular result, that very thing one obtains. Thus it is said: by that very *bhāva* and by that very desire, whatever one wishes for, that alone is obtained. It is thereby demonstrated that all substances can yield all results. (4.234)
He who accepts what has been honored, or he who gives what has been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell. (4.235)

It should be given preceded by worship, and it should likewise be accepted in that same manner; one must not give with contempt—this is the purport of the verse. "Arcitam" (honored) is an adverbial modifier of the action. 4.235.

One should not take pride in one's asceticism, nor speak untruth after performing a sacrifice; even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, and having given a gift, one should not boast of it. (4.236)

One should not feel pride because of the austerity one has performed. One should not think in one's mind, "I have practiced extremely intense and very difficult penance. Having sacrificed—that is, having performed a ritual—one should not speak untruth. Although lying is prohibited without distinction as a general rule for human conduct, its prohibition here again is intended to indicate that it is specifically an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice; for if this prohibition is transgressed, the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites become deficient in their constituent parts. Even when afflicted or distressed, one should not revile or slander Brāhmaṇas. Having given away wealth such as cows or other goods, one should not boast of it before anyone, saying, "This was given by me. (4.236)
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; life-span perishes through reviling Brahmins; and a gift perishes through boasting of it. (4.237)

This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) for the preceding prohibition. By means of falsehood as a cause, the sacrifice flows away—that is, it leaks and becomes fruitless; that for which it was performed does not come to pass. This applies everywhere. (4.237)
One should gradually accumulate merit, like termites building an anthill, for the sake of a companion in the next world, without causing pain to any living beings. (4.238)

If one is unable to perform great acts of charity, great asceticism, or great sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, then one must not remain indifferent. Rather, little by little, through small acts of charity, small asceticism, assistance to others according to one's capacity, and through the recitation of prayers (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*) prescribed by the *Smṛti*, one should accumulate merit. Just as ants and termites build up a mound of earth, so should one accumulate merit for the sake of a companion in the next world; this is a restatement of the fruits of dharma. "Without causing pain to any living beings": one must not cause suffering to beings by making requests for the sake of dharma. (4.238)
For in the next world, neither father nor mother remain for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—only the Dharma stands alone. (4.239)

This is a statement of fact: in another birth hereafter, no one—neither friend nor kinsman—has the power to rescue anyone from the sufferings of hell and other such realms; only the Dharma practiced while alive can deliver one. (4.239)
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone that of its evil deeds. (4.240)

Just as a living being, a creature, is born alone and not together with friends, kinsmen, and so forth, and likewise perishes alone—friends and kinsmen do not undergo death along with him—even if a wife or another devoted person should kill themselves at the time of his death, nevertheless that act of dying is entirely separate. By this [act], they do not experience a single womb together, as in the case of Atri. In the same way, they experience their good and evil deeds separately as well.

But has it not been stated that "neither son nor wife" [should be given] (MDh 4.239)? For a son indeed benefits his deceased father through rites such as the *śrāddha*, and so too does a wife. True; however, this statement refers to the fact that only the son of a righteous man becomes such [a benefactor]. Just as someone becomes a helper to a living person by taking him by the hand, so too does a son benefit a deceased person solely through the medium of *dharma*. 4.240.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of clay, the relatives depart with averted faces; only Dharma follows him. (4.241)

It goes along with him. This is established by direct perception and is stated here for the sake of reflection: having cast the body of the deceased upon the earth like a useless piece of wood, the relatives turn away and depart; but dharma alone follows the person. (4.241)
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate Dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with Dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse. 4.242

This is a summary: darkness is difficult to cross because it is traversed with great hardship; "darkness" here means suffering. Even that becomes easy to cross when accompanied by Dharma as one's companion; for one does not sink into such darkness—this is the meaning. (4.242)
The radiant one, whose body is ethereal, swiftly leads that man who is devoted to dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity to the next world.

He for whom dharma is primary is *dharmapradhānaḥ*, one who is devoted to dharma and a performer of actions as they have been prescribed. "With his sins destroyed by austerity" (*tapasā hatakilbiṣam*): even if some transgression has occurred through negligence, his impurity is destroyed by austerity—that is, by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). When the fault arising from a transgression against the scriptures has been eliminated by that expiation, he leads [the soul] to the radiant other world; he causes it to reach the other world, the celestial abode such as heaven. Who is it? By virtue of the context, it is dharma itself. "The embodied person" (*śarīriṇam puruṣam*): he whose body is space (*kha*) is a "space-bodied one" (*khaśarīrī*). His body is not composed of the five elements like the bodies of other persons; rather, his body is space itself—namely, Brahman. By this, his omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is expressed. (4.243)
One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form alliances with the most eminent; he should avoid those who are inferior. (4.244)

Because the "excellent" (uttama) is of many kinds, there is a distributive repetition (vīpsā) with respect to it: one may be excellent by birth, another by learning, and another by conduct; or else, due to the difference in relations, it refers to whatever relation is appropriate with whichever person is excellent.

One who desires to lead one's lineage to excellence, eminence, and preeminence should enter into alliances—characterized by the giving of a daughter in marriage and so forth—with those who are superior, most excellent, and distinguished by birth and other qualities; and one should avoid those who are inferior and base. Since the avoidance of the inferior is already established by the injunction to associate only with the superior, this statement of avoidance is intended to permit the acceptance of middling persons when superiors are unavailable. "Inferior" means lowly. (4.244)
By approaching only the most excellent and avoiding those who are inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; through the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra. (4.245)

By associating with and forming connections with those who are superior, a Brāhmaṇa attains excellence. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to include the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya as well. By transgression—that is, by acting in the opposite manner and forming connections with those who are inferior—he descends to the state of a Śūdra through pratiloma (inverse order). Since there is no loss of caste, what is meant is that he attains equality with them. (4.245)
Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not dwelling with those of cruel conduct, one who is non-violent and observes such vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and charity. (4.246)

One who is firm in resolve regarding duties to be performed is one who acts with steadfastness; whatever he undertakes, he necessarily completes, and having begun a task, he does not desist before finishing it—this is the meaning of "not being unstable. As it has been said: "Carrying through to the end of what has been begun" (ŚSūktā 79). "Gentle" means not harsh. He forms no association with those of cruel conduct, such as thieves and the like; that is, he does not associate with them. Likewise, by means of self-restraint (*dama*) and generosity (*dāna*), he shall conquer—that is, attain—heaven. "Likewise observant of vows" (*tathāvrataḥ*): maintaining this vow, which is a religious observance (*niyama*). Since self-restraint (*dama*) is mentioned separately, one should understand that the "self-controlled" (*dānta*) person is one who endures the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*). 4.246.
One may accept from everyone fuel, water, roots, fruits, and food that is offered; likewise, honey and the gift of safety. (4.247)

Fuel (*edhas*) means firewood, such as wood and the like; food (*anna*) means that which is either cooked or raw. When it is "offered" (*abhyudyata*), meaning brought forward toward one, all of this may be accepted from everyone—except from outcastes (*patita*), those accused of crimes (*abhiśasta*), Caṇḍālas, and others of the inverse castes (*pratiloma*); however, it may be accepted from a Śūdra or from another who has committed only slight sins. Honey (*madhu*) refers to that produced by bees. "Fearlessness" (*abhaya*) is like a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is mentioned for the sake of illustration. For "acceptance" (*pratigraha*) is the taking of another's property through their consent; it does not, however, consist of the form of food itself. In this case, no one's ownership ceases, nor does anyone's ownership arise anew. Therefore, the term *dakṣiṇā* is used here as a figure of speech (*stuti*). Just as accepting protection from thieves and the like in a forest or wilderness—even from Caṇḍālas and others—is not a fault, so too there is no fault in accepting this fuel and the rest. And this rule applies when there is no distress (*anāpad*); but in times of distress, he will state later that it may be accepted even from Caṇḍālas and others. Furthermore, the word "offered" (*abhyudyata*) is connected specifically with "food" due to proximity, and not with fuel and the other items. Thus, regarding fuel and the rest, there is no contradiction with the practice of begging. Since the rule "Acceptance [of gifts] should be made from righteous twice-born men" implies that it is not permitted from unrighteous twice-born men or from Śūdras, and yet the solicitation of specific types of objects is desired, this verse is intended for that purpose. (4.247)
Prajāpati has declared that alms brought forward and offered spontaneously, without having been previously solicited, may be accepted even from one of evil deeds. (4.248)

By the word *edha* (fuel), any other substance that exceeds [the norm] is also indicated as being acceptable by this specific qualification. Furthermore, the word *bhikṣā* (alms) is employed here in a sense of praise; it is not intended to mean alms alone, even though this term usually denotes a small quantity of prepared food. For alms, due to their meagerness, do not bring excessive fault, and for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), they are prescribed as being acceptable from all castes. In the same way, any other similar thing is seen to be equivalent by this specific qualification. Thus, the word *bhikṣā* is used with the intention of conveying such a meaning. As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:
Having gone together to the workshop of Bhārgava, those two high-souled sons of Pṛthā approached Pṛthā,
and being exceedingly delighted, they [presented] Yājñasenī.
"Alms!"—thus did those two foremost of men announce themselves. (MBh 1.182.1)

*Āhṛta-upahṛtā* means brought to that place where the recipient is stationed; *abhyudyatā* means placed before him, announced by word or gesture as "Please accept this. *Purastāt* means previously; *apracoditā* means unasked for by the recipient, either directly or through another, such that the donor had not previously said, "I have this object; please accept it out of favor. It is merely presented unexpectedly, with the intention revealed at that very moment. Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha considered such alms to be acceptable even from one who has performed evil deeds (*duṣkṛtakarman*). One whose actions are evil is a *duṣkṛtakarman*. (4.248)
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years from him who treats her with contempt, nor does the fire carry his sacrificial offerings. (4.249)

Now follows an explanatory passage (arthavāda) intended to censure non-acceptance: "Furthermore, when someone disregards this [gift], his ancestors do not eat the *śrāddha* offering nor do they accept it; and Agni does not carry the oblation to the gods. The meaning is that one obtains no fruit from rites dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*) or to the gods (*daiva*).
Regarding this, someone says: "Even if it is of no practical use, such a thing must necessarily be accepted for the sake of favoring the donor."

But that is incorrect; for it is the faultlessness of this acceptance of what is not solicited that is being stated. For this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), and a counter-exception applies to that which has been prohibited. And the acquisition [of wealth] through worldly means when one is in distress has been prohibited; that very same [acquisition] is here permitted as a counter-exception. (4.249)
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or even vegetables. (4.250)

One should not reject nor refuse beds and other such items even if they have not been brought forward. If certain objects are present in the house and someone says, "I shall bring this and that; please wait for it," then those things should not be refused. 4.250.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from all sources, but he himself should not be satisfied by them alone. (4.251)
Gurus are many, owing to the direct instructions and extended applications [of the law]. Servants and dependents, however, are enumerated in another Smṛti:
"The aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son... (MDh 11.5, with an added verse).

Desiring to uplift those who are sinking from hunger, and wishing to honor the deities and guests for the sake of fulfilling his daily duties—this is the meaning—he may accept alms from all quarters, both from the virtuous and the unvirtuous; however, he should not satisfy himself with that. "Satisfaction" means the cessation of hunger and its enjoyment; he should not do that. He should accept that [food] solely for the purpose of serving his teacher and others, and not for his own sake. (4.251)

How, then, should one maintain oneself? To this he says: "But when the teachers have passed away, or living at home without them, seeking a livelihood for oneself, one should always accept [gifts] from the virtuous. (4.252)

If, when the [ancestors] have passed away or are deceased, or even in their absence, they continue to live separately, then—[the mention of the "guru"] being for the purpose of indicating all dependents as well—one who seeks his own livelihood, that is, his means of subsistence, should receive it from the virtuous, meaning from those who are righteous. Since no specific caste is mentioned here, there is acceptance [of gifts] even from a Śūdra provided he is righteous. Thus it has been said: "One should not eat [the food] of a Śūdra," and so forth (MDh 4.223). 4.252.
A partner in a business, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]. (4.253)

One who is called an *ardhasīrī*, an *ardhika*, a *kuṭumbī*, or a *bhūmikarṣaka* [is one whose food may be eaten]. The terms *gopa* (cowherd) and *dāsa* (servant) are relative words: he who herds another's cattle is to be fed by that person; and he who offers himself, saying, "I am your refuge; I shall live under you with confidence"—he too, who thus surrenders himself, is one whose food may be eaten. (4.253)
Whatever his nature may be, whatever he intends to do, and how he would treat him, in that manner should one present oneself. (4.254)

He clarifies the very nature of self-surrender (*ātmanivedana*): what kind of self this *śūdra* may have—his lineage, his country, his craft, and what he desires to do. [He says: "I have sought refuge in you for many tasks, whether by way of duty (*dharma*) or some other purpose, such as the protection of the royal household. Or, as to how he should serve: "I shall attend upon you with this craft; I shall perform the salutation of your feet and all duties of the household. When all this is reported, the self is truly surrendered.

Others, however, considering the word *ātman* in the passage “The self (*ātman*), indeed, is the name of the son” (ŚB 14.9.4.26) to refer to offspring, say that this [text] declares the food of that Śūdra to be edible whose daughter, having married out of her own desire, is taken in marriage.

That is incorrect. First of all, this word *ātman* is not clearly used here with reference to a daughter; for the word *putra* (son) is far more commonly established as referring specifically to a male. Furthermore, there is no purpose in teaching through an indirect term; it would have been proper simply to say, “and he who gives away his daughter.”

Others, however, explain that the mention of "the half-caste" (*ardhika*) and so forth is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Śūdra; by this, the fact that the food of a Pāraśava and of a father-in-law is fit to be eaten is established. (4.254)
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is among virtuous people is a doer of evil; he is a thief in the world of darkness, a robber of his own self. (4.255)

One who, while being otherwise, unrighteous, and wicked, speaks otherwise among the virtuous and disciplined, saying "I am righteous"; or one who, having relied upon one purpose, displays another—such a person is the greatest of all evildoers. He is a thief, a robber; for while another thief or robber steals external property, this one steals his very self. This is an expression of extreme censure. (4.255)
All objects of speech are fixed; they are rooted in speech and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals this speech is a thief of everything. (4.256)

Because of the eternal relationship between word and meaning, meanings are said to be fixed within speech, that is, in the word. They are said to be rooted in speech because the speaker’s manifestation of his own intention is dependent upon it; they are said to be rooted in that [speech]. They are said to have issued forth from speech because they are produced from it, and because the listener’s comprehension is likewise dependent on it. Nor should one strive here to resolve any suspicion of tautology, since this is a restatement and serves to clarify the matter in whatever way possible.

He who steals that speech—meaning he who deceives by saying one thing while doing another, who acts with one intention but displays something else—is a perpetrator of every kind of theft. There is no substance, such as gold or the like, which has not been stolen by him; this is a declamatory statement (arthavāda) intended to censure the speaking of falsehood. 4.256.

Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule, and having entrusted everything to his son, he should live maintaining an attitude of neutrality. 4.257

This is stated as another alternative for the householder alone. Having fulfilled the debt to the great sages through Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), to the ancestors through the procreation of offspring, and to the gods through sacrifices—as it is said, "One is burdened by three debts" (TS 6.3.10.5)—and having performed these three, he should entrust the entire management of his household and family to his son who has attained legal capacity, and dwell in the home itself after renouncing [worldly ties]. Established in neutrality (*mādhyasthya*) and having abandoned egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), he should remain having completely relinquished the notion that "this is my wealth," "these are my wife and children," or "these are my male and female slaves. Neutrality is the state of having abandoned craving for possessions, thinking, "I belong to no one, and no one belongs to me. Furthermore, this renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) applies to desires and to actions seen [in this world], but not to all [actions]; we shall demonstrate this later. (4.257)
One should always reflect alone in solitude upon what is beneficial for oneself;
for by reflecting alone, one indeed attains the supreme good. (4.258)

Once the renunciation of all actions has been performed, this must be done by him in particular: being alone and without companion, without conversation, in an undisturbed, secluded, and solitary place, he should reflect and meditate upon what is beneficial; he should practice those meditations on Brahman which are prescribed in the Upaniṣads regarding the Self. Through such reflection and through that practice, he attains and reaches the supreme good known as liberation. 4.258.
Thus has been declared the eternal mode of life for a Brahmin householder,
as well as the ritual rules for the vows of a Snātaka, which are auspicious and increase one's inner strength.

The summary of the chapter’s subject matter: This eternal (śāśvatī), that is, constant (nityā) mode of life for a householder Brahmin has been declared; however, the non-constant mode to be practiced in times of distress will be described later. By the mention of "vipra," this rule (kalpa)—the injunction (vidhi)—for the observances of a Snātaka pertains to the Brāhmaṇa alone. It increases his quality of goodness (sattva), which is auspicious (śubha) and praiseworthy (praśasta). This is a statement of praise. (4.259)
A Brahmin who, knowing the Vedas and the Shastras, conducts himself according to this mode of life,
being eternally freed from all taint, is glorified in the world of Brahma.

This is the statement of the fruit for all of this. A Brahmin living by means of this, being a knower of the Vedic scriptures and free from stain—where "stain" refers to the sin born of the transgression of prohibitions, which has been removed or eliminated through expiations—attains greatness in the world of Brahmā. By this it is meant that, because he performs what is prescribed, does not practice what is prohibited, and because whatever was done [by mistake] has been redeemed through expiations, he attains magnificence in a specific station within the world of Brahmā. According to another philosophical view, it is established that he becomes one with the nature of Brahmā. (4.260)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu. || 4 ||
